title: Completed revenue share by plan tier
description: Return plan_tier, total_completed_revenue, and revenue_share_pct for each plan tier based on 'completed' orders only. revenue_share_pct should be the percentage contribution of that tier's total_completed_revenue to the overall revenue from 'completed' orders across all plan tiers, rounded to 2 decimal places. Include only plan tiers that have at least one 'completed' order. Order by total_completed_revenue descending, then plan_tier ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT plan_tier, total_completed_revenue,
  ROUND(100.0 * total_completed_revenue / SUM(total_completed_revenue) OVER (), 2) AS revenue_share_pct
FROM (
  SELECT u.plan_tier, SUM(o.net_amount) AS total_completed_revenue
  FROM users u
  JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY u.plan_tier
) tier_revenue
ORDER BY total_completed_revenue DESC, plan_tier ASC
solution_query:
SELECT plan_tier, total_completed_revenue,
  ROUND(100.0 * total_completed_revenue / SUM(total_completed_revenue) OVER (), 2) AS revenue_share_pct
FROM (
  SELECT u.plan_tier, SUM(o.net_amount) AS total_completed_revenue
  FROM users u
  JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY u.plan_tier
) tier_revenue
ORDER BY total_completed_revenue DESC, plan_tier ASC;
explanation: The inner query performs the first stage: join users to orders, filter to completed orders, and aggregate net_amount by plan_tier. That produces one revenue total per tier. The outer query then applies a window function across those aggregated rows. SUM(total_completed_revenue) OVER () gives the grand total across all tiers without collapsing the result into a single row, which makes it possible to compute each tier's percentage share alongside its own subtotal. This is a classic hard-level pattern because the window function operates on the result of an earlier aggregation step rather than on raw rows.
hints: Create row-to-row context within each entity first; the final filter or comparison happens after that derived state exists.
Then use a window SUM over the aggregated result to get the grand total for the percentage calculation.
complexity_hint: Two-stage pattern: aggregate first (subquery), then apply a window function on the aggregated rows. The window SUM(...) OVER () computes the grand total without collapsing rows.

alternative_solution.query:
WITH tier_revenue AS (
  SELECT u.plan_tier, SUM(o.net_amount) AS total_completed_revenue
  FROM users u
  JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY u.plan_tier
)
SELECT plan_tier, total_completed_revenue,
  ROUND(100.0 * total_completed_revenue / SUM(total_completed_revenue) OVER (), 2) AS revenue_share_pct
FROM tier_revenue
ORDER BY total_completed_revenue DESC, plan_tier ASC
alternative_solution.explanation: This version uses a CTE (WITH clause) instead of an inline subquery. Both approaches produce identical results. CTEs are generally preferred when the intermediate result is referenced more than once, or when readability is the priority — the named step makes the two-stage intent explicit.

title: Top completed-revenue user in each acquisition channel
description: For orders placed in 2024, return the single user with the highest revenue from 'completed' orders in each acquisition_channel. Columns: acquisition_channel, user_id, name, total_completed_revenue. If multiple users in the same acquisition_channel tie on total_completed_revenue, choose the user whose first 'completed' order in 2024 is earlier. If there is still a tie, choose the lower user_id. Order by acquisition_channel ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT acquisition_channel, user_id, name, total_completed_revenue
FROM (
  SELECT
    u.acquisition_channel,
    u.user_id,
    u.name,
    SUM(o.net_amount) AS total_completed_revenue,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
      PARTITION BY u.acquisition_channel
      ORDER BY SUM(o.net_amount) DESC, MIN(o.order_date) ASC, u.user_id ASC
    ) AS rn
  FROM users u
  JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    AND EXTRACT(YEAR FROM o.order_date) = 2024
  GROUP BY u.acquisition_channel, u.user_id, u.name
) ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY acquisition_channel ASC
solution_query:
SELECT acquisition_channel, user_id, name, total_completed_revenue
FROM (
  SELECT
    u.acquisition_channel,
    u.user_id,
    u.name,
    SUM(o.net_amount) AS total_completed_revenue,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
      PARTITION BY u.acquisition_channel
      ORDER BY SUM(o.net_amount) DESC, MIN(o.order_date) ASC, u.user_id ASC
    ) AS rn
  FROM users u
  JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    AND EXTRACT(YEAR FROM o.order_date) = 2024
  GROUP BY u.acquisition_channel, u.user_id, u.name
) ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY acquisition_channel ASC;
explanation: This query combines aggregation and partitioned ranking. The grouped subquery computes each user's completed revenue within an acquisition channel for 2024. After that aggregation, ROW_NUMBER() is applied with PARTITION BY acquisition_channel so ranking restarts independently inside each channel. The ORDER BY inside the window is deliberately multi-step: highest total revenue first, then earliest completed order date, then lowest user_id. That guarantees exactly one deterministic winner per channel even when totals tie.
hints: Create row-to-row context within each entity first; the final filter or comparison happens after that derived state exists.
Use ROW_NUMBER() with PARTITION BY acquisition_channel and include every tie-breaker in the window ORDER BY.

title: First completed order where cumulative revenue reaches 1000
description: Return the first 'completed' order for each user where that user's cumulative revenue from 'completed' orders reaches or exceeds 1000 for the first time. Columns: user_id, order_id, order_date, net_amount, running_completed_revenue. Build the cumulative revenue in order_date ascending order, breaking ties on order_id ascending. Exclude users who never reach 1000. Order by user_id ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT user_id, order_id, order_date, net_amount, running_completed_revenue
FROM (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    order_id,
    order_date,
    net_amount,
    SUM(net_amount) OVER (
      PARTITION BY user_id
      ORDER BY order_date ASC, order_id ASC
      ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS running_completed_revenue
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'completed'
) running
WHERE running_completed_revenue >= 1000
  AND running_completed_revenue - net_amount < 1000
ORDER BY user_id ASC
solution_query:
SELECT user_id, order_id, order_date, net_amount, running_completed_revenue
FROM (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    order_id,
    order_date,
    net_amount,
    SUM(net_amount) OVER (
      PARTITION BY user_id
      ORDER BY order_date ASC, order_id ASC
      ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS running_completed_revenue
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'completed'
) running
WHERE running_completed_revenue >= 1000
  AND running_completed_revenue - net_amount < 1000
ORDER BY user_id ASC;
explanation: The inner query calculates a running completed-revenue total per user with a windowed SUM. PARTITION BY user_id ensures each user's accumulation is independent, while ORDER BY order_date and order_id defines the exact sequence. The explicit ROWS frame makes the cumulative logic unambiguous. The outer filter is the key dependency step: running_completed_revenue >= 1000 identifies rows at or beyond the threshold, and running_completed_revenue - net_amount < 1000 guarantees that the previous cumulative total was still below 1000. Together, those conditions isolate the first threshold-crossing order for each user.
hints: Create per-entity running context first, then isolate the exact moment the threshold or transition is reached.
After you have the running total, keep only rows where the threshold is reached now but had not been reached before this row.
complexity_hint: O(n) window scan per user partition. The two-condition filter (current >= 1000 AND current - net_amount < 1000) precisely isolates the first threshold-crossing row without a self-join.

title: User-months above each user's 2024 monthly average
description: For 2024 only, return every user-month where the user's revenue from 'completed' orders for that month is strictly greater than their own average monthly revenue from 'completed' orders across all 2024 months that contain at least one 'completed' order. Columns: user_id, order_month, monthly_completed_revenue, avg_monthly_completed_revenue. order_month should be the numeric month extracted from order_date. Order by user_id ascending, then order_month ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT user_id, order_month, monthly_completed_revenue, avg_monthly_completed_revenue
FROM (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    order_month,
    monthly_completed_revenue,
    ROUND(AVG(monthly_completed_revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id), 2) AS avg_monthly_completed_revenue
  FROM (
    SELECT
      user_id,
      EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date) AS order_month,
      SUM(net_amount) AS monthly_completed_revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
      AND EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) = 2024
    GROUP BY user_id, EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date)
  ) monthly
) scored
WHERE monthly_completed_revenue > avg_monthly_completed_revenue
ORDER BY user_id ASC, order_month ASC
solution_query:
SELECT user_id, order_month, monthly_completed_revenue, avg_monthly_completed_revenue
FROM (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    order_month,
    monthly_completed_revenue,
    ROUND(AVG(monthly_completed_revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id), 2) AS avg_monthly_completed_revenue
  FROM (
    SELECT
      user_id,
      EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date) AS order_month,
      SUM(net_amount) AS monthly_completed_revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
      AND EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) = 2024
    GROUP BY user_id, EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date)
  ) monthly
) scored
WHERE monthly_completed_revenue > avg_monthly_completed_revenue
ORDER BY user_id ASC, order_month ASC;
explanation: This is a two-stage aggregation problem. The inner subquery collapses raw orders into one row per user per month, but only for completed orders in 2024. The outer query then computes each user's average monthly revenue across those already-aggregated monthly rows with AVG(...) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id). That is the critical hard-level move: the window function is not operating on raw orders, but on monthly totals produced by a prior aggregation. Once both numbers exist on the same row, the final filter simply keeps months whose revenue is above the user's own baseline.
hints: Create row-to-row context within each entity first; the final filter or comparison happens after that derived state exists.
After you have monthly totals, use a window AVG partitioned by user_id to compute each user's monthly baseline.
complexity_hint: Double-nested subquery: the inner subquery aggregates by month, the outer window computes each user's monthly average on top of those aggregates. This pattern can be rewritten with two CTEs for readability.

title: Products added to cart but never purchased afterward
description: Return each user-product pair where the user added the product to cart at least once, but never recorded a 'purchase' event for that same product at or after their first 'add_to_cart' event for that product. Columns: user_id, name, product_id, product_name, first_add_to_cart_time. If a user added the same product multiple times, base the comparison on the earliest 'add_to_cart' time for that user-product pair. Order by user_id ascending, then product_id ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT a.user_id, u.name, a.product_id, p.product_name, a.first_add_to_cart_time
FROM (
  SELECT user_id, product_id, MIN(event_time) AS first_add_to_cart_time
  FROM events
  WHERE event_name = 'add_to_cart'
    AND product_id IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY user_id, product_id
) a
JOIN users u ON a.user_id = u.user_id
JOIN products p ON a.product_id = p.product_id
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM events e
  WHERE e.user_id = a.user_id
    AND e.product_id = a.product_id
    AND e.event_name = 'purchase'
    AND e.event_time >= a.first_add_to_cart_time
)
ORDER BY a.user_id ASC, a.product_id ASC
solution_query:
SELECT a.user_id, u.name, a.product_id, p.product_name, a.first_add_to_cart_time
FROM (
  SELECT user_id, product_id, MIN(event_time) AS first_add_to_cart_time
  FROM events
  WHERE event_name = 'add_to_cart'
    AND product_id IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY user_id, product_id
) a
JOIN users u ON a.user_id = u.user_id
JOIN products p ON a.product_id = p.product_id
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM events e
  WHERE e.user_id = a.user_id
    AND e.product_id = a.product_id
    AND e.event_name = 'purchase'
    AND e.event_time >= a.first_add_to_cart_time
)
ORDER BY a.user_id ASC, a.product_id ASC;
explanation: The inner query establishes the dependency point by reducing all add_to_cart events to one earliest timestamp per user-product pair. That first add_to_cart time becomes the reference event for later filtering. The outer query enriches those pairs with user and product details, then applies a correlated NOT EXISTS check against the events table. The correlated subquery asks a precise business question: does this same user ever have a purchase event for this same product at or after that first add_to_cart? If the answer is no, the pair stays in the result. This is hard because the filter depends on a value computed in an earlier stage rather than on a simple raw-column predicate.
hints: Break the problem into stages so the reusable intermediate result exists before the final filter or comparison.
Then use a correlated NOT EXISTS to check whether a later purchase exists for that same user-product pair.

title: Signup cohort retention by month offset
description: For signup cohorts based on the calendar month of signup_date, return retention metrics for month offsets 0, 1, and 2. A user counts as retained in a month offset if they placed at least one 'completed' order in that calendar month offset from their signup month. Count each user at most once per offset even if they placed multiple 'completed' orders in the same month. Columns: cohort_month, months_since_signup, cohort_size, retained_users, retained_pct. retained_pct should be rounded to 2 decimal places. Include only cohort-month and offset combinations that have at least one retained user. Order by cohort_month ascending, then months_since_signup ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT cohort_month, months_since_signup, cohort_size, retained_users,
  ROUND(100.0 * retained_users / cohort_size, 2) AS retained_pct
FROM (
  SELECT a.cohort_month, a.months_since_signup, c.cohort_size, COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) AS retained_users
  FROM (
    SELECT DISTINCT
      u.user_id,
      DATE_TRUNC('month', u.signup_date) AS cohort_month,
      DATE_DIFF('month', DATE_TRUNC('month', u.signup_date), DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date)) AS months_since_signup
    FROM users u
    JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
      AND DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date) >= DATE_TRUNC('month', u.signup_date)
      AND DATE_DIFF('month', DATE_TRUNC('month', u.signup_date), DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date)) BETWEEN 0 AND 2
  ) a
  JOIN (
    SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', signup_date) AS cohort_month, COUNT(*) AS cohort_size
    FROM users
    GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', signup_date)
  ) c ON a.cohort_month = c.cohort_month
  GROUP BY a.cohort_month, a.months_since_signup, c.cohort_size
) retained
ORDER BY cohort_month ASC, months_since_signup ASC
solution_query:
SELECT cohort_month, months_since_signup, cohort_size, retained_users,
  ROUND(100.0 * retained_users / cohort_size, 2) AS retained_pct
FROM (
  SELECT a.cohort_month, a.months_since_signup, c.cohort_size, COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) AS retained_users
  FROM (
    SELECT DISTINCT
      u.user_id,
      DATE_TRUNC('month', u.signup_date) AS cohort_month,
      DATE_DIFF('month', DATE_TRUNC('month', u.signup_date), DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date)) AS months_since_signup
    FROM users u
    JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
      AND DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date) >= DATE_TRUNC('month', u.signup_date)
      AND DATE_DIFF('month', DATE_TRUNC('month', u.signup_date), DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date)) BETWEEN 0 AND 2
  ) a
  JOIN (
    SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', signup_date) AS cohort_month, COUNT(*) AS cohort_size
    FROM users
    GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', signup_date)
  ) c ON a.cohort_month = c.cohort_month
  GROUP BY a.cohort_month, a.months_since_signup, c.cohort_size
) retained
ORDER BY cohort_month ASC, months_since_signup ASC;
explanation: This problem has two separate time-based steps. First, each user is assigned to a cohort month using the month of signup_date, and completed-order activity is converted into month offsets relative to that cohort month. DISTINCT is necessary because a user should count only once per month offset even if they placed multiple completed orders in the same calendar month. Second, those retained-user counts are joined to cohort sizes so retention percentage can be computed. The hard part is reasoning across two time axes at once: absolute calendar months and relative months since signup.
hints: Bring together the sources that hold the required attributes, then summarize at the business grain named in the prompt.
Deduplicate to one row per user and month offset before counting retained users.

title: Sessionize events with a 30-minute inactivity gap
description: Create derived sessions from the events table using this rule: within each user_id, a new session starts on the first event or whenever the gap from the previous event is more than 30 minutes. A gap of exactly 30 minutes stays in the same session. Return one row per derived session with columns: user_id, derived_session_id, session_start_time, session_end_time, event_count, duration_minutes. derived_session_id should start at 1 for each user and increase in event order. Use event_time ascending and event_id ascending to break ties. Order by user_id ascending, then derived_session_id ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT user_id, derived_session_id, session_start_time, session_end_time, event_count, duration_minutes
FROM (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    session_number AS derived_session_id,
    MIN(event_time) AS session_start_time,
    MAX(event_time) AS session_end_time,
    COUNT(*) AS event_count,
    DATE_DIFF('minute', MIN(event_time), MAX(event_time)) AS duration_minutes
  FROM (
    SELECT
      user_id,
      event_time,
      SUM(is_new_session) OVER (
        PARTITION BY user_id
        ORDER BY event_time ASC, event_id ASC
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
      ) AS session_number
    FROM (
      SELECT
        event_id,
        user_id,
        event_time,
        CASE
          WHEN prev_event_time IS NULL THEN 1
          WHEN DATE_DIFF('minute', prev_event_time, event_time) > 30 THEN 1
          ELSE 0
        END AS is_new_session
      FROM (
        SELECT
          event_id,
          user_id,
          event_time,
          LAG(event_time) OVER (
            PARTITION BY user_id
            ORDER BY event_time ASC, event_id ASC
          ) AS prev_event_time
        FROM events
      ) lagged
    ) flagged
  ) assigned
  GROUP BY user_id, session_number
) sessions
ORDER BY user_id ASC, derived_session_id ASC
solution_query:
SELECT user_id, derived_session_id, session_start_time, session_end_time, event_count, duration_minutes
FROM (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    session_number AS derived_session_id,
    MIN(event_time) AS session_start_time,
    MAX(event_time) AS session_end_time,
    COUNT(*) AS event_count,
    DATE_DIFF('minute', MIN(event_time), MAX(event_time)) AS duration_minutes
  FROM (
    SELECT
      user_id,
      event_time,
      SUM(is_new_session) OVER (
        PARTITION BY user_id
        ORDER BY event_time ASC, event_id ASC
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
      ) AS session_number
    FROM (
      SELECT
        event_id,
        user_id,
        event_time,
        CASE
          WHEN prev_event_time IS NULL THEN 1
          WHEN DATE_DIFF('minute', prev_event_time, event_time) > 30 THEN 1
          ELSE 0
        END AS is_new_session
      FROM (
        SELECT
          event_id,
          user_id,
          event_time,
          LAG(event_time) OVER (
            PARTITION BY user_id
            ORDER BY event_time ASC, event_id ASC
          ) AS prev_event_time
        FROM events
      ) lagged
    ) flagged
  ) assigned
  GROUP BY user_id, session_number
) sessions
ORDER BY user_id ASC, derived_session_id ASC;
explanation: Sessionization is inherently multi-step. The first step uses LAG(event_time) to look at the previous event for the same user in chronological order. The next step converts that row-to-row comparison into a boundary flag that marks the start of each new session. Finally, a running SUM of those flags turns boundaries into stable derived session ids, which can then be aggregated into session-level metrics like start time, end time, and duration. The reasoning challenge is that the final group identifier is not stored anywhere in the data; it has to be derived from event gaps.
hints: Create row-to-row context within each entity first; the final filter or comparison happens after that derived state exists.
Once you can mark the first event of each session with a flag, think about how a running aggregation can turn those flags into stable, contiguous identifiers.

title: Acquisition-channel funnel progression by ordered product events
description: For each acquisition_channel, compute funnel counts based on ordered product-level behavior. A user is counted in viewed_users if they had at least one product journey with a 'view_product' event. They are counted in cart_after_view_users if they had at least one product where an 'add_to_cart' event occurred after the first 'view_product' event for that same product. They are counted in purchase_after_cart_users if they had at least one product where a 'purchase' event occurred after that 'add_to_cart' event for the same product. Return acquisition_channel, viewed_users, cart_after_view_users, purchase_after_cart_users, drop_off_after_view, and drop_off_after_cart. drop_off_after_view is viewed_users minus cart_after_view_users. drop_off_after_cart is cart_after_view_users minus purchase_after_cart_users. Order by acquisition_channel ascending. All funnel steps must occur on the same product_id within a single user-product journey.
expected_query:
SELECT acquisition_channel,
  SUM(reached_view) AS viewed_users,
  SUM(reached_cart_after_view) AS cart_after_view_users,
  SUM(reached_purchase_after_cart) AS purchase_after_cart_users,
  SUM(reached_view) - SUM(reached_cart_after_view) AS drop_off_after_view,
  SUM(reached_cart_after_view) - SUM(reached_purchase_after_cart) AS drop_off_after_cart
FROM (
  SELECT
    acquisition_channel,
    user_id,
    MAX(CASE WHEN first_view_time IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS reached_view,
    MAX(CASE WHEN first_cart_time IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS reached_cart_after_view,
    MAX(CASE WHEN first_purchase_time IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS reached_purchase_after_cart
  FROM (
    SELECT
      c.acquisition_channel,
      c.user_id,
      c.product_id,
      c.first_view_time,
      c.first_cart_time,
      MIN(e.event_time) AS first_purchase_time
    FROM (
      SELECT
        v.acquisition_channel,
        v.user_id,
        v.product_id,
        v.first_view_time,
        MIN(e.event_time) AS first_cart_time
      FROM (
        SELECT
          u.acquisition_channel,
          e.user_id,
          e.product_id,
          MIN(e.event_time) AS first_view_time
        FROM events e
        JOIN users u ON e.user_id = u.user_id
        JOIN products p ON e.product_id = p.product_id
        WHERE e.event_name = 'view_product'
        GROUP BY u.acquisition_channel, e.user_id, e.product_id
      ) v
      LEFT JOIN events e ON e.user_id = v.user_id
       AND e.product_id = v.product_id
       AND e.event_name = 'add_to_cart'
       AND e.event_time > v.first_view_time
      GROUP BY v.acquisition_channel, v.user_id, v.product_id, v.first_view_time
    ) c
    LEFT JOIN events e ON e.user_id = c.user_id
     AND e.product_id = c.product_id
     AND e.event_name = 'purchase'
     AND e.event_time > c.first_cart_time
    GROUP BY c.acquisition_channel, c.user_id, c.product_id, c.first_view_time, c.first_cart_time
  ) journeys
  GROUP BY acquisition_channel, user_id
) user_funnel
GROUP BY acquisition_channel
ORDER BY acquisition_channel ASC
solution_query:
SELECT acquisition_channel,
  SUM(reached_view) AS viewed_users,
  SUM(reached_cart_after_view) AS cart_after_view_users,
  SUM(reached_purchase_after_cart) AS purchase_after_cart_users,
  SUM(reached_view) - SUM(reached_cart_after_view) AS drop_off_after_view,
  SUM(reached_cart_after_view) - SUM(reached_purchase_after_cart) AS drop_off_after_cart
FROM (
  SELECT
    acquisition_channel,
    user_id,
    MAX(CASE WHEN first_view_time IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS reached_view,
    MAX(CASE WHEN first_cart_time IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS reached_cart_after_view,
    MAX(CASE WHEN first_purchase_time IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS reached_purchase_after_cart
  FROM (
    SELECT
      c.acquisition_channel,
      c.user_id,
      c.product_id,
      c.first_view_time,
      c.first_cart_time,
      MIN(e.event_time) AS first_purchase_time
    FROM (
      SELECT
        v.acquisition_channel,
        v.user_id,
        v.product_id,
        v.first_view_time,
        MIN(e.event_time) AS first_cart_time
      FROM (
        SELECT
          u.acquisition_channel,
          e.user_id,
          e.product_id,
          MIN(e.event_time) AS first_view_time
        FROM events e
        JOIN users u ON e.user_id = u.user_id
        JOIN products p ON e.product_id = p.product_id
        WHERE e.event_name = 'view_product'
        GROUP BY u.acquisition_channel, e.user_id, e.product_id
      ) v
      LEFT JOIN events e ON e.user_id = v.user_id
       AND e.product_id = v.product_id
       AND e.event_name = 'add_to_cart'
       AND e.event_time > v.first_view_time
      GROUP BY v.acquisition_channel, v.user_id, v.product_id, v.first_view_time
    ) c
    LEFT JOIN events e ON e.user_id = c.user_id
     AND e.product_id = c.product_id
     AND e.event_name = 'purchase'
     AND e.event_time > c.first_cart_time
    GROUP BY c.acquisition_channel, c.user_id, c.product_id, c.first_view_time, c.first_cart_time
  ) journeys
  GROUP BY acquisition_channel, user_id
) user_funnel
GROUP BY acquisition_channel
ORDER BY acquisition_channel ASC;
explanation: This funnel is hard because stage membership depends on ordered events for the same user-product journey, not just on whether a user has ever produced each event type. The first subquery finds the initial view for each user-product pair. The next stage searches for an add_to_cart that happens after that view, and the final stage searches for a purchase that happens after that cart. Only after the ordered product-level journeys are built can the query roll up to the user level and then to acquisition channels. The conditional MAX expressions are what convert multiple product journeys into a single yes-or-no stage flag per user.
hints: Bring together the sources that hold the required attributes, then summarize at the business grain named in the prompt.
After deriving ordered stage timestamps, roll those journeys up to one stage flag per user before aggregating by acquisition_channel.

title: Products contributing to the first 80% of completed revenue
description: Identify the products that make up the first 80% of 'completed'-order revenue when products are ordered by product_revenue descending. Columns: product_id, product_name, product_revenue, cumulative_revenue, cumulative_revenue_pct. product_revenue should be the sum of line_amount from 'completed' orders only. cumulative_revenue should be the running total in product_revenue descending order, breaking ties on product_id ascending. Include the product that causes the cumulative total to reach or cross 80% even if it pushes the running percentage above 80. Order by product_revenue descending, then product_id ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT product_id, product_name, product_revenue, cumulative_revenue, cumulative_revenue_pct
FROM (
  SELECT
    product_id,
    product_name,
    product_revenue,
    SUM(product_revenue) OVER (
      ORDER BY product_revenue DESC, product_id ASC
      ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS cumulative_revenue,
    SUM(product_revenue) OVER () AS total_revenue,
    ROUND(
      100.0 * SUM(product_revenue) OVER (
        ORDER BY product_revenue DESC, product_id ASC
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
      ) / SUM(product_revenue) OVER (),
      2
    ) AS cumulative_revenue_pct
  FROM (
    SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name, SUM(oi.line_amount) AS product_revenue
    FROM products p
    JOIN order_items oi ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
    JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name
  ) product_totals
) ranked
WHERE cumulative_revenue - product_revenue < 0.8 * total_revenue
ORDER BY product_revenue DESC, product_id ASC
solution_query:
SELECT product_id, product_name, product_revenue, cumulative_revenue, cumulative_revenue_pct
FROM (
  SELECT
    product_id,
    product_name,
    product_revenue,
    SUM(product_revenue) OVER (
      ORDER BY product_revenue DESC, product_id ASC
      ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS cumulative_revenue,
    SUM(product_revenue) OVER () AS total_revenue,
    ROUND(
      100.0 * SUM(product_revenue) OVER (
        ORDER BY product_revenue DESC, product_id ASC
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
      ) / SUM(product_revenue) OVER (),
      2
    ) AS cumulative_revenue_pct
  FROM (
    SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name, SUM(oi.line_amount) AS product_revenue
    FROM products p
    JOIN order_items oi ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
    JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name
  ) product_totals
) ranked
WHERE cumulative_revenue - product_revenue < 0.8 * total_revenue
ORDER BY product_revenue DESC, product_id ASC;
explanation: Pareto analysis is more than just ranking products by revenue. The first stage aggregates completed-order revenue per product. The second stage adds two window calculations over that ranked product list: a running cumulative revenue and the total revenue across all products. The final filter is the important reasoning step. Instead of keeping only rows whose cumulative percentage is already below 80, it keeps rows whose cumulative total before the current product was still below 80% of the grand total. That logic ensures the threshold-crossing product is included, which is exactly how cumulative-contribution analysis is normally reported.
hints: Create row-to-row context within each entity first; the final filter or comparison happens after that derived state exists.
To include the threshold-crossing row, compare the cumulative total before the current product to 80% of the grand total.

title: Detect three-attempt decreasing payment sequences
description: Return each payment row that completes a sequence of three consecutive payment attempts for the same order where the amounts are strictly decreasing from oldest to newest. Consider attempts ordered by payment_date ascending, then payment_id ascending. Columns: order_id, payment_id, payment_date, amount, previous_amount, amount_two_payments_ago. Ignore orders with fewer than three payment attempts. Order by order_id ascending, then payment_date ascending, then payment_id ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT order_id, payment_id, payment_date, amount, previous_amount, amount_two_payments_ago
FROM (
  SELECT
    order_id,
    payment_id,
    payment_date,
    amount,
    LAG(amount, 1) OVER (
      PARTITION BY order_id
      ORDER BY payment_date ASC, payment_id ASC
    ) AS previous_amount,
    LAG(amount, 2) OVER (
      PARTITION BY order_id
      ORDER BY payment_date ASC, payment_id ASC
    ) AS amount_two_payments_ago
  FROM payments
) ordered_payments
WHERE amount_two_payments_ago IS NOT NULL
  AND amount_two_payments_ago > previous_amount
  AND previous_amount > amount
ORDER BY order_id ASC, payment_date ASC, payment_id ASC
solution_query:
SELECT order_id, payment_id, payment_date, amount, previous_amount, amount_two_payments_ago
FROM (
  SELECT
    order_id,
    payment_id,
    payment_date,
    amount,
    LAG(amount, 1) OVER (
      PARTITION BY order_id
      ORDER BY payment_date ASC, payment_id ASC
    ) AS previous_amount,
    LAG(amount, 2) OVER (
      PARTITION BY order_id
      ORDER BY payment_date ASC, payment_id ASC
    ) AS amount_two_payments_ago
  FROM payments
) ordered_payments
WHERE amount_two_payments_ago IS NOT NULL
  AND amount_two_payments_ago > previous_amount
  AND previous_amount > amount
ORDER BY order_id ASC, payment_date ASC, payment_id ASC;
explanation: This question uses row-to-row comparison to validate a sequential anomaly pattern. LAG(amount, 1) and LAG(amount, 2) bring the previous two payment amounts onto the current row within each order's payment history. Once those values are aligned, the anomaly becomes a simple boolean test: oldest amount greater than previous amount, and previous amount greater than current amount. The subquery is necessary because those lagged values need to be computed before the final filter can reason about a three-row pattern. Ordering by payment_date and payment_id guarantees deterministic sequence evaluation even when two attempts share the same timestamp.
hints: Create row-to-row context within each entity first; the final filter or comparison happens after that derived state exists.
Apply the decreasing-sequence filter only after the lagged columns have been computed in a subquery.

title: Users whose order size drops after crossing a spend threshold
description: Using 'completed' orders only, identify users whose average order net_amount becomes smaller after they first reach a cumulative spend on 'completed' orders of at least 500. Treat the threshold-crossing order as part of the after-threshold period. Exclude users who never reach the threshold, and exclude users who do not have at least one 'completed' order before the threshold and at least one 'completed' order at or after the threshold. Return user_id, name, threshold_order_date, avg_before_threshold, avg_after_threshold, and delta_after_minus_before rounded to 2 decimal places. Build order sequence by order_date ascending, then order_id ascending. Order by delta_after_minus_before ascending, then user_id ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT
  u.user_id,
  u.name,
  MIN(CASE WHEN c.order_seq = t.threshold_seq THEN c.order_date END) AS threshold_order_date,
  ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN c.order_seq < t.threshold_seq THEN c.net_amount END), 2) AS avg_before_threshold,
  ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN c.order_seq >= t.threshold_seq THEN c.net_amount END), 2) AS avg_after_threshold,
  ROUND(
    AVG(CASE WHEN c.order_seq >= t.threshold_seq THEN c.net_amount END)
    - AVG(CASE WHEN c.order_seq < t.threshold_seq THEN c.net_amount END),
    2
  ) AS delta_after_minus_before
FROM (
  SELECT
    order_id,
    user_id,
    order_date,
    net_amount,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
      PARTITION BY user_id
      ORDER BY order_date ASC, order_id ASC
    ) AS order_seq,
    SUM(net_amount) OVER (
      PARTITION BY user_id
      ORDER BY order_date ASC, order_id ASC
      ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS running_completed_spend
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'completed'
) c
JOIN (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(order_seq) AS threshold_seq
  FROM (
    SELECT
      user_id,
      ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
        PARTITION BY user_id
        ORDER BY order_date ASC, order_id ASC
      ) AS order_seq,
      SUM(net_amount) OVER (
        PARTITION BY user_id
        ORDER BY order_date ASC, order_id ASC
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
      ) AS running_completed_spend
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
  ) thresholds
  WHERE running_completed_spend >= 500
  GROUP BY user_id
) t ON c.user_id = t.user_id
JOIN users u ON c.user_id = u.user_id
GROUP BY u.user_id, u.name, t.threshold_seq
HAVING COUNT(CASE WHEN c.order_seq < t.threshold_seq THEN 1 END) >= 1
   AND COUNT(CASE WHEN c.order_seq >= t.threshold_seq THEN 1 END) >= 1
   AND AVG(CASE WHEN c.order_seq >= t.threshold_seq THEN c.net_amount END)
       < AVG(CASE WHEN c.order_seq < t.threshold_seq THEN c.net_amount END)
ORDER BY delta_after_minus_before ASC, u.user_id ASC
solution_query:
SELECT
  u.user_id,
  u.name,
  MIN(CASE WHEN c.order_seq = t.threshold_seq THEN c.order_date END) AS threshold_order_date,
  ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN c.order_seq < t.threshold_seq THEN c.net_amount END), 2) AS avg_before_threshold,
  ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN c.order_seq >= t.threshold_seq THEN c.net_amount END), 2) AS avg_after_threshold,
  ROUND(
    AVG(CASE WHEN c.order_seq >= t.threshold_seq THEN c.net_amount END)
    - AVG(CASE WHEN c.order_seq < t.threshold_seq THEN c.net_amount END),
    2
  ) AS delta_after_minus_before
FROM (
  SELECT
    order_id,
    user_id,
    order_date,
    net_amount,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
      PARTITION BY user_id
      ORDER BY order_date ASC, order_id ASC
    ) AS order_seq,
    SUM(net_amount) OVER (
      PARTITION BY user_id
      ORDER BY order_date ASC, order_id ASC
      ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS running_completed_spend
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'completed'
) c
JOIN (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(order_seq) AS threshold_seq
  FROM (
    SELECT
      user_id,
      ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
        PARTITION BY user_id
        ORDER BY order_date ASC, order_id ASC
      ) AS order_seq,
      SUM(net_amount) OVER (
        PARTITION BY user_id
        ORDER BY order_date ASC, order_id ASC
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
      ) AS running_completed_spend
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
  ) thresholds
  WHERE running_completed_spend >= 500
  GROUP BY user_id
) t ON c.user_id = t.user_id
JOIN users u ON c.user_id = u.user_id
GROUP BY u.user_id, u.name, t.threshold_seq
HAVING COUNT(CASE WHEN c.order_seq < t.threshold_seq THEN 1 END) >= 1
   AND COUNT(CASE WHEN c.order_seq >= t.threshold_seq THEN 1 END) >= 1
   AND AVG(CASE WHEN c.order_seq >= t.threshold_seq THEN c.net_amount END)
       < AVG(CASE WHEN c.order_seq < t.threshold_seq THEN c.net_amount END)
ORDER BY delta_after_minus_before ASC, u.user_id ASC;
explanation: This problem deliberately forces a compute, filter, then recompute workflow. The first stage computes running completed spend per user so the threshold-crossing order can be identified. The second stage keeps only users who actually cross the threshold and records the first sequence number where that happens. Only after that threshold position is known can the query recompute two different averages for the same user: one before the threshold and one at or after it. The hard part is that the business split is not present in the raw data; it is derived from an earlier window calculation and then reused inside grouped conditional aggregation.
hints: Create per-entity running context first, then isolate the exact moment the threshold or transition is reached.
Once you know the first order that crosses 500, use conditional aggregation to compute before-versus-after averages on the same joined set.

title: Acquisition-channel rank improvements across months
description: For 2024 only, compute 'completed'-order revenue per acquisition_channel for each calendar month, rank channels within each month by monthly revenue, and return only the month-channel rows where the channel improved relative to its previous revenue-bearing month. Improvement means the current monthly rank is numerically smaller than the previous monthly rank. If channels tie on monthly revenue within a month, break ties by acquisition_channel ascending. When comparing a channel to its previous revenue-bearing month, order months by order_month ascending and use monthly_rank ascending as the explicit tie-breaker. Columns: order_month, acquisition_channel, monthly_completed_revenue, monthly_rank, previous_month_rank, rank_change. order_month should be the first day of the month. rank_change should be previous_month_rank minus monthly_rank. Order by order_month ascending, monthly_rank ascending, acquisition_channel ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT order_month, acquisition_channel, monthly_completed_revenue, monthly_rank, previous_month_rank,
  previous_month_rank - monthly_rank AS rank_change
FROM (
  SELECT
    order_month,
    acquisition_channel,
    monthly_completed_revenue,
    monthly_rank,
    LAG(monthly_rank) OVER (
      PARTITION BY acquisition_channel
      ORDER BY order_month ASC, monthly_rank ASC
    ) AS previous_month_rank
  FROM (
    SELECT
      order_month,
      acquisition_channel,
      monthly_completed_revenue,
      ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
        PARTITION BY order_month
        ORDER BY monthly_completed_revenue DESC, acquisition_channel ASC
      ) AS monthly_rank
    FROM (
      SELECT
        DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date) AS order_month,
        u.acquisition_channel,
        SUM(o.net_amount) AS monthly_completed_revenue
      FROM orders o
      JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.user_id
      WHERE o.status = 'completed'
        AND EXTRACT(YEAR FROM o.order_date) = 2024
      GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date), u.acquisition_channel
    ) monthly_revenue
  ) ranked
) compared
WHERE previous_month_rank IS NOT NULL
  AND monthly_rank < previous_month_rank
ORDER BY order_month ASC, monthly_rank ASC, acquisition_channel ASC
solution_query:
SELECT order_month, acquisition_channel, monthly_completed_revenue, monthly_rank, previous_month_rank,
  previous_month_rank - monthly_rank AS rank_change
FROM (
  SELECT
    order_month,
    acquisition_channel,
    monthly_completed_revenue,
    monthly_rank,
    LAG(monthly_rank) OVER (
      PARTITION BY acquisition_channel
      ORDER BY order_month ASC, monthly_rank ASC
    ) AS previous_month_rank
  FROM (
    SELECT
      order_month,
      acquisition_channel,
      monthly_completed_revenue,
      ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
        PARTITION BY order_month
        ORDER BY monthly_completed_revenue DESC, acquisition_channel ASC
      ) AS monthly_rank
    FROM (
      SELECT
        DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date) AS order_month,
        u.acquisition_channel,
        SUM(o.net_amount) AS monthly_completed_revenue
      FROM orders o
      JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.user_id
      WHERE o.status = 'completed'
        AND EXTRACT(YEAR FROM o.order_date) = 2024
      GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date), u.acquisition_channel
    ) monthly_revenue
  ) ranked
) compared
WHERE previous_month_rank IS NOT NULL
  AND monthly_rank < previous_month_rank
ORDER BY order_month ASC, monthly_rank ASC, acquisition_channel ASC;
explanation: This question combines time bucketing with ranking and then compares ranks across periods. The inner aggregation creates one monthly revenue row per acquisition channel. The next layer ranks channels within each month, which answers a different question than their absolute revenue. Only after those monthly ranks exist can LAG compare each channel's current rank to its previous revenue-bearing month. The reasoning challenge is that the query moves between three levels: raw orders, monthly channel aggregates, and cross-month rank deltas for the same channel.

title: Country-level order outcome mix using the latest payment attempt
description: For each user country, classify every order into exactly one outcome bucket using this logic. If order status is 'cancelled', count it as cancelled_orders regardless of any payment rows. Otherwise, look only at the latest payment attempt for that order, where latest means payment_date descending and payment_id descending. Count 'completed' orders with latest payment status 'paid' as completed_paid_orders, latest status in ('refunded', 'chargeback') as completed_reversed_orders, latest status 'failed' as completed_failed_orders, and orders with no payment rows as completed_no_payment_orders. Also return net_paid_revenue, defined as the sum of net_amount for completed_paid_orders only, and reversal_rate_pct, defined as completed_reversed_orders divided by all 'completed' orders in that country, rounded to 2 decimal places. Order by reversal_rate_pct descending, then country ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT
  u.country,
  SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled_orders,
  SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'completed' AND lp.payment_status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS completed_paid_orders,
  SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'completed' AND lp.payment_status IN ('refunded', 'chargeback') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS completed_reversed_orders,
  SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'completed' AND lp.payment_status = 'failed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS completed_failed_orders,
  SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'completed' AND lp.payment_status IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS completed_no_payment_orders,
  SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'completed' AND lp.payment_status = 'paid' THEN o.net_amount ELSE 0 END) AS net_paid_revenue,
  ROUND(
    100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'completed' AND lp.payment_status IN ('refunded', 'chargeback') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
    / NULLIF(SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'completed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 0),
    2
  ) AS reversal_rate_pct
FROM orders o
JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.user_id
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT order_id, status AS payment_status
  FROM (
    SELECT
      order_id,
      status,
      ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
        PARTITION BY order_id
        ORDER BY payment_date DESC, payment_id DESC
      ) AS rn
    FROM payments
  ) ranked_payments
  WHERE rn = 1
) lp ON o.order_id = lp.order_id
GROUP BY u.country
ORDER BY reversal_rate_pct DESC, u.country ASC
solution_query:
SELECT
  u.country,
  SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled_orders,
  SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'completed' AND lp.payment_status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS completed_paid_orders,
  SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'completed' AND lp.payment_status IN ('refunded', 'chargeback') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS completed_reversed_orders,
  SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'completed' AND lp.payment_status = 'failed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS completed_failed_orders,
  SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'completed' AND lp.payment_status IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS completed_no_payment_orders,
  SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'completed' AND lp.payment_status = 'paid' THEN o.net_amount ELSE 0 END) AS net_paid_revenue,
  ROUND(
    100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'completed' AND lp.payment_status IN ('refunded', 'chargeback') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
    / NULLIF(SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'completed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 0),
    2
  ) AS reversal_rate_pct
FROM orders o
JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.user_id
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT order_id, status AS payment_status
  FROM (
    SELECT
      order_id,
      status,
      ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
        PARTITION BY order_id
        ORDER BY payment_date DESC, payment_id DESC
      ) AS rn
    FROM payments
  ) ranked_payments
  WHERE rn = 1
) lp ON o.order_id = lp.order_id
GROUP BY u.country
ORDER BY reversal_rate_pct DESC, u.country ASC;
explanation: The core challenge is that the business logic is branchy: the same order can fall into different outcome buckets depending on order status and, for completed orders, the latest payment status. That means the latest payment row has to be derived first with a window function before conditional aggregation can classify orders correctly. Once the latest-payment subquery exists, a single grouped query can produce multiple operational metrics from the same set of orders by using separate CASE expressions. This is harder than ordinary aggregation because the logic branches by both data source and business rule.
hints: Create row-to-row context within each entity first; the final filter or comparison happens after that derived state exists.
Use separate CASE expressions inside SUM to count each outcome bucket and to sum revenue only for the paid bucket.

title: Payment-method recovery summary after failed attempts
description: A recovery attempt is a payment row whose status is 'paid' and whose immediately previous payment attempt for the same order had status 'failed'. For this question, only count recovery attempts where the paid attempt happens between 0 and 24 hours after the failed attempt, inclusive of both endpoints. Summarize those recovery attempts by the payment_method of the paid row. Return payment_method, recovered_attempt_count, recovered_order_count, total_recovered_amount, and avg_hours_to_recovery rounded to 2 decimal places. recovered_attempt_count counts qualifying paid rows. recovered_order_count counts distinct orders with at least one qualifying recovery attempt. Order by recovered_attempt_count descending, then payment_method ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT
  payment_method,
  COUNT(*) AS recovered_attempt_count,
  COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS recovered_order_count,
  SUM(amount) AS total_recovered_amount,
  ROUND(AVG(hours_to_recovery), 2) AS avg_hours_to_recovery
FROM (
  SELECT
    order_id,
    payment_method,
    amount,
    DATE_DIFF('hour', previous_payment_date, payment_date) AS hours_to_recovery
  FROM (
    SELECT
      order_id,
      payment_date,
      payment_method,
      amount,
      status,
      LAG(status) OVER (
        PARTITION BY order_id
        ORDER BY payment_date ASC, payment_id ASC
      ) AS previous_status,
      LAG(payment_date) OVER (
        PARTITION BY order_id
        ORDER BY payment_date ASC, payment_id ASC
      ) AS previous_payment_date
    FROM payments
  ) ordered_attempts
  WHERE status = 'paid'
    AND previous_status = 'failed'
    AND DATE_DIFF('hour', previous_payment_date, payment_date) BETWEEN 0 AND 24
) recoveries
GROUP BY payment_method
ORDER BY recovered_attempt_count DESC, payment_method ASC
solution_query:
SELECT
  payment_method,
  COUNT(*) AS recovered_attempt_count,
  COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS recovered_order_count,
  SUM(amount) AS total_recovered_amount,
  ROUND(AVG(hours_to_recovery), 2) AS avg_hours_to_recovery
FROM (
  SELECT
    order_id,
    payment_method,
    amount,
    DATE_DIFF('hour', previous_payment_date, payment_date) AS hours_to_recovery
  FROM (
    SELECT
      order_id,
      payment_date,
      payment_method,
      amount,
      status,
      LAG(status) OVER (
        PARTITION BY order_id
        ORDER BY payment_date ASC, payment_id ASC
      ) AS previous_status,
      LAG(payment_date) OVER (
        PARTITION BY order_id
        ORDER BY payment_date ASC, payment_id ASC
      ) AS previous_payment_date
    FROM payments
  ) ordered_attempts
  WHERE status = 'paid'
    AND previous_status = 'failed'
    AND DATE_DIFF('hour', previous_payment_date, payment_date) BETWEEN 0 AND 24
) recoveries
GROUP BY payment_method
ORDER BY recovered_attempt_count DESC, payment_method ASC;
explanation: The interesting part here is that the pattern has to be detected before it can be summarized. LAG brings the previous payment status and timestamp onto each row inside an order's attempt history. The recovery rows are then filtered to the business-defined pattern: a paid attempt immediately following a failed attempt within 24 hours. Only after that sequence logic is resolved does aggregation make sense, because the final output is not individual rows but operational summaries by payment method. This is hard because it combines sequence detection with grouped reporting in a single pipeline.
hints: Create row-to-row context within each entity first; the final filter or comparison happens after that derived state exists.
Filter to qualifying recovery rows first, then aggregate that reduced set by the paid row's payment_method.

title: Reactivated users after a dormant period
description: A 'reactivated user' can be interpreted in many ways, so use this exact definition for the question. Consider a user's events ordered by event_time ascending, then event_id ascending. A reactivation candidate is an event that occurs after at least 14 full days with no prior events from that user. A user qualifies as reactivated if, starting from that candidate event time, they record at least 3 total events in the half-open interval >= reactivation_time and < reactivation_time + 7 days, including the candidate event itself. If a user has multiple qualifying reactivation candidates, keep only the earliest one by reactivation_time ascending, breaking ties on event_id ascending. Return user_id, name, reactivation_time, inactivity_days, and events_in_next_7_days. Order by reactivation_time ascending, then user_id ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT user_id, name, reactivation_time, inactivity_days, events_in_next_7_days
FROM (
  SELECT
    u.user_id,
    u.name,
    q.reactivation_time,
    q.inactivity_days,
    q.events_in_next_7_days,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
      PARTITION BY u.user_id
      ORDER BY q.reactivation_time ASC, q.reactivation_event_id ASC
    ) AS rn
  FROM users u
  JOIN (
    SELECT
      c.user_id,
      c.reactivation_time,
      c.reactivation_event_id,
      c.inactivity_days,
      COUNT(e2.event_id) AS events_in_next_7_days
    FROM (
      SELECT
        user_id,
        event_id AS reactivation_event_id,
        event_time AS reactivation_time,
        DATE_DIFF('day', previous_event_time, event_time) AS inactivity_days
      FROM (
        SELECT
          user_id,
          event_id,
          event_time,
          LAG(event_time) OVER (
            PARTITION BY user_id
            ORDER BY event_time ASC, event_id ASC
          ) AS previous_event_time
        FROM events
      ) ordered_events
      WHERE previous_event_time IS NOT NULL
        AND DATE_DIFF('day', previous_event_time, event_time) >= 14
    ) c
    JOIN events e2 ON e2.user_id = c.user_id
     AND e2.event_time >= c.reactivation_time
     AND e2.event_time < c.reactivation_time + INTERVAL 7 DAY
    GROUP BY c.user_id, c.reactivation_time, c.reactivation_event_id, c.inactivity_days
    HAVING COUNT(e2.event_id) >= 3
  ) q ON u.user_id = q.user_id
) ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY reactivation_time ASC, user_id ASC

      FROM (

            PARTITION BY user_id
            ORDER BY event_time ASC, event_id ASC

First, LAG identifies candidate return events that follow at least 14 days of inactivity. Second, each candidate is evaluated in a forward-looking 7-day window to see whether the user becomes active enough to qualify. Finally, if a user qualifies more than once, ROW_NUMBER keeps the earliest qualifying comeback. title: High-growth stable products among top revenue leaders
description: Consider only products that have revenue in at least 3 distinct calendar months from 'completed' orders. For each such product, compute total_revenue, volatility, and latest_mom_growth_pct. volatility is the sample standard deviation of monthly revenue across all of that product's revenue-bearing months. latest_mom_growth_pct is the percentage growth from the previous revenue-bearing month to the latest revenue-bearing month, rounded to 2 decimal places. Identify the latest and previous revenue-bearing months by order_month descending, with product_id ascending as the explicit tie-breaker. Return only products that satisfy all three conditions: they are in the top 20% of products by total_revenue, latest_mom_growth_pct is positive, and volatility is at or below the 75th percentile of volatility across all eligible products (i.e. not in the most-volatile quartile). If two products tie on total_revenue, break ties on product_id ascending when determining the top 20%. Columns: product_id, product_name, total_revenue, volatility, latest_mom_growth_pct. Order by total_revenue descending, then product_id ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT product_id, product_name, total_revenue, ROUND(volatility, 2) AS volatility, latest_mom_growth_pct
FROM (
  SELECT
    m.product_id,
    p.product_name,
    m.total_revenue,
    m.volatility,
    ROUND(100.0 * (m.latest_month_revenue - m.previous_month_revenue) / NULLIF(m.previous_month_revenue, 0), 2) AS latest_mom_growth_pct,
    CUME_DIST() OVER (ORDER BY m.total_revenue DESC, m.product_id ASC) AS revenue_cume_dist,
    CUME_DIST() OVER (ORDER BY m.volatility ASC, m.product_id ASC) AS volatility_cume_dist,
    m.latest_month_revenue,
    m.previous_month_revenue
  FROM (
    SELECT
      s.product_id,
      s.total_revenue,
      s.volatility,
      MAX(CASE WHEN s.recency_rank = 1 THEN s.monthly_revenue END) AS latest_month_revenue,
      MAX(CASE WHEN s.recency_rank = 2 THEN s.monthly_revenue END) AS previous_month_revenue
    FROM (
      SELECT
        product_id,
        order_month,
        monthly_revenue,
        SUM(monthly_revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY product_id) AS total_revenue,
        STDDEV_SAMP(monthly_revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY product_id) AS volatility,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
          PARTITION BY product_id
          ORDER BY order_month DESC, product_id ASC
        ) AS recency_rank,
        COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY product_id) AS month_count
      FROM (
        SELECT
          oi.product_id,
          DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date) AS order_month,
          SUM(oi.line_amount) AS monthly_revenue
        FROM order_items oi
        JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
        WHERE o.status = 'completed'
        GROUP BY oi.product_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date)
      ) monthly_product_revenue
    ) s
    WHERE s.month_count >= 3
    GROUP BY s.product_id, s.total_revenue, s.volatility
  ) m
  JOIN products p ON m.product_id = p.product_id
) final_metrics
WHERE revenue_cume_dist <= 0.20
  AND previous_month_revenue IS NOT NULL
  AND latest_month_revenue > previous_month_revenue
  AND volatility_cume_dist <= 0.75
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC, product_id ASC
solution_query:

    CUME_DIST() OVER (ORDER BY m.total_revenue DESC, m.product_id ASC) AS revenue_cume_dist,
    CUME_DIST() OVER (ORDER BY m.volatility ASC, m.product_id ASC) AS volatility_cume_dist,
    m.latest_month_revenue,
    m.previous_month_revenue
  FROM (
    SELECT
      s.product_id,
      s.total_revenue,
      s.volatility,
      MAX(CASE WHEN s.recency_rank = 1 THEN s.monthly_revenue END) AS latest_month_revenue,
      MAX(CASE WHEN s.recency_rank = 2 THEN s.monthly_revenue END) AS previous_month_revenue
    FROM (
      SELECT
        product_id,
        order_month,
        monthly_revenue,
        SUM(monthly_revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY product_id) AS total_revenue,
        STDDEV_SAMP(monthly_revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY product_id) AS volatility,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
          PARTITION BY product_id
          ORDER BY order_month DESC, product_id ASC
        ) AS recency_rank,
        COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY product_id) AS month_count
      FROM (
        SELECT
          oi.product_id,
          DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date) AS order_month,
          SUM(oi.line_amount) AS monthly_revenue
        FROM order_items oi
        JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
        WHERE o.status = 'completed'
        GROUP BY oi.product_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date)
      ) monthly_product_revenue
    ) s
    WHERE s.month_count >= 3

  ) m

explanation: This question forces several metrics that pull in different directions. The first stage aggregates monthly revenue per product from completed orders. The next stage computes three product-level signals from those monthly rows: total revenue, volatility, and the latest month-over-month change. Only after those metrics exist can the final screening logic be applied. The hard part is that none of the filter conditions lives at the same granularity as the raw data: one is based on the full revenue distribution, one is based on the latest two months, and one is based on volatility across all months. That makes this a genuine competing-metrics problem rather than a simple ranking exercise.

title: Returned users after 30-day order inactivity
description: Using 'completed' orders only, identify users who returned after a churn gap of more than 30 days between consecutive 'completed' orders. The return order is the later order in that gap. If a user has multiple qualifying churn-return gaps, keep only the earliest return. Compare behavior in the half-open interval >= return_order_date - 30 days and < return_order_date to behavior in the half-open interval >= return_order_date and < return_order_date + 30 days. Return user_id, name, return_order_date, inactivity_days, orders_before_30d, orders_after_30d, avg_before_30d, and avg_after_30d, where the averages are based on net_amount and rounded to 2 decimal places. The post-return window always contains at least the return order itself; the pre-return window can be empty — when it is, `orders_before_30d` is 0 and `avg_before_30d` is NULL. Order by return_order_date ascending, then user_id ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT user_id, name, return_order_date, inactivity_days, orders_before_30d, orders_after_30d, avg_before_30d, avg_after_30d
FROM (
  SELECT
    u.user_id,
    u.name,
    r.return_order_date,
    r.inactivity_days,
    COUNT(CASE WHEN o.order_date < r.return_order_date AND o.order_date >= r.return_order_date - INTERVAL 30 DAY THEN 1 END) AS orders_before_30d,
    COUNT(CASE WHEN o.order_date >= r.return_order_date AND o.order_date < r.return_order_date + INTERVAL 30 DAY THEN 1 END) AS orders_after_30d,
    ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN o.order_date < r.return_order_date AND o.order_date >= r.return_order_date - INTERVAL 30 DAY THEN o.net_amount END), 2) AS avg_before_30d,
    ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN o.order_date >= r.return_order_date AND o.order_date < r.return_order_date + INTERVAL 30 DAY THEN o.net_amount END), 2) AS avg_after_30d
  FROM users u
  JOIN (
    SELECT user_id, return_order_date, inactivity_days
    FROM (
      SELECT
        user_id,
        order_date AS return_order_date,
        DATE_DIFF('day', previous_order_date, order_date) AS inactivity_days,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
          PARTITION BY user_id
          ORDER BY order_date ASC, order_id ASC
        ) AS return_rank
      FROM (
        SELECT
          order_id,
          user_id,
          order_date,
          LAG(order_date) OVER (
            PARTITION BY user_id
            ORDER BY order_date ASC, order_id ASC
          ) AS previous_order_date
        FROM orders
        WHERE status = 'completed'
      ) ordered_orders
      WHERE previous_order_date IS NOT NULL
        AND DATE_DIFF('day', previous_order_date, order_date) > 30
    ) churn_returns
    WHERE return_rank = 1
  ) r ON u.user_id = r.user_id
  JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id AND o.status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY u.user_id, u.name, r.return_order_date, r.inactivity_days
) compared
ORDER BY return_order_date ASC, user_id ASC
solution_query:
SELECT user_id, name, return_order_date, inactivity_days, orders_before_30d, orders_after_30d, avg_before_30d, avg_after_30d
FROM (
  SELECT
    u.user_id,
    u.name,
    r.return_order_date,
    r.inactivity_days,
    COUNT(CASE WHEN o.order_date < r.return_order_date AND o.order_date >= r.return_order_date - INTERVAL 30 DAY THEN 1 END) AS orders_before_30d,
    COUNT(CASE WHEN o.order_date >= r.return_order_date AND o.order_date < r.return_order_date + INTERVAL 30 DAY THEN 1 END) AS orders_after_30d,
    ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN o.order_date < r.return_order_date AND o.order_date >= r.return_order_date - INTERVAL 30 DAY THEN o.net_amount END), 2) AS avg_before_30d,
    ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN o.order_date >= r.return_order_date AND o.order_date < r.return_order_date + INTERVAL 30 DAY THEN o.net_amount END), 2) AS avg_after_30d
  FROM users u
  JOIN (
    SELECT user_id, return_order_date, inactivity_days
    FROM (
      SELECT
        user_id,
        order_date AS return_order_date,
        DATE_DIFF('day', previous_order_date, order_date) AS inactivity_days,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
          PARTITION BY user_id
          ORDER BY order_date ASC, order_id ASC
        ) AS return_rank
      FROM (
        SELECT
          order_id,
          user_id,
          order_date,
          LAG(order_date) OVER (
            PARTITION BY user_id
            ORDER BY order_date ASC, order_id ASC
          ) AS previous_order_date
        FROM orders
        WHERE status = 'completed'
      ) ordered_orders
      WHERE previous_order_date IS NOT NULL
        AND DATE_DIFF('day', previous_order_date, order_date) > 30
    ) churn_returns
    WHERE return_rank = 1
  ) r ON u.user_id = r.user_id
  JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id AND o.status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY u.user_id, u.name, r.return_order_date, r.inactivity_days
) compared
ORDER BY return_order_date ASC, user_id ASC;
explanation: This is a state-transition problem because the interesting event is not an order by itself but the user's change from inactive to active again. LAG detects the gap between consecutive completed orders, which is what defines churn and return here. Once the first qualifying return order is identified per user, the query has to switch to a different time frame and compare two forward- and backward-looking 30-day windows around that return date. The hard part is coordinating these two layers of reasoning: the return event is derived from the order sequence, but the behavior comparison is measured over date windows around that derived event.

After you keep the earliest qualifying return per user, use conditional aggregation over 30-day windows before and after that date.

title: Users whose top spending category changes from Q1 to Q2
description: For 2024 only, find users whose top product category by 'completed'-order spend changes from Q1 to Q2. Define top category separately within each quarter using total line_amount. If multiple categories tie for the top spend within a user-quarter, choose the smaller category_id. Only include users who have at least one 'completed'-order line item in both Q1 and Q2. Return user_id, name, q1_top_category_id, q1_spend, q2_top_category_id, and q2_spend. Order by user_id ascending.
expected_query:
WITH quarter_category_spend AS (
  SELECT
    o.user_id,
    p.category_id,
    CASE WHEN EXTRACT(QUARTER FROM o.order_date) = 1 THEN 'Q1' ELSE 'Q2' END AS quarter_label,
    SUM(oi.line_amount) AS quarter_spend
  FROM orders o
  JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
  JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    AND EXTRACT(YEAR FROM o.order_date) = 2024
    AND EXTRACT(QUARTER FROM o.order_date) IN (1, 2)
  GROUP BY o.user_id, p.category_id, CASE WHEN EXTRACT(QUARTER FROM o.order_date) = 1 THEN 'Q1' ELSE 'Q2' END
),
ranked_categories AS (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    category_id,
    quarter_spend,
    quarter_label,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
      PARTITION BY user_id, quarter_label
      ORDER BY quarter_spend DESC, category_id ASC
    ) AS rn
  FROM quarter_category_spend
),
q1 AS (SELECT user_id, category_id, quarter_spend FROM ranked_categories WHERE quarter_label = 'Q1' AND rn = 1),
q2 AS (SELECT user_id, category_id, quarter_spend FROM ranked_categories WHERE quarter_label = 'Q2' AND rn = 1)
SELECT
  q1.user_id,
  u.name,
  q1.category_id AS q1_top_category_id,
  q1.quarter_spend AS q1_spend,
  q2.category_id AS q2_top_category_id,
  q2.quarter_spend AS q2_spend
FROM q1
JOIN q2 ON q1.user_id = q2.user_id
JOIN users u ON q1.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE q1.category_id <> q2.category_id
ORDER BY q1.user_id ASC
solution_query:
WITH quarter_category_spend AS (
  SELECT
    o.user_id,
    p.category_id,
    CASE WHEN EXTRACT(QUARTER FROM o.order_date) = 1 THEN 'Q1' ELSE 'Q2' END AS quarter_label,
    SUM(oi.line_amount) AS quarter_spend
  FROM orders o
  JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
  JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    AND EXTRACT(YEAR FROM o.order_date) = 2024
    AND EXTRACT(QUARTER FROM o.order_date) IN (1, 2)
  GROUP BY o.user_id, p.category_id, CASE WHEN EXTRACT(QUARTER FROM o.order_date) = 1 THEN 'Q1' ELSE 'Q2' END
),
ranked_categories AS (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    category_id,
    quarter_spend,
    quarter_label,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
      PARTITION BY user_id, quarter_label
      ORDER BY quarter_spend DESC, category_id ASC
    ) AS rn
  FROM quarter_category_spend
),
q1 AS (SELECT user_id, category_id, quarter_spend FROM ranked_categories WHERE quarter_label = 'Q1' AND rn = 1),
q2 AS (SELECT user_id, category_id, quarter_spend FROM ranked_categories WHERE quarter_label = 'Q2' AND rn = 1)
SELECT
  q1.user_id,
  u.name,
  q1.category_id AS q1_top_category_id,
  q1.quarter_spend AS q1_spend,
  q2.category_id AS q2_top_category_id,

WHERE q1.category_id <> q2.category_id

explanation: This question works across multiple granularities at once. The raw data lives at the order-item level, but the business comparison happens at the user-category-quarter level. Spend is aggregated once per user-category-quarter, then ranked within each user-quarter to determine the dominant category. Only then can the query compare quarter-level winners across time slices for the same user. The reasoning challenge is moving cleanly from item-level transactions to quarter-level preference shifts without losing deterministic tie-breaking.
hints: Create row-to-row context within each entity first; the final filter or comparison happens after that derived state exists.
Use ROW_NUMBER with category_id as a tie-breaker so each user-quarter has exactly one top category.

title: Resolve final order status from conflicting payment evidence
description: Determine a resolved final_status for every order using this precedence logic: if the order has any payment with status 'chargeback', final_status is 'chargeback'; else if it has any payment with status 'refunded', final_status is 'refunded'; else if the latest payment for that order has status 'paid', final_status is 'paid'; else if the latest payment has status 'failed', final_status is 'failed'; else final_status is 'unknown'. Latest payment means payment_date descending and payment_id descending. Then summarize by user country. Return country, chargeback_orders, refunded_orders, paid_orders, failed_orders, unknown_orders, and resolved_paid_revenue, where resolved_paid_revenue is the sum of net_amount for orders whose final_status is 'paid'. Order by country ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT
  u.country,
  SUM(CASE WHEN r.final_status = 'chargeback' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS chargeback_orders,
  SUM(CASE WHEN r.final_status = 'refunded' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS refunded_orders,
  SUM(CASE WHEN r.final_status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS paid_orders,
  SUM(CASE WHEN r.final_status = 'failed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS failed_orders,
  SUM(CASE WHEN r.final_status = 'unknown' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS unknown_orders,
  SUM(CASE WHEN r.final_status = 'paid' THEN o.net_amount ELSE 0 END) AS resolved_paid_revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.user_id
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT
    x.order_id,
    CASE
      WHEN x.has_chargeback = 1 THEN 'chargeback'
      WHEN x.has_refunded = 1 THEN 'refunded'
      WHEN x.latest_status = 'paid' THEN 'paid'
      WHEN x.latest_status = 'failed' THEN 'failed'
      ELSE 'unknown'
    END AS final_status
  FROM (
    SELECT
      order_id,
      MAX(CASE WHEN status = 'chargeback' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS has_chargeback,
      MAX(CASE WHEN status = 'refunded' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS has_refunded,
      MAX(CASE WHEN rn = 1 THEN status END) AS latest_status
    FROM (
      SELECT
        order_id,
        status,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
          PARTITION BY order_id
          ORDER BY payment_date DESC, payment_id DESC
        ) AS rn
      FROM payments
    ) ranked_payments
    GROUP BY order_id
  ) x
) r ON o.order_id = r.order_id
GROUP BY u.country
ORDER BY u.country ASC
solution_query:
SELECT
  u.country,
  SUM(CASE WHEN r.final_status = 'chargeback' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS chargeback_orders,
  SUM(CASE WHEN r.final_status = 'refunded' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS refunded_orders,
  SUM(CASE WHEN r.final_status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS paid_orders,
  SUM(CASE WHEN r.final_status = 'failed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS failed_orders,
  SUM(CASE WHEN r.final_status = 'unknown' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS unknown_orders,
  SUM(CASE WHEN r.final_status = 'paid' THEN o.net_amount ELSE 0 END) AS resolved_paid_revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.user_id
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT
    x.order_id,
    CASE
      WHEN x.has_chargeback = 1 THEN 'chargeback'
      WHEN x.has_refunded = 1 THEN 'refunded'
      WHEN x.latest_status = 'paid' THEN 'paid'
      WHEN x.latest_status = 'failed' THEN 'failed'
      ELSE 'unknown'
    END AS final_status
  FROM (
    SELECT
      order_id,
      MAX(CASE WHEN status = 'chargeback' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS has_chargeback,
      MAX(CASE WHEN status = 'refunded' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS has_refunded,
      MAX(CASE WHEN rn = 1 THEN status END) AS latest_status
    FROM (
      SELECT
        order_id,
        status,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
          PARTITION BY order_id
          ORDER BY payment_date DESC, payment_id DESC
        ) AS rn
      FROM payments
    ) ranked_payments
    GROUP BY order_id
  ) x
) r ON o.order_id = r.order_id
GROUP BY u.country
ORDER BY u.country ASC;
explanation: This is a noisy-data resolution problem because multiple payment rows can tell conflicting stories about the same order. The query first reduces those rows into three competing signals: whether any chargeback exists, whether any refund exists, and what the latest payment status says. Only then can the precedence rules be applied to derive a single final status per order. After that resolution step, country-level metrics are straightforward. The hard part is explicitly separating evidence gathering from precedence evaluation so the final status is stable and deterministic.
hints: Create row-to-row context within each entity first; the final filter or comparison happens after that derived state exists.
Apply the precedence rules in a CASE expression only after all order-level payment evidence has been collected.

title: Users whose monthly revenue declines after their peak month
description: Using 'completed' orders in 2024 only, find users whose average monthly revenue from 'completed' orders declines after their peak month. First aggregate to one row per user per calendar month. Define the peak month as the month with the highest monthly revenue from 'completed' orders; if multiple months tie, choose the earliest month. Then compare the user's average monthly revenue from 'completed' orders before the peak month to the average monthly revenue from 'completed' orders after the peak month. Exclude users who do not have at least one revenue-bearing month before the peak and one after the peak. Return user_id, name, peak_month, peak_month_revenue, avg_before_peak, avg_after_peak, and decline_amount, where decline_amount is avg_before_peak minus avg_after_peak rounded to 2 decimal places. Include only users where avg_after_peak is strictly lower than avg_before_peak. Order by decline_amount descending, then user_id ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT
  u.user_id,
  u.name,
  p.peak_month,
  p.peak_month_revenue,
  ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN m.order_month < p.peak_month THEN m.monthly_revenue END), 2) AS avg_before_peak,
  ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN m.order_month > p.peak_month THEN m.monthly_revenue END), 2) AS avg_after_peak,
  ROUND(
    AVG(CASE WHEN m.order_month < p.peak_month THEN m.monthly_revenue END)
    - AVG(CASE WHEN m.order_month > p.peak_month THEN m.monthly_revenue END),
    2
  ) AS decline_amount
FROM users u
JOIN (
  SELECT user_id, order_month AS peak_month, monthly_revenue AS peak_month_revenue
  FROM (
    SELECT
      user_id,
      order_month,
      monthly_revenue,
      ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
        PARTITION BY user_id
        ORDER BY monthly_revenue DESC, order_month ASC
      ) AS rn
    FROM (
      SELECT
        user_id,
        DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS order_month,
        SUM(net_amount) AS monthly_revenue
      FROM orders
      WHERE status = 'completed'
        AND EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) = 2024
      GROUP BY user_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)
    ) monthly_user_revenue
  ) ranked_months
  WHERE rn = 1
) p ON u.user_id = p.user_id
JOIN (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS order_month,
    SUM(net_amount) AS monthly_revenue
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'completed'
    AND EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) = 2024
  GROUP BY user_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)
) m ON u.user_id = m.user_id
GROUP BY u.user_id, u.name, p.peak_month, p.peak_month_revenue
HAVING COUNT(CASE WHEN m.order_month < p.peak_month THEN 1 END) >= 1
   AND COUNT(CASE WHEN m.order_month > p.peak_month THEN 1 END) >= 1
   AND AVG(CASE WHEN m.order_month > p.peak_month THEN m.monthly_revenue END)
       < AVG(CASE WHEN m.order_month < p.peak_month THEN m.monthly_revenue END)
ORDER BY decline_amount DESC, u.user_id ASC
solution_query:
SELECT
  u.user_id,
  u.name,
  p.peak_month,
  p.peak_month_revenue,
  ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN m.order_month < p.peak_month THEN m.monthly_revenue END), 2) AS avg_before_peak,
  ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN m.order_month > p.peak_month THEN m.monthly_revenue END), 2) AS avg_after_peak,
  ROUND(
    AVG(CASE WHEN m.order_month < p.peak_month THEN m.monthly_revenue END)
    - AVG(CASE WHEN m.order_month > p.peak_month THEN m.monthly_revenue END),
    2
  ) AS decline_amount
FROM users u
JOIN (
  SELECT user_id, order_month AS peak_month, monthly_revenue AS peak_month_revenue
  FROM (
    SELECT
      user_id,
      order_month,
      monthly_revenue,
      ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
        PARTITION BY user_id
        ORDER BY monthly_revenue DESC, order_month ASC
      ) AS rn
    FROM (
      SELECT
        user_id,
        DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS order_month,
        SUM(net_amount) AS monthly_revenue
      FROM orders
      WHERE status = 'completed'
        AND EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) = 2024
      GROUP BY user_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)
    ) monthly_user_revenue
  ) ranked_months
  WHERE rn = 1
) p ON u.user_id = p.user_id
JOIN (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS order_month,
    SUM(net_amount) AS monthly_revenue
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'completed'
    AND EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date) = 2024
  GROUP BY user_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)
) m ON u.user_id = m.user_id
GROUP BY u.user_id, u.name, p.peak_month, p.peak_month_revenue
HAVING COUNT(CASE WHEN m.order_month < p.peak_month THEN 1 END) >= 1
   AND COUNT(CASE WHEN m.order_month > p.peak_month THEN 1 END) >= 1
   AND AVG(CASE WHEN m.order_month > p.peak_month THEN m.monthly_revenue END)
       < AVG(CASE WHEN m.order_month < p.peak_month THEN m.monthly_revenue END)
