title: Revenue slices with GROUPING SETS
description: Write a query using `GROUPING SETS` to produce three independent revenue summaries in one pass: (1) by `category_name`, (2) by order `status`, and (3) by user `country`. Return `category_name`, `status`, `country`, and `revenue` (`SUM(oi.line_amount)` rounded to 2 dp). Use `COALESCE` to replace GROUPING SET NULLs with `'—'`. Order by `category_name`, `status`, `country`.
expected_query:
SELECT COALESCE(c.category_name, '—') AS category_name,
       COALESCE(o.status, '—') AS status,
       COALESCE(u.country, '—') AS country,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.line_amount), 2) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
JOIN categories c ON p.category_id = c.category_id
JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.user_id
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS (
    (c.category_name),
    (o.status),
    (u.country)
)
ORDER BY category_name, status, country
solution_query:
SELECT COALESCE(c.category_name, '—') AS category_name,
       COALESCE(o.status, '—') AS status,
       COALESCE(u.country, '—') AS country,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.line_amount), 2) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
JOIN categories c ON p.category_id = c.category_id
JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.user_id
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS (
    (c.category_name),
    (o.status),
    (u.country)
)
ORDER BY category_name, status, country;
hints: GROUPING SETS((...), (...)) enumerates each aggregation level explicitly — rows for each set are unioned in one pass with no UNION ALL.
Columns not in the current grouping set appear as NULL; COALESCE replaces them with a display label.
Contrast with ROLLUP (a fixed hierarchy of subtotals) and CUBE (all possible combinations) — GROUPING SETS gives you exactly the levels you need.
explanation: GROUPING SETS((...), (...)) is the most flexible extended GROUP BY clause. Unlike ROLLUP (fixed hierarchy) or CUBE (all 2^n combinations), GROUPING SETS lets you enumerate precisely which groupings you need. Each grouping set produces a separate set of rows that are unioned together, with columns outside the current set filled with NULL. The GROUPING(col) function returns 1 for rollup NULLs and 0 for real NULLs, which can distinguish a row with a NULL category_name from a rollup total — more precise than COALESCE alone in production pipelines.

title: Ordered product arrays per user
description: Write a query that returns each `user_id` and an array of the distinct `product_name` values they have ordered, sorted alphabetically within the array. Alias the array column as `ordered_products`. Only include users who have placed at least one order. Order by `user_id` ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT o.user_id,
       ARRAY_AGG(DISTINCT p.product_name ORDER BY p.product_name) AS ordered_products
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY o.user_id
ORDER BY o.user_id
solution_query:
SELECT o.user_id,
       ARRAY_AGG(DISTINCT p.product_name ORDER BY p.product_name) AS ordered_products
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY o.user_id
ORDER BY o.user_id;
hints: You need an ordered, deduplicated collection of values per group — all in a single cell. Which aggregate function builds an array from grouped values, and does it support ordering and deduplication?
The ORDER BY inside ARRAY_AGG controls the order of elements within each array, not the order of rows in the output.
explanation: ARRAY_AGG(expr) builds an array from grouped rows. Adding DISTINCT deduplicates, and ORDER BY inside the function sorts elements within each array. The resulting array type is compatible with JSON export, Spark/Pandas processing, and BI tools that can unnest arrays. ARRAY_AGG vs STRING_AGG is a common interview comparison: ARRAY_AGG preserves type and structure (elements are individually indexable); STRING_AGG produces a flat string (compact for display, lossy for processing). Use ARRAY_AGG when downstream code needs to iterate or index individual elements.

title: Fill monthly revenue gaps with a date spine
description: Using a recursive CTE, generate a monthly date spine from the earliest to the latest `order_date` in the `orders` table (both truncated to the first of the month). LEFT JOIN it to actual monthly revenue. Return `month`, `revenue` (0.00 if no orders that month), and `has_orders` (boolean). Order by `month` ascending.
expected_query:
WITH RECURSIVE spine AS (
    SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(order_date))::DATE AS month
    FROM orders
    UNION ALL
    SELECT (month + INTERVAL '1 month')::DATE
    FROM spine
    WHERE (month + INTERVAL '1 month')::DATE
          <= (SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', MAX(order_date))::DATE FROM orders)
),
monthly_revenue AS (
    SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)::DATE AS month,
           ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS revenue
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)::DATE
)
SELECT s.month,
       COALESCE(m.revenue, 0.00) AS revenue,
       m.revenue IS NOT NULL AS has_orders
FROM spine s
LEFT JOIN monthly_revenue m ON s.month = m.month
ORDER BY s.month
solution_query:
WITH RECURSIVE spine AS (
    SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(order_date))::DATE AS month
    FROM orders
    UNION ALL
    SELECT (month + INTERVAL '1 month')::DATE
    FROM spine
    WHERE (month + INTERVAL '1 month')::DATE
          <= (SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', MAX(order_date))::DATE FROM orders)
),
monthly_revenue AS (
    SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)::DATE AS month,
           ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS revenue
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)::DATE
)
SELECT s.month,
       COALESCE(m.revenue, 0.00) AS revenue,
       m.revenue IS NOT NULL AS has_orders
FROM spine s
LEFT JOIN monthly_revenue m ON s.month = m.month
ORDER BY s.month;
hints: A date spine generates every expected period whether or not data exists. Which SQL construct lets you iterate from an anchor date forward in steps until you reach an end date?
LEFT JOIN the spine to the monthly revenue CTE — months with no orders become NULL in the revenue column, which COALESCE turns to 0.
Use a scalar subquery in the recursive member's WHERE clause to compare against the dynamically computed max date.
explanation: The recursive CTE generates every month between the data's earliest and latest months, regardless of whether orders exist. The LEFT JOIN produces NULL for months with no data, which COALESCE turns to 0 and IS NOT NULL computes the boolean flag. Without the spine, a plain GROUP BY would silently skip empty months — charts built on that data would have invisible gaps, which is a common data quality issue. Subquerying MIN/MAX inside the anchor makes the spine self-adapting; hard-coded dates break when the data range changes.

title: Top 2 products per category with LATERAL
description: Write a query using a `LATERAL` join to return the top 2 products by revenue (`SUM(oi.line_amount)` rounded to 2 dp) for each category. Return `category_name`, `product_name`, and `revenue`. Order by `category_name`, then `revenue` descending.
expected_query:
SELECT c.category_name, top.product_name, top.revenue
FROM categories c
JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT p.product_name,
           ROUND(SUM(oi.line_amount), 2) AS revenue
    FROM products p
    JOIN order_items oi ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
    WHERE p.category_id = c.category_id
    GROUP BY p.product_name
    ORDER BY revenue DESC
    LIMIT 2
) top ON 1=1
ORDER BY c.category_name, top.revenue DESC
solution_query:
SELECT c.category_name, top.product_name, top.revenue
FROM categories c
JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT p.product_name,
           ROUND(SUM(oi.line_amount), 2) AS revenue
    FROM products p
    JOIN order_items oi ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
    WHERE p.category_id = c.category_id
    GROUP BY p.product_name
    ORDER BY revenue DESC
    LIMIT 2
) top ON 1=1
ORDER BY c.category_name, top.revenue DESC;
hints: A LATERAL subquery executes once per outer row and can reference columns from the outer FROM clause — use c.category_id inside the lateral subquery to filter to the current category.
CROSS JOIN LATERAL produces one row in the outer result for each row returned by the subquery — for each category, the LIMIT 2 gives at most 2 product rows.
explanation: A LATERAL subquery (or correlated subquery in FROM) executes once per outer row and can reference those outer columns. CROSS JOIN LATERAL produces the cross-product of the outer table with each lateral result. For top-N per group, LATERAL with ORDER BY + LIMIT is competitive with the window function approach (ROW_NUMBER OVER PARTITION + WHERE rn <= 2). LATERAL is preferred when the per-group logic is complex or when the database's query planner handles it better than a dense-ranking subquery. PostgreSQL and DuckDB support LATERAL; BigQuery uses a different syntax.

title: Most recent order per user with QUALIFY
description: Write a query using the `QUALIFY` clause to return each user's most recent order — `user_id`, `order_id`, `order_date`, and `net_amount`. Use `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY order_date DESC)` inside QUALIFY to filter to the latest row per user. Order by `user_id` ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT user_id, order_id, order_date, net_amount
FROM orders
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY order_date DESC) = 1
ORDER BY user_id
solution_query:
SELECT user_id, order_id, order_date, net_amount
FROM orders
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY order_date DESC) = 1
ORDER BY user_id;
hints: Window functions produce a column you can't filter on in the same clause as the data. What SQL keyword is designed specifically for filtering on computed window-function results?
Without QUALIFY you would need a subquery or CTE: WITH r AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) AS rn FROM orders) SELECT ... FROM r WHERE rn = 1.
explanation: QUALIFY is supported in DuckDB, Snowflake, BigQuery, and Teradata. It evaluates after window functions in SELECT, so you can filter directly on ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), or any window expression without a subquery wrapper. The equivalent without QUALIFY is to wrap in a CTE and add WHERE rn = 1 — QUALIFY collapses this into one query level. It is a major ergonomic improvement for deduplication, latest-record, and top-N queries. Not available in PostgreSQL or MySQL — in those engines, use the CTE pattern.

title: Daily revenue spine with GENERATE_SERIES
description: Using `GENERATE_SERIES` to build a daily date spine from `2023-01-01` to `2025-12-31`, LEFT JOIN it to daily order revenue (`SUM(net_amount)` per `order_date`). Return `day`, `revenue` (0.00 if no orders), and `is_weekend` (true when the day is Saturday or Sunday, using `EXTRACT(ISODOW FROM day) >= 6`). Order by `day` ascending.
expected_query:
WITH spine AS (
    SELECT generate_series::DATE AS day
    FROM generate_series(DATE '2023-01-01', DATE '2025-12-31', INTERVAL '1 day')
),
daily_revenue AS (
    SELECT order_date::DATE AS day,
           ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS revenue
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY order_date::DATE
)
SELECT s.day,
       COALESCE(r.revenue, 0.00) AS revenue,
       EXTRACT(ISODOW FROM s.day) >= 6 AS is_weekend
FROM spine s
LEFT JOIN daily_revenue r ON s.day = r.day
ORDER BY s.day
solution_query:
WITH spine AS (
    SELECT generate_series::DATE AS day
    FROM generate_series(DATE '2023-01-01', DATE '2025-12-31', INTERVAL '1 day')
),
daily_revenue AS (
    SELECT order_date::DATE AS day,
           ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS revenue
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY order_date::DATE
)
SELECT s.day,
       COALESCE(r.revenue, 0.00) AS revenue,
       EXTRACT(ISODOW FROM s.day) >= 6 AS is_weekend
FROM spine s
LEFT JOIN daily_revenue r ON s.day = r.day
ORDER BY s.day;
hints: GENERATE_SERIES(start, stop, step) is a DuckDB table-valued function — use it in FROM and alias the result column as day with ::DATE.
LEFT JOIN the spine to actual revenue data — days with no orders have NULL revenue, which COALESCE turns to 0.
EXTRACT(ISODOW FROM date) returns ISO day of week: Monday = 1, Sunday = 7 — so >= 6 selects Saturday (6) and Sunday (7).
explanation: GENERATE_SERIES(start, stop, interval) is DuckDB's table-valued function for producing dense sequences. The column it produces is named 'generate_series', which you cast to ::DATE to get a proper date. Unlike a recursive CTE, GENERATE_SERIES is a single function call with no recursion limit concerns. The spine → LEFT JOIN → COALESCE pattern guarantees every day in the range has a row, making downstream time-series charts gap-free. EXTRACT(ISODOW ...) uses the ISO standard where Monday = 1 and Sunday = 7, so Saturday = 6 and Sunday = 7 means >= 6 correctly identifies weekends.

title: Per-user revenue and purchase events without fan-out
description: For each user with at least one completed order, report their total completed-order revenue alongside the number of purchase events they logged. The two metrics must be computed independently — joining orders directly to events would multiply every order against every event for that user, inflating both counts. Output columns: user_id, total_revenue, purchase_events. Order by total_revenue descending, user_id ascending; limit to the top 10.
expected_query:
WITH user_revenue AS (
    SELECT user_id, SUM(net_amount) AS total_revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY user_id
),
user_purchases AS (
    SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS purchase_events
    FROM events
    WHERE event_name = 'purchase'
    GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT ur.user_id, ur.total_revenue, COALESCE(up.purchase_events, 0) AS purchase_events
FROM user_revenue ur
LEFT JOIN user_purchases up ON ur.user_id = up.user_id
ORDER BY ur.total_revenue DESC, ur.user_id ASC
LIMIT 10
solution_query:
WITH user_revenue AS (
  SELECT user_id,
         SUM(net_amount) AS total_revenue
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY user_id
),
user_purchases AS (
  SELECT user_id,
         COUNT(*) AS purchase_events
  FROM events
  WHERE event_name = 'purchase'
  GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT ur.user_id,
       ur.total_revenue,
       COALESCE(up.purchase_events, 0) AS purchase_events
FROM user_revenue ur
LEFT JOIN user_purchases up ON ur.user_id = up.user_id
ORDER BY ur.total_revenue DESC, ur.user_id ASC
LIMIT 10;
explanation: Joining orders to events directly before aggregating creates a cross between every order row and every event row for the same user. With ~85 events per user on average, this inflates net_amount roughly 85× for each user. The correct architecture is two independent CTEs — one that aggregates revenue at the user grain, one that aggregates event counts at the user grain — then a LEFT JOIN on user_id to combine them. The LEFT JOIN preserves users who have revenue but zero purchase events; COALESCE handles the NULL that arises when no matching event row exists.
hints: When a user has multiple orders and multiple events, joining those tables directly multiplies rows — each order pairs with every event, inflating both metrics. Compute each metric in isolation before combining.
Pre-aggregate both CTEs to the user grain, then join them on user_id; the result is one row per user with both metrics correct.
LEFT JOIN the purchases CTE so users with no purchase events still appear; use COALESCE to substitute 0 for the NULL purchase_events.

title: Top revenue product per brand in last 6 months
description: The merchandising team wants to know which single product drives the most revenue per brand in the last 6 months. Define 'last 6 months' as orders with `order_date >= 2025-07-01`. Write a query that returns `brand`, `product_name`, `revenue_6m` (total `line_amount` for completed orders in that window, rounded to 2 dp), and `brand_rank` (DENSE_RANK within brand by revenue, 1 = highest). Include only rows where `brand_rank = 1`. Order by `brand` ascending.
expected_query:
WITH recent AS (
    SELECT oi.product_id, SUM(oi.line_amount) AS revenue_6m
    FROM order_items oi
    JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
      AND CAST(o.order_date AS DATE) >= DATE '2025-07-01'
    GROUP BY oi.product_id
),
ranked AS (
    SELECT p.brand, p.product_name,
           ROUND(r.revenue_6m, 2) AS revenue_6m,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY p.brand ORDER BY r.revenue_6m DESC) AS brand_rank
    FROM recent r
    JOIN products p ON r.product_id = p.product_id
)
SELECT brand, product_name, revenue_6m, brand_rank
FROM ranked
WHERE brand_rank = 1
ORDER BY brand
solution_query:
WITH recent AS (
    SELECT oi.product_id, SUM(oi.line_amount) AS revenue_6m
    FROM order_items oi
    JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
      AND CAST(o.order_date AS DATE) >= DATE '2025-07-01'
    GROUP BY oi.product_id
),
ranked AS (
    SELECT p.brand, p.product_name,
           ROUND(r.revenue_6m, 2) AS revenue_6m,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY p.brand ORDER BY r.revenue_6m DESC) AS brand_rank
    FROM recent r
    JOIN products p ON r.product_id = p.product_id
)
SELECT brand, product_name, revenue_6m, brand_rank
FROM ranked
WHERE brand_rank = 1
ORDER BY brand;
explanation: First CTE computes product-level revenue within the time window. Second CTE joins to products and applies DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY brand ORDER BY revenue DESC) to rank products within each brand. WHERE brand_rank = 1 keeps only the top product per brand — DENSE_RANK handles ties by giving tied products the same rank (both would appear at rank 1).
hints: Each product's total revenue must be computed first — you cannot determine position within a brand group until you have the per-product totals to compare.
DENSE_RANK means two products with equal revenue both get rank 1 — they both appear in the output.

title: Per-user payment vs order net amount reconciliation
description: Finance suspects some users have paid more or less than their completed order totals. Write a query that returns `user_id`, `order_net_sum` (sum of `net_amount` from completed orders, rounded to 2 dp), `payment_sum` (sum of `amount` from paid payments linked to those orders, rounded to 2 dp — use 0 if no paid payments exist), and `discrepancy` (absolute difference between the two, rounded to 2 dp). Include only users where `discrepancy > 1`. Order by `discrepancy` descending. Limit to 20 rows.
expected_query:
WITH order_totals AS (
    SELECT user_id, SUM(net_amount) AS order_net_sum
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY user_id
),
payment_totals AS (
    SELECT o.user_id, SUM(p.amount) AS payment_sum
    FROM payments p
    JOIN orders o ON p.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE p.status = 'paid'
    GROUP BY o.user_id
)
SELECT ot.user_id,
       ROUND(ot.order_net_sum, 2) AS order_net_sum,
       ROUND(COALESCE(pt.payment_sum, 0), 2) AS payment_sum,
       ROUND(ABS(ot.order_net_sum - COALESCE(pt.payment_sum, 0)), 2) AS discrepancy
FROM order_totals ot
LEFT JOIN payment_totals pt ON ot.user_id = pt.user_id
WHERE ABS(ot.order_net_sum - COALESCE(pt.payment_sum, 0)) > 1
ORDER BY discrepancy DESC
LIMIT 20
solution_query:
WITH order_totals AS (
    SELECT user_id, SUM(net_amount) AS order_net_sum
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY user_id
),
payment_totals AS (
    SELECT o.user_id, SUM(p.amount) AS payment_sum
    FROM payments p
    JOIN orders o ON p.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE p.status = 'paid'
    GROUP BY o.user_id
)
SELECT ot.user_id,
       ROUND(ot.order_net_sum, 2) AS order_net_sum,
       ROUND(COALESCE(pt.payment_sum, 0), 2) AS payment_sum,
       ROUND(ABS(ot.order_net_sum - COALESCE(pt.payment_sum, 0)), 2) AS discrepancy
FROM order_totals ot
LEFT JOIN payment_totals pt ON ot.user_id = pt.user_id
WHERE ABS(ot.order_net_sum - COALESCE(pt.payment_sum, 0)) > 1
ORDER BY discrepancy DESC
LIMIT 20;
explanation: Two CTEs compute independent totals: order_totals aggregates completed order net_amounts; payment_totals joins payments to orders to get user_id, then sums paid amounts. A LEFT JOIN from order_totals to payment_totals preserves users with no paid payments (COALESCE turns their NULL to 0). The discrepancy uses ABS() so over- and under-payment are both surfaced. WHERE discrepancy > 1 uses a tolerance of ¤1 to ignore floating-point rounding.
hints: When reconciling two tables, keep each one intact until you are ready to compare — silently dropping rows that exist in one but not the other would hide the discrepancies you are trying to surface.
COALESCE(payment_sum, 0) handles users who have completed orders but no paid payments.

title: Users with 3 consecutive months of declining average order value
description: The customer success team wants to flag users whose purchase behaviour is deteriorating. Write a query that finds users who have at least one run of three of their consecutive ORDERING months (three successive months in which they placed completed orders) where the average completed order value strictly decreased each step (month N < month N-1 < month N-2). These three months need not be calendar-adjacent — gaps between ordering months are ignored; only the succession of months with orders matters. Return `user_id` and `name` for each qualifying user (no duplicates). Order by `user_id` ascending.
expected_query:
WITH monthly_aov AS (
    SELECT u.user_id, u.name,
           strftime(CAST(o.order_date AS DATE), '%Y-%m') AS order_month,
           ROUND(AVG(o.net_amount), 2) AS avg_order_value
    FROM users u
    JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY u.user_id, u.name, order_month
),
lagged AS (
    SELECT user_id, name, order_month, avg_order_value,
           LAG(avg_order_value, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY order_month) AS prev_aov,
           LAG(avg_order_value, 2) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY order_month) AS prev2_aov
    FROM monthly_aov
)
SELECT DISTINCT user_id, name
FROM lagged
WHERE avg_order_value < prev_aov
  AND prev_aov < prev2_aov
  AND prev2_aov IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY user_id
solution_query:
WITH monthly_aov AS (
    SELECT u.user_id, u.name,
           strftime(CAST(o.order_date AS DATE), '%Y-%m') AS order_month,
           ROUND(AVG(o.net_amount), 2) AS avg_order_value
    FROM users u
    JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY u.user_id, u.name, order_month
),
lagged AS (
    SELECT user_id, name, order_month, avg_order_value,
           LAG(avg_order_value, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY order_month) AS prev_aov,
           LAG(avg_order_value, 2) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY order_month) AS prev2_aov
    FROM monthly_aov
)
SELECT DISTINCT user_id, name
FROM lagged
WHERE avg_order_value < prev_aov
  AND prev_aov < prev2_aov
  AND prev2_aov IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY user_id;
explanation: The first CTE computes per-user per-month average order value. The second applies LAG(1) and LAG(2) partitioned by user_id and ordered by month to bring in the prior two months' AOVs alongside the current. The WHERE checks all three descend: current < prev < prev2. The IS NOT NULL guard ensures we have at least 3 months of history. DISTINCT removes users who appear multiple times if they have multiple qualifying windows.
hints: Detecting three consecutive declining months requires comparing each month against the two prior months in the same row — think about how to pull those prior values alongside the current row.
Add IS NOT NULL on prev2_aov to ensure 3 months of history exist — otherwise the first two months will always pass the condition vacuously.

title: Completed orders with no paid payment on record
description: The payments integrity team wants to find completed orders that have no associated paid payment — a potential data quality issue. Write a query on `orders` and `payments` that returns `order_id`, `user_id`, `order_date` (as a DATE), `net_amount`, `payment_status` (from orders), `payment_attempts` (total payment rows for the order), and `paid_payments` (count of rows with payment status = 'paid'). Include only completed orders where `paid_payments = 0`. Order by `order_date` descending. Limit to 20 rows.
expected_query:
SELECT o.order_id, o.user_id, CAST(o.order_date AS DATE) AS order_date,
       o.net_amount, o.payment_status,
       COUNT(p.payment_id) AS payment_attempts,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN p.status = 'paid' THEN 1 END) AS paid_payments
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN payments p ON o.order_id = p.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY o.order_id, o.user_id, order_date, o.net_amount, o.payment_status
HAVING COUNT(CASE WHEN p.status = 'paid' THEN 1 END) = 0
ORDER BY order_date DESC
LIMIT 20
solution_query:
SELECT o.order_id, o.user_id, CAST(o.order_date AS DATE) AS order_date,
       o.net_amount, o.payment_status,
       COUNT(p.payment_id) AS payment_attempts,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN p.status = 'paid' THEN 1 END) AS paid_payments
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN payments p ON o.order_id = p.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY o.order_id, o.user_id, order_date, o.net_amount, o.payment_status
HAVING COUNT(CASE WHEN p.status = 'paid' THEN 1 END) = 0
ORDER BY order_date DESC
LIMIT 20;
explanation: LEFT JOIN retains orders even when there are no payment rows. COUNT(payment_id) counts all payment attempts (0 when no rows joined). COUNT(CASE WHEN status='paid') counts successful ones. HAVING keeps only orders where the paid count is zero — meaning completed orders that never got a paid payment. This is a classic data integrity check: status fields in one table contradicted by absence of evidence in another.
hints: Finding records that are absent in another table requires an approach that explicitly surfaces the non-matching case — not one that silently drops those rows.
HAVING COUNT(CASE WHEN p.status = 'paid' THEN 1 END) = 0 filters after aggregation — it can't go in WHERE because it depends on the aggregate.

title: Monthly user activity segments: new, retained, returned
description: The growth team tracks three user types each month, based on active months derived from the orders table (any order placed in that month, any status). For each user: 'new' is their first-ever active month; 'retained' means their previous active month was 60 days or fewer before this one (gap ≤ 60 days); 'returned' means their previous active month was more than 60 days ago. Output columns: active_month (YYYY-MM string), user_type ('new' / 'retained' / 'returned'), user_count. Order by active_month ascending, then user_type ascending.
expected_query:
WITH user_months AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT user_id,
           strftime(CAST(order_date AS DATE), '%Y-%m') AS active_month
    FROM orders
),
with_prev AS (
    SELECT user_id, active_month,
           LAG(active_month) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY active_month) AS prev_month
    FROM user_months
),
first_ever AS (
    SELECT user_id, MIN(active_month) AS first_month FROM user_months GROUP BY user_id
),
classified AS (
    SELECT w.user_id, w.active_month,
           CASE
               WHEN w.active_month = fe.first_month THEN 'new'
               WHEN w.prev_month IS NULL OR
                    (CAST(w.active_month || '-01' AS DATE) - CAST(w.prev_month || '-01' AS DATE)) > 60
                    THEN 'returned'
               ELSE 'retained'
           END AS user_type
    FROM with_prev w
    JOIN first_ever fe ON w.user_id = fe.user_id
)
SELECT active_month, user_type,
       COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS user_count
FROM classified
GROUP BY active_month, user_type
ORDER BY active_month, user_type
solution_query:
WITH user_months AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT user_id,
           strftime(CAST(order_date AS DATE), '%Y-%m') AS active_month
    FROM orders
),
with_prev AS (
    SELECT user_id, active_month,
           LAG(active_month) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY active_month) AS prev_month
    FROM user_months
),
first_ever AS (
    SELECT user_id, MIN(active_month) AS first_month FROM user_months GROUP BY user_id
),
classified AS (
    SELECT w.user_id, w.active_month,
           CASE
               WHEN w.active_month = fe.first_month THEN 'new'
               WHEN w.prev_month IS NULL OR
                    (CAST(w.active_month || '-01' AS DATE) - CAST(w.prev_month || '-01' AS DATE)) > 60
                    THEN 'returned'
               ELSE 'retained'
           END AS user_type
    FROM with_prev w
    JOIN first_ever fe ON w.user_id = fe.user_id
)
SELECT active_month, user_type,
       COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS user_count
FROM classified
GROUP BY active_month, user_type
ORDER BY active_month, user_type;
explanation: Four CTEs build up the classification: (1) distinct user-month activity pairs; (2) LAG to get each user's previous active month; (3) MIN month per user (to detect 'new'); (4) CASE to assign user_type based on whether it's their first month, whether prev_month is absent or > 60 days ago. Date subtraction (date1 - date2) in DuckDB returns an integer number of days, enabling the 60-day gap check without strftime or epoch conversion.
hints: To classify each month's activity as new, retained, or returned, you need to know whether the user was active in the prior month — consider how to look back one row within each user's ordered timeline.
A user with NULL prev_month who is not in their first_month is a returning user — their activity gap extends back before your data window.

title: 30-day rolling GMV with day-over-day growth rate
description: Finance wants a daily GMV (gross merchandise value = sum of `gross_amount` from all orders regardless of status) with a 30-day rolling total and day-over-day growth percentage. Write a query that returns `order_day` (DATE), `daily_gmv` (rounded to 2 dp), `rolling_30d_gmv` (sum of daily_gmv over the 30-row window ending on the current day, rounded to 2 dp), and `dod_growth_pct` (percentage change from the previous day's daily_gmv, rounded to 2 dp; NULL when there is no prior day). Order by `order_day` ascending.
expected_query:
WITH daily AS (
    SELECT CAST(order_date AS DATE) AS order_day,
           ROUND(SUM(gross_amount), 2) AS daily_gmv
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY order_day
),
with_rolling AS (
    SELECT order_day,
           daily_gmv,
           ROUND(SUM(daily_gmv) OVER (
               ORDER BY order_day
               ROWS BETWEEN 29 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
           ), 2) AS rolling_30d_gmv,
           LAG(daily_gmv) OVER (ORDER BY order_day) AS prev_day_gmv
    FROM daily
)
SELECT order_day,
       daily_gmv,
       rolling_30d_gmv,
       CASE
           WHEN prev_day_gmv IS NULL OR prev_day_gmv = 0 THEN NULL
           ELSE ROUND((daily_gmv - prev_day_gmv) * 100.0 / prev_day_gmv, 2)
       END AS dod_growth_pct
FROM with_rolling
ORDER BY order_day
solution_query:
WITH daily AS (
    SELECT CAST(order_date AS DATE) AS order_day,
           ROUND(SUM(gross_amount), 2) AS daily_gmv
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY order_day
),
with_rolling AS (
    SELECT order_day,
           daily_gmv,
           ROUND(SUM(daily_gmv) OVER (
               ORDER BY order_day
               ROWS BETWEEN 29 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
           ), 2) AS rolling_30d_gmv,
           LAG(daily_gmv) OVER (ORDER BY order_day) AS prev_day_gmv
    FROM daily
)
SELECT order_day,
       daily_gmv,
       rolling_30d_gmv,
       CASE
           WHEN prev_day_gmv IS NULL OR prev_day_gmv = 0 THEN NULL
           ELSE ROUND((daily_gmv - prev_day_gmv) * 100.0 / prev_day_gmv, 2)
       END AS dod_growth_pct
FROM with_rolling
ORDER BY order_day;
explanation: Two window functions in the second CTE: SUM OVER with ROWS BETWEEN 29 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW for the 30-day rolling total (29 preceding + current = 30 rows), and LAG(1) for the previous day's GMV. The CASE in the final SELECT handles both NULL (no prior day) and zero (division-by-zero) guards for the growth percentage. gross_amount includes all orders — the problem says regardless of status, so no WHERE filter on status.
hints: ROWS BETWEEN 29 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW gives a 30-row window — 29 before plus the current row.
Guard the growth rate with CASE WHEN prev_day_gmv IS NULL OR prev_day_gmv = 0 THEN NULL to avoid division errors on the first day or zero-GMV days.

title: Q1 2024 purchasers who did not return in Q2 2024
description: The retention team wants to measure Q1-to-Q2 churn: users who placed at least one order in Q1 2024 (January–March) but placed no order in Q2 2024 (April–June). Write a query using EXCEPT (or equivalent) that returns `user_id`, `name`, `country`, and `acquisition_channel` for all such users. Order by `user_id` ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT u.user_id, u.name, u.country, u.acquisition_channel
FROM users u
WHERE u.user_id IN (
    SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM orders
    WHERE strftime(CAST(order_date AS DATE), '%Y') = '2024'
      AND strftime(CAST(order_date AS DATE), '%m') IN ('01','02','03')
    EXCEPT
    SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM orders
    WHERE strftime(CAST(order_date AS DATE), '%Y') = '2024'
      AND strftime(CAST(order_date AS DATE), '%m') IN ('04','05','06')
)
ORDER BY u.user_id
solution_query:
SELECT u.user_id, u.name, u.country, u.acquisition_channel
FROM users u
WHERE u.user_id IN (
    SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM orders
    WHERE strftime(CAST(order_date AS DATE), '%Y') = '2024'
      AND strftime(CAST(order_date AS DATE), '%m') IN ('01','02','03')
    EXCEPT
    SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM orders
    WHERE strftime(CAST(order_date AS DATE), '%Y') = '2024'
      AND strftime(CAST(order_date AS DATE), '%m') IN ('04','05','06')
)
ORDER BY u.user_id;
explanation: EXCEPT removes from the Q1 user set any user_id also present in the Q2 user set — exactly the definition of 'ordered in Q1 but not Q2'. The result is used as a subquery filter to pull user metadata. This is cleaner than a NOT IN / NOT EXISTS with a multi-condition subquery and directly expresses the business intent as a set difference.
hints: EXCEPT subtracts the second set from the first — Q1 users EXCEPT Q2 users gives users who churned after Q1.
Wrap the EXCEPT in IN (...) to join back to the users table for name, country, and acquisition_channel.

title: Products purchased by more than the median number of distinct buyers
description: The catalogue team wants to identify broadly popular products — those bought by more distinct users than the median across all products. Write a query that returns `product_name`, `brand`, `distinct_buyers` (count of distinct user_ids who completed at least one order containing this product), and `median_buyers` (the 50th percentile distinct buyer count across all products, rounded to 1 dp). Include only products where `distinct_buyers` strictly exceeds `median_buyers`. Order by `distinct_buyers` descending.
expected_query:
WITH product_buyer_counts AS (
    SELECT oi.product_id,
           COUNT(DISTINCT o.user_id) AS distinct_buyers
    FROM order_items oi
    JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY oi.product_id
),
median_val AS (
    SELECT PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY distinct_buyers) AS median_buyers
    FROM product_buyer_counts
)
SELECT p.product_name, p.brand, pbc.distinct_buyers,
       ROUND(mv.median_buyers, 1) AS median_buyers
FROM product_buyer_counts pbc
JOIN products p ON pbc.product_id = p.product_id
JOIN median_val mv ON 1=1
WHERE pbc.distinct_buyers > mv.median_buyers
ORDER BY pbc.distinct_buyers DESC
solution_query:
WITH product_buyer_counts AS (
    SELECT oi.product_id,
           COUNT(DISTINCT o.user_id) AS distinct_buyers
    FROM order_items oi
    JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY oi.product_id
),
median_val AS (
    SELECT PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY distinct_buyers) AS median_buyers
    FROM product_buyer_counts
)
SELECT p.product_name, p.brand, pbc.distinct_buyers,
       ROUND(mv.median_buyers, 1) AS median_buyers
FROM product_buyer_counts pbc
JOIN products p ON pbc.product_id = p.product_id
JOIN median_val mv ON 1=1
WHERE pbc.distinct_buyers > mv.median_buyers
ORDER BY pbc.distinct_buyers DESC;
explanation: PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY distinct_buyers) computes the median across all product buyer counts. CROSS JOIN attaches this single value to every product row. The WHERE clause then filters to products exceeding it. This is a scalar subquery pattern — CROSS JOIN a one-row CTE is equivalent to a scalar subquery in the WHERE clause but makes the median visible in the output.
hints: The comparison requires a single benchmark value — the median buyer count across all products. SQL has an ordered-set aggregate function that computes this directly.
CROSS JOIN the median CTE (one row) so you can reference it in both SELECT and WHERE without repeating the subquery.

title: Session-to-purchase conversion rate by traffic source (24-hour window)
description: Marketing wants to know which traffic sources drive sessions that actually lead to a completed purchase within 24 hours. Write a query that returns `traffic_source`, `total_sessions`, `converted_sessions` (sessions followed by at least one completed order for the same user within 24 hours of `session_start`), and `conversion_rate_pct` (converted / total × 100, rounded to 1 dp). Order by `conversion_rate_pct` descending.
expected_query:
WITH session_purchases AS (
    SELECT s.session_id
    FROM sessions s
    JOIN orders o ON s.user_id = o.user_id
      AND o.status = 'completed'
      AND CAST(o.order_date AS TIMESTAMP) >= s.session_start
      AND CAST(o.order_date AS TIMESTAMP) <= s.session_start + INTERVAL 24 HOUR
    GROUP BY s.session_id
)
SELECT s.traffic_source,
       COUNT(DISTINCT s.session_id) AS total_sessions,
       COUNT(DISTINCT sp.session_id) AS converted_sessions,
       ROUND(COUNT(DISTINCT sp.session_id) * 100.0 / COUNT(DISTINCT s.session_id), 1) AS conversion_rate_pct
FROM sessions s
LEFT JOIN session_purchases sp ON s.session_id = sp.session_id
GROUP BY s.traffic_source
ORDER BY conversion_rate_pct DESC
solution_query:
WITH session_purchases AS (
    SELECT s.session_id
    FROM sessions s
    JOIN orders o ON s.user_id = o.user_id
      AND o.status = 'completed'
      AND CAST(o.order_date AS TIMESTAMP) >= s.session_start
      AND CAST(o.order_date AS TIMESTAMP) <= s.session_start + INTERVAL 24 HOUR
    GROUP BY s.session_id
)
SELECT s.traffic_source,
       COUNT(DISTINCT s.session_id) AS total_sessions,
       COUNT(DISTINCT sp.session_id) AS converted_sessions,
       ROUND(COUNT(DISTINCT sp.session_id) * 100.0 / COUNT(DISTINCT s.session_id), 1) AS conversion_rate_pct
FROM sessions s
LEFT JOIN session_purchases sp ON s.session_id = sp.session_id
GROUP BY s.traffic_source
ORDER BY conversion_rate_pct DESC;
explanation: The CTE finds sessions with at least one completed order within 24 hours by joining on user_id with a time-range condition on order_date (cast to TIMESTAMP to match session_start type). GROUP BY session_id deduplicates so each session appears once. The main query LEFT JOINs sessions to session_purchases so unconverted sessions still count in total_sessions. Conversion rate uses COUNT(DISTINCT sp.session_id) which is 0 when sp.session_id is NULL.
hints: Linking a session to an order requires more than the same user — the order must also fall within a specific time window after the session started.
GROUP BY session_id in the CTE deduplicates — a session is either converted or not, regardless of how many orders the user placed.

title: High-value power users: 5+ orders by plan tier
description: The VIP programme team wants to understand how many high-value customers (users with 5 or more completed orders) exist in each plan tier and what their revenue profile looks like. Write a query that returns `plan_tier`, `user_count`, `avg_orders` (average order count per power user, rounded to 1 dp), `avg_lifetime_spend` (average total spend per power user, rounded to 2 dp), and `segment_revenue` (total spend from all power users in that tier, rounded to 2 dp). Order by `segment_revenue` descending.
expected_query:
WITH power_users AS (
    SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count,
           ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS total_spend
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY user_id
    HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5
)
SELECT u.plan_tier,
       COUNT(DISTINCT pu.user_id) AS user_count,
       ROUND(AVG(pu.order_count), 1) AS avg_orders,
       ROUND(AVG(pu.total_spend), 2) AS avg_lifetime_spend,
       ROUND(SUM(pu.total_spend), 2) AS segment_revenue
FROM power_users pu
JOIN users u ON pu.user_id = u.user_id
GROUP BY u.plan_tier
ORDER BY segment_revenue DESC
solution_query:
WITH power_users AS (
    SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count,
           ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS total_spend
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY user_id
    HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5
)
SELECT u.plan_tier,
       COUNT(DISTINCT pu.user_id) AS user_count,
       ROUND(AVG(pu.order_count), 1) AS avg_orders,
       ROUND(AVG(pu.total_spend), 2) AS avg_lifetime_spend,
       ROUND(SUM(pu.total_spend), 2) AS segment_revenue
FROM power_users pu
JOIN users u ON pu.user_id = u.user_id
GROUP BY u.plan_tier
ORDER BY segment_revenue DESC;
explanation: The CTE uses HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5 to pre-filter to power users — these users are a small subset of the full user base. The main query then joins to users for plan_tier and aggregates at the tier level. avg_orders averages per-user order counts (not total orders / users — that would be the same thing here, but the CTE makes it explicit). segment_revenue is the cohort's total spend, a useful size signal.
hints: Isolate the qualifying users before computing per-tier counts — pre-filtering to the target population keeps the final aggregation clean.
avg_orders averages the per-user order count from the CTE — not raw COUNT(*) in the outer GROUP BY.

title: Top spending category shift from Q1 to Q2 2024
description: The product team wants to identify users who changed their top spending category between Q1 2024 (Jan–Mar) and Q2 2024 (Apr–Jun) — a sign of evolving preferences or seasonal effects. Count only completed orders when computing category spend. Write a query that returns `user_id`, `q1_category` (top spending category in Q1 among completed orders), and `q2_category` (top spending category in Q2 among completed orders) for users who: had a clear top category in both quarters AND whose top category changed between the two quarters. Order by `user_id` ascending. If two categories tie for the top in a quarter, pick the one that comes first alphabetically.
expected_query:
WITH category_spend AS (
    SELECT o.user_id,
           c.category_name,
           CASE
               WHEN strftime(CAST(o.order_date AS DATE), '%m') IN ('01','02','03') THEN 'Q1'
               WHEN strftime(CAST(o.order_date AS DATE), '%m') IN ('04','05','06') THEN 'Q2'
           END AS quarter,
           SUM(oi.line_amount) AS spend
    FROM orders o
    JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
    JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
    JOIN categories c ON p.category_id = c.category_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
      AND strftime(CAST(o.order_date AS DATE), '%Y') = '2024'
      AND strftime(CAST(o.order_date AS DATE), '%m') IN ('01','02','03','04','05','06')
    GROUP BY o.user_id, c.category_name, quarter
),
top_per_user_quarter AS (
    SELECT user_id, quarter, category_name,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY user_id, quarter
               ORDER BY spend DESC, category_name ASC
           ) AS rnk
    FROM category_spend
),
q1_top AS (
    SELECT user_id, category_name AS q1_category
    FROM top_per_user_quarter WHERE quarter = 'Q1' AND rnk = 1
),
q2_top AS (
    SELECT user_id, category_name AS q2_category
    FROM top_per_user_quarter WHERE quarter = 'Q2' AND rnk = 1
)
SELECT q1.user_id, q1.q1_category, q2.q2_category
FROM q1_top q1
JOIN q2_top q2 ON q1.user_id = q2.user_id
WHERE q1.q1_category <> q2.q2_category
ORDER BY q1.user_id
solution_query:
WITH category_spend AS (
    SELECT o.user_id,
           c.category_name,
           CASE
               WHEN strftime(CAST(o.order_date AS DATE), '%m') IN ('01','02','03') THEN 'Q1'
               WHEN strftime(CAST(o.order_date AS DATE), '%m') IN ('04','05','06') THEN 'Q2'
           END AS quarter,
           SUM(oi.line_amount) AS spend
    FROM orders o
    JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
    JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
    JOIN categories c ON p.category_id = c.category_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
      AND strftime(CAST(o.order_date AS DATE), '%Y') = '2024'
      AND strftime(CAST(o.order_date AS DATE), '%m') IN ('01','02','03','04','05','06')
    GROUP BY o.user_id, c.category_name, quarter
),
top_per_user_quarter AS (
    SELECT user_id, quarter, category_name,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY user_id, quarter
               ORDER BY spend DESC, category_name ASC
           ) AS rnk
    FROM category_spend
),
q1_top AS (
    SELECT user_id, category_name AS q1_category
    FROM top_per_user_quarter WHERE quarter = 'Q1' AND rnk = 1
),
q2_top AS (
    SELECT user_id, category_name AS q2_category
    FROM top_per_user_quarter WHERE quarter = 'Q2' AND rnk = 1
)
SELECT q1.user_id, q1.q1_category, q2.q2_category
FROM q1_top q1
JOIN q2_top q2 ON q1.user_id = q2.user_id
WHERE q1.q1_category <> q2.q2_category
ORDER BY q1.user_id;
explanation: Four CTEs build up the answer: (1) per-user-category-quarter spend via a 4-table join; (2) ROW_NUMBER() within each user-quarter by spend DESC, category_name ASC (alphabetical tie-breaking) to assign rank; (3 & 4) extract rank-1 category for Q1 and Q2. The final JOIN keeps only users present in both quarters, and WHERE ... <> filters to those who shifted categories. ROW_NUMBER() (not DENSE_RANK) ensures exactly one winner per user-quarter.
hints: When ranking to select exactly one winner per group, consider whether ties should both make the cut or only one should — that choice determines which ranking approach is correct.
Add category_name ASC as a secondary sort in the window function to break ties deterministically — the question says 'alphabetically first'.

title: Users reactivated after a 90+ day order gap
description: The re-engagement team tracks users who lapsed and came back. A reactivation event occurs when a user places an order at least 90 days after their previous order. Write a query that returns `user_id`, `name`, `acquisition_channel`, `last_order_before_gap` (the order_date before the gap, as a DATE), `reactivation_date` (the order_date when they returned, as a DATE), and `days_gap` (integer days between the two dates). Include all reactivation events (a user may have multiple). Order by `days_gap` descending, then `user_id` ascending. Limit to 20 rows.
expected_query:
WITH user_orders AS (
    SELECT user_id, CAST(order_date AS DATE) AS order_day
    FROM orders
),
with_next AS (
    SELECT user_id, order_day,
           LEAD(order_day) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY order_day) AS next_order_day
    FROM user_orders
)
SELECT DISTINCT w.user_id, u.name, u.acquisition_channel,
       w.order_day AS last_order_before_gap,
       w.next_order_day AS reactivation_date,
       (w.next_order_day - w.order_day) AS days_gap
FROM with_next w
JOIN users u ON w.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE w.next_order_day IS NOT NULL
  AND (w.next_order_day - w.order_day) >= 90
ORDER BY days_gap DESC, w.user_id
LIMIT 20
solution_query:
WITH user_orders AS (
    SELECT user_id, CAST(order_date AS DATE) AS order_day
    FROM orders
),
with_next AS (
    SELECT user_id, order_day,
           LEAD(order_day) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY order_day) AS next_order_day
    FROM user_orders
)
SELECT DISTINCT w.user_id, u.name, u.acquisition_channel,
       w.order_day AS last_order_before_gap,
       w.next_order_day AS reactivation_date,
       (w.next_order_day - w.order_day) AS days_gap
FROM with_next w
JOIN users u ON w.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE w.next_order_day IS NOT NULL
  AND (w.next_order_day - w.order_day) >= 90
ORDER BY days_gap DESC, w.user_id
LIMIT 20;
explanation: LEAD(order_day) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY order_day) attaches the NEXT order date alongside the current one in the same row. Subtracting DATEs in DuckDB returns an integer (days). The WHERE filters to gaps >= 90 days and excludes the last order per user (where LEAD returns NULL). The DISTINCT isn't strictly needed if each (user_id, order_day) pair is unique, but it protects against duplicate orders on the same day.
hints: To detect reactivation, you need to compare each order's date against the next order for that user — look forward in the user's ordered sequence, not backward.
DATE subtraction in DuckDB returns an integer (number of days), so (next_order_day - order_day) >= 90 works directly.

title: Support ticket resolution performance by country and plan tier
description: The customer experience team wants to know where ticket volume and resolution speed differ across country-plan combinations. Write a query that returns `country`, `plan_tier`, `users_with_tickets` (distinct user count who filed at least one ticket), `total_tickets`, and `avg_resolution_hours` (average resolution time across all tickets for that segment, rounded to 1 dp). Include only country-plan combinations where `total_tickets >= 5`. Order by `avg_resolution_hours` descending.
expected_query:
SELECT u.country, u.plan_tier,
       COUNT(DISTINCT u.user_id) AS users_with_tickets,
       COUNT(t.ticket_id) AS total_tickets,
       ROUND(AVG(t.resolution_hours), 1) AS avg_resolution_hours
FROM users u
JOIN support_tickets t ON u.user_id = t.user_id
GROUP BY u.country, u.plan_tier
HAVING COUNT(t.ticket_id) >= 5
ORDER BY avg_resolution_hours DESC
solution_query:
SELECT u.country, u.plan_tier,
       COUNT(DISTINCT u.user_id) AS users_with_tickets,
       COUNT(t.ticket_id) AS total_tickets,
       ROUND(AVG(t.resolution_hours), 1) AS avg_resolution_hours
FROM users u
JOIN support_tickets t ON u.user_id = t.user_id
GROUP BY u.country, u.plan_tier
HAVING COUNT(t.ticket_id) >= 5
ORDER BY avg_resolution_hours DESC;
explanation: Joining users to support_tickets links the demographic dimensions (country, plan_tier) to the operational metric (resolution_hours). COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) counts unique users — one user can file multiple tickets. HAVING COUNT(ticket_id) >= 5 removes thin segments where averages are unstable. avg_resolution_hours includes NULL values in the AVG denominator reduction — tickets with no resolution_hours are excluded from the average by SQL's default NULL handling in AVG.
hints: The metric is the number of users who filed tickets, not the number of tickets — a user who filed multiple tickets should count once.
HAVING filters on total ticket count after grouping — it belongs after GROUP BY, not in WHERE.

title: Viewed but never purchased products
description: The catalogue team wants to identify products that users viewed (event_name = 'view_product') but that were never purchased in any completed order. Write a query that returns `product_id`, `product_name`, `brand`, `price`, and `category_name` for all such products. Order by `price` descending.
expected_query:
WITH viewed_products AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT product_id
    FROM events
    WHERE event_name = 'view_product'
),
purchased_products AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT oi.product_id
    FROM order_items oi
    JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
)
SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name, p.brand, p.price, c.category_name
FROM viewed_products vp
JOIN products p ON vp.product_id = p.product_id
JOIN categories c ON p.category_id = c.category_id
WHERE vp.product_id NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM purchased_products)
ORDER BY p.price DESC
solution_query:
WITH viewed_products AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT product_id
    FROM events
    WHERE event_name = 'view_product'
),
purchased_products AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT oi.product_id
    FROM order_items oi
    JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
)
SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name, p.brand, p.price, c.category_name
FROM viewed_products vp
JOIN products p ON vp.product_id = p.product_id
JOIN categories c ON p.category_id = c.category_id
WHERE vp.product_id NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM purchased_products)
ORDER BY p.price DESC;
explanation: Two CTEs define the two product sets: viewed (via events) and purchased (via order_items + orders). The NOT IN subquery filters to viewed products not in the purchased set — this is the set difference pattern. Starting from viewed_products in the FROM clause means the base set is already scoped to products users were interested in. High-price items that were never bought despite being viewed are high-priority catalogue issues.
hints: Build two CTEs — one for viewed product IDs, one for purchased product IDs — then filter the first set using NOT IN.
Join to products and categories after the NOT IN filter to enrich the output without affecting the set logic.

title: Acquisition channel lifetime value: paying vs all users
description: The growth team wants to compare LTV (lifetime value = sum of completed order net_amounts) across acquisition channels, distinguishing between paying users and the broader user base. Write a query that returns `acquisition_channel`, `total_users` (all users from that channel), `paying_users` (users with at least one completed order), `avg_ltv_paying` (average LTV among paying users only, rounded to 2 dp), and `avg_ltv_all` (total channel LTV divided by total channel users — includes non-paying users in denominator — rounded to 2 dp). Order by `avg_ltv_paying` descending.
expected_query:
WITH user_ltv AS (
    SELECT u.user_id, u.acquisition_channel,
           COALESCE(SUM(o.net_amount), 0) AS lifetime_value
    FROM users u
    LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id AND o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY u.user_id, u.acquisition_channel
)
SELECT acquisition_channel,
       COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS total_users,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN lifetime_value > 0 THEN user_id END) AS paying_users,
       ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN lifetime_value > 0 THEN lifetime_value END), 2) AS avg_ltv_paying,
       ROUND(SUM(lifetime_value) / COUNT(DISTINCT user_id), 2) AS avg_ltv_all
FROM user_ltv
GROUP BY acquisition_channel
ORDER BY avg_ltv_paying DESC
solution_query:
WITH user_ltv AS (
    SELECT u.user_id, u.acquisition_channel,
           COALESCE(SUM(o.net_amount), 0) AS lifetime_value
    FROM users u
    LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id AND o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY u.user_id, u.acquisition_channel
)
SELECT acquisition_channel,
       COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS total_users,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN lifetime_value > 0 THEN user_id END) AS paying_users,
       ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN lifetime_value > 0 THEN lifetime_value END), 2) AS avg_ltv_paying,
       ROUND(SUM(lifetime_value) / COUNT(DISTINCT user_id), 2) AS avg_ltv_all
FROM user_ltv
GROUP BY acquisition_channel
ORDER BY avg_ltv_paying DESC;
explanation: The CTE computes per-user LTV using LEFT JOIN so users with no orders get 0 (via COALESCE). The main query then computes two averages: avg_ltv_paying uses CASE WHEN lifetime_value > 0 inside AVG — SQL's NULL handling means 0-LTV users are excluded from AVG automatically since they're filtered by the CASE. avg_ltv_all divides total revenue by all users (the 'blended' LTV used in growth modelling). These two denominators tell different stories about channel quality.
hints: Your denominator includes all users who signed up through each channel, not just those who made a purchase — the combination must preserve non-buyers so they contribute to the channel count.
avg_ltv_paying uses CASE WHEN lifetime_value > 0 THEN lifetime_value END inside AVG — CASE returns NULL for 0-LTV users, and SQL's AVG automatically excludes NULLs.

title: 7-day signup-to-first-purchase conversion by cohort month
description: The growth team tracks how quickly new users convert. Write a query that groups users by `signup_month` (YYYY-MM from `signup_date`) and returns `signup_month`, `cohort_size` (users in that signup month), `converted_7d` (users who placed their first completed order within 7 days of signup), and `conversion_7d_pct` (converted_7d / cohort_size × 100, rounded to 1 dp). A user converts if their earliest completed order_date minus signup_date is <= 7 days. Order by `signup_month` ascending.
expected_query:
WITH cohort AS (
    SELECT user_id, signup_date
    FROM users
),
first_purchase AS (
    SELECT user_id, MIN(CAST(order_date AS DATE)) AS first_order_date
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT strftime(c.signup_date, '%Y-%m') AS signup_month,
       COUNT(DISTINCT c.user_id) AS cohort_size,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE
           WHEN (fp.first_order_date - c.signup_date) <= 7 THEN c.user_id
       END) AS converted_7d,
       ROUND(COUNT(DISTINCT CASE
           WHEN (fp.first_order_date - c.signup_date) <= 7 THEN c.user_id
       END) * 100.0 / COUNT(DISTINCT c.user_id), 1) AS conversion_7d_pct
FROM cohort c
LEFT JOIN first_purchase fp ON c.user_id = fp.user_id
GROUP BY signup_month
ORDER BY signup_month
solution_query:
WITH cohort AS (
    SELECT user_id, signup_date
    FROM users
),
first_purchase AS (
    SELECT user_id, MIN(CAST(order_date AS DATE)) AS first_order_date
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT strftime(c.signup_date, '%Y-%m') AS signup_month,
       COUNT(DISTINCT c.user_id) AS cohort_size,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE
           WHEN (fp.first_order_date - c.signup_date) <= 7 THEN c.user_id
       END) AS converted_7d,
       ROUND(COUNT(DISTINCT CASE
           WHEN (fp.first_order_date - c.signup_date) <= 7 THEN c.user_id
       END) * 100.0 / COUNT(DISTINCT c.user_id), 1) AS conversion_7d_pct
FROM cohort c
LEFT JOIN first_purchase fp ON c.user_id = fp.user_id
GROUP BY signup_month
ORDER BY signup_month;
explanation: The first CTE holds user signup dates. The second computes each user's first completed purchase date using MIN. The LEFT JOIN retains all users (including those who never purchased). The CASE WHEN checks whether the date gap is <= 7 (DATE subtraction returns integer days in DuckDB). COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) inside the CASE ensures each user is counted once even if the CASE matches multiple times.
hints: Conversion rates require non-converters in the denominator — the approach must keep users who never purchased in the result, not silently exclude them.
DATE subtraction (first_order_date - signup_date) returns an integer in DuckDB — no DATEDIFF needed.

title: Top completed-order product per country by line revenue
description: The regional team wants the single product that generates the most revenue in each country, based on completed orders. Return country, product_name, order_count (distinct completed orders containing that product in that country), and total_revenue (sum of line_amount, rounded to 2 dp). Return exactly one row per country — the top product by total_revenue, breaking ties by product_name ascending. Output columns: country, product_name, order_count, total_revenue. Order by country ascending.
expected_query: WITH cpr AS (SELECT u.country, p.product_name, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS order_count, ROUND(SUM(oi.line_amount), 2) AS total_revenue FROM orders o JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.user_id JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id WHERE o.status = 'completed' GROUP BY u.country, p.product_name), ranked AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY country ORDER BY total_revenue DESC, product_name ASC) AS rn FROM cpr) SELECT country, product_name, order_count, total_revenue FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY country
solution_query: WITH cpr AS (SELECT u.country, p.product_name, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS order_count, ROUND(SUM(oi.line_amount), 2) AS total_revenue FROM orders o JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.user_id JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id WHERE o.status = 'completed' GROUP BY u.country, p.product_name), ranked AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY country ORDER BY total_revenue DESC, product_name ASC) AS rn FROM cpr) SELECT country, product_name, order_count, total_revenue FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY country;
explanation: The query builds country-product revenue aggregates in the cpr CTE, then uses ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY country ORDER BY total_revenue DESC, product_name ASC) to assign rank 1 to the top product in each country. Filtering WHERE rn = 1 returns exactly one row per country. Ties in total_revenue are broken by product_name ASC for deterministic output. COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) avoids inflation when an order contains the same product on multiple line items.
hints: To return a single top product per country, you need to enforce top-N-per-group selection — compute country-product aggregates first, then apply a per-partition selection.
A window function that assigns a sequence number within each country partition, ordered by revenue descending, lets you filter to exactly one row per country.

title: Quantify order-count fan-out from joining order_items
description: After reviewing the product-per-country query, the interviewer asks: 'What goes wrong with order_count if you forget COUNT(DISTINCT) and just use COUNT(*)? Show me the inflation.' Write a query that returns `country`, `order_rows_with_items` (COUNT(*) after joining orders to order_items — i.e., one row per order-item pair), `actual_distinct_orders` (COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)), and `fanout_inflation` (the difference). Include only completed orders. Order by `fanout_inflation` descending.
expected_query:
SELECT u.country,
       COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_rows_with_items,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS actual_distinct_orders,
       COUNT(o.order_id) - COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS fanout_inflation
FROM orders o
JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.user_id
JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY u.country
ORDER BY fanout_inflation DESC
solution_query:
SELECT u.country,
       COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_rows_with_items,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS actual_distinct_orders,
       COUNT(o.order_id) - COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS fanout_inflation
FROM orders o
JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.user_id
JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY u.country
ORDER BY fanout_inflation DESC;
explanation: After joining to order_items, each order appears once per line item — an order with 5 items produces 5 rows. COUNT(*) or COUNT(order_id) counts all those rows, inflating the order count by the average items-per-order. The fanout_inflation column makes this visible. This is the canonical example of the double-counting bug: a JOIN to a child table multiplies parent rows.
hints: After joining orders to order_items, the row count expands — each order appears once per line item. Verify that your count measures orders rather than line items.
The point of this query is to make the bug measurable — showing inflation = COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT) proves you understand the mechanism.

title: Products contributing to the first 80% of completed revenue (Pareto)
description: The product catalogue team applies the Pareto principle: identify the products that collectively generate the first 80% of total completed revenue. Write a query that returns `product_name`, `brand`, `product_revenue` (per-product sum of line_amount for completed orders, rounded to 2 dp), and `cumulative_pct` (running cumulative revenue as a percentage of total, rounded to 2 dp). Include only products where their addition to the running total has not yet crossed the 80% threshold (i.e., the cumulative total before adding this product was still below 80% of total). Order by `product_revenue` descending.
expected_query:
WITH product_revenue AS (
    SELECT oi.product_id, SUM(oi.line_amount) AS revenue
    FROM order_items oi
    JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY oi.product_id
),
total AS (
    SELECT SUM(revenue) AS total_revenue FROM product_revenue
),
running AS (
    SELECT pr.product_id, pr.revenue,
           SUM(pr.revenue) OVER (ORDER BY pr.revenue DESC) AS running_revenue,
           t.total_revenue
    FROM product_revenue pr
    JOIN total t ON 1=1
)
SELECT p.product_name, p.brand,
       ROUND(r.revenue, 2) AS product_revenue,
       ROUND(r.running_revenue * 100.0 / r.total_revenue, 2) AS cumulative_pct
FROM running r
JOIN products p ON r.product_id = p.product_id
WHERE r.running_revenue - r.revenue < r.total_revenue * 0.8
ORDER BY r.revenue DESC
solution_query:
WITH product_revenue AS (
    SELECT oi.product_id, SUM(oi.line_amount) AS revenue
    FROM order_items oi
    JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY oi.product_id
),
total AS (
    SELECT SUM(revenue) AS total_revenue FROM product_revenue
),
running AS (
    SELECT pr.product_id, pr.revenue,
           SUM(pr.revenue) OVER (ORDER BY pr.revenue DESC) AS running_revenue,
           t.total_revenue
    FROM product_revenue pr
    JOIN total t ON 1=1
)
SELECT p.product_name, p.brand,
       ROUND(r.revenue, 2) AS product_revenue,
       ROUND(r.running_revenue * 100.0 / r.total_revenue, 2) AS cumulative_pct
FROM running r
JOIN products p ON r.product_id = p.product_id
WHERE r.running_revenue - r.revenue < r.total_revenue * 0.8
ORDER BY r.revenue DESC;
explanation: Three CTEs: product_revenue aggregates per-product, total computes the grand total, running adds a cumulative sum window. The WHERE condition (running_revenue - revenue < 0.8 × total) includes a product if the cumulative total BEFORE this product was still under 80% — meaning this product's revenue is still 'within' the top 80% contribution group. This includes the product that crosses 80%.
hints: The 80% threshold test should be applied before the current product's revenue is added in — that way you include products that push the running total past the cutoff.
CROSS JOIN a single-row CTE to attach the total revenue scalar to every product row.

title: Session engagement metrics by device and traffic source
description: The product analytics team wants to understand user engagement by session type. Write a query that returns `device_type`, `traffic_source`, `sessions` (total distinct sessions), `avg_events_per_session` (average event count per session, rounded to 1 dp), `bounce_sessions` (sessions with exactly 1 event — 'bounced'), and `converting_sessions` (sessions with at least one 'purchase' event). Order by `avg_events_per_session` descending.
expected_query:
WITH session_stats AS (
    SELECT s.session_id, s.device_type, s.traffic_source,
           COUNT(e.event_id) AS event_count,
           COUNT(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'purchase' THEN 1 END) AS purchases
    FROM sessions s
    LEFT JOIN events e ON s.session_id = e.session_id
    GROUP BY s.session_id, s.device_type, s.traffic_source
)
SELECT device_type, traffic_source,
       COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) AS sessions,
       ROUND(AVG(event_count), 1) AS avg_events_per_session,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN event_count = 1 THEN 1 END) AS bounce_sessions,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN purchases > 0 THEN 1 END) AS converting_sessions
FROM session_stats
GROUP BY device_type, traffic_source
ORDER BY avg_events_per_session DESC
solution_query:
WITH session_stats AS (
    SELECT s.session_id, s.device_type, s.traffic_source,
           COUNT(e.event_id) AS event_count,
           COUNT(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'purchase' THEN 1 END) AS purchases
    FROM sessions s
    LEFT JOIN events e ON s.session_id = e.session_id
    GROUP BY s.session_id, s.device_type, s.traffic_source
)
SELECT device_type, traffic_source,
       COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) AS sessions,
       ROUND(AVG(event_count), 1) AS avg_events_per_session,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN event_count = 1 THEN 1 END) AS bounce_sessions,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN purchases > 0 THEN 1 END) AS converting_sessions
FROM session_stats
GROUP BY device_type, traffic_source
ORDER BY avg_events_per_session DESC;
explanation: Two-level aggregation: CTE aggregates events at the session level (event_count, purchases), then the main query aggregates sessions at the device×source level. LEFT JOIN in the CTE preserves sessions with no events (event_count = 0). The bounce definition (event_count = 1) and conversion definition (purchases > 0) are computed as CASE conditions in the outer GROUP BY.
hints: Aggregate to the session level in a CTE first (event_count, purchase_flag), then aggregate sessions to the device×source level in the outer query.
LEFT JOIN sessions to events so sessions with no events are preserved — they have event_count = 0 and still affect the average.

title: Monthly payment success rate by method with month-over-month change
description: The payments team monitors success rates over time. Write a query that returns `payment_method`, `payment_month` (YYYY-MM from `payment_date`), `total_attempts`, `paid_count` (status = 'paid'), `success_rate_pct` (paid / total × 100, rounded to 1 dp), and `rate_change_pct` (success_rate_pct minus the previous month's success_rate_pct for the same payment_method, rounded to 1 dp; NULL for the first month of each method). Order by `payment_method` ascending, then `payment_month` ascending.
expected_query:
WITH monthly_payments AS (
    SELECT payment_method,
           strftime(payment_date, '%Y-%m') AS payment_month,
           COUNT(*) AS total_attempts,
           COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 END) AS paid_count,
           ROUND(COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 END) * 100.0 / COUNT(*), 1) AS success_rate_pct
    FROM payments
    GROUP BY payment_method, payment_month
)
SELECT payment_method, payment_month, total_attempts, paid_count, success_rate_pct,
       ROUND(success_rate_pct - LAG(success_rate_pct) OVER (
           PARTITION BY payment_method ORDER BY payment_month
       ), 1) AS rate_change_pct
FROM monthly_payments
ORDER BY payment_method, payment_month
solution_query:
WITH monthly_payments AS (
    SELECT payment_method,
           strftime(payment_date, '%Y-%m') AS payment_month,
           COUNT(*) AS total_attempts,
           COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 END) AS paid_count,
           ROUND(COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 END) * 100.0 / COUNT(*), 1) AS success_rate_pct
    FROM payments
    GROUP BY payment_method, payment_month
)
SELECT payment_method, payment_month, total_attempts, paid_count, success_rate_pct,
       ROUND(success_rate_pct - LAG(success_rate_pct) OVER (
           PARTITION BY payment_method ORDER BY payment_month
       ), 1) AS rate_change_pct
FROM monthly_payments
ORDER BY payment_method, payment_month;
explanation: CTE computes monthly aggregates including the success rate. The outer query applies LAG() OVER (PARTITION BY payment_method ORDER BY payment_month) to bring the prior month's rate alongside the current, then subtracts to get the change. PARTITION BY payment_method ensures LAG looks backwards within the same payment method only — without it, the lag would cross method boundaries.
hints: Computing a period-over-period change requires two steps: calculate the per-period metric first, then compare each period to its predecessor in a separate pass.
PARTITION BY payment_method in the LAG window ensures each method's timeline is independent — without it, the lag would cross method boundaries.

title: Average days between orders for repeat buyers
description: The retention team wants to understand repurchase velocity. Write a query that, for each user who has placed at least 3 orders (any status), returns `user_id`, `order_count`, `avg_days_between_orders` (average gap between consecutive orders in days, rounded to 1 dp), `max_gap_days` (longest gap), and `min_gap_days` (shortest gap). Order by `avg_days_between_orders` ascending. Limit to 20 rows.
expected_query:
WITH ordered_orders AS (
    SELECT user_id, CAST(order_date AS DATE) AS order_day,
           LAG(CAST(order_date AS DATE)) OVER (
               PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY order_date
           ) AS prev_order_day
    FROM orders
)
SELECT user_id,
       COUNT(*) + 1 AS order_count,
       ROUND(AVG(order_day - prev_order_day), 1) AS avg_days_between_orders,
       MAX(order_day - prev_order_day) AS max_gap_days,
       MIN(order_day - prev_order_day) AS min_gap_days
FROM ordered_orders
WHERE prev_order_day IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY user_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY avg_days_between_orders ASC
LIMIT 20
solution_query:
WITH ordered_orders AS (
    SELECT user_id, CAST(order_date AS DATE) AS order_day,
           LAG(CAST(order_date AS DATE)) OVER (
               PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY order_date
           ) AS prev_order_day
    FROM orders
)
SELECT user_id,
       COUNT(*) + 1 AS order_count,
       ROUND(AVG(order_day - prev_order_day), 1) AS avg_days_between_orders,
       MAX(order_day - prev_order_day) AS max_gap_days,
       MIN(order_day - prev_order_day) AS min_gap_days
FROM ordered_orders
WHERE prev_order_day IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY user_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY avg_days_between_orders ASC
LIMIT 20;
explanation: LAG(order_day) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY order_date) gives the previous order date alongside the current. WHERE prev_order_day IS NOT NULL excludes the first order per user (which has no predecessor) — the remaining rows are inter-order gaps. The prompt asks for users with at least 3 orders; because the first order was dropped, 3 orders survive as 2 gaps — so the correct filter is `HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2`. The `order_count` column adds 1 back to `COUNT(*)` so it reports total orders (not gaps). DATE subtraction returns integer days.
hints: The average inter-order gap requires bringing each order's predecessor date into the same row. Users' first orders have no predecessor — account for that in the filter.

After `LAG` and the `IS NOT NULL` filter, each surviving row is a gap, not an order. So a user with N orders contributes N-1 rows here — set `HAVING` accordingly to match the prompt's order-count threshold.

title: Department salary quartile distribution
description: HR wants to understand how salary is distributed across departments. Write a query that uses NTILE(4) to assign each employee to a salary quartile (1 = lowest, 4 = highest) globally, then aggregates by `department_name` and `region`. Return `department_name`, `region`, `employee_count`, `avg_salary` (rounded to 2 dp), `min_salary` (rounded to 2 dp), `max_salary` (rounded to 2 dp), and `top_quartile_count` (employees in quartile 4). Order by `avg_salary` descending.
expected_query:
WITH salary_bands AS (
    SELECT e.employee_id, e.salary, d.department_name, d.region,
           NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY e.salary) AS salary_quartile
    FROM employees e
    JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id
)
SELECT department_name, region,
       COUNT(*) AS employee_count,
       ROUND(AVG(salary), 2) AS avg_salary,
       ROUND(MIN(salary), 2) AS min_salary,
       ROUND(MAX(salary), 2) AS max_salary,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN salary_quartile = 4 THEN 1 END) AS top_quartile_count
FROM salary_bands
GROUP BY department_name, region
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC
solution_query:
WITH salary_bands AS (
    SELECT e.employee_id, e.salary, d.department_name, d.region,
           NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY e.salary) AS salary_quartile
    FROM employees e
    JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id
)
SELECT department_name, region,
       COUNT(*) AS employee_count,
       ROUND(AVG(salary), 2) AS avg_salary,
       ROUND(MIN(salary), 2) AS min_salary,
       ROUND(MAX(salary), 2) AS max_salary,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN salary_quartile = 4 THEN 1 END) AS top_quartile_count
FROM salary_bands
GROUP BY department_name, region
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC;
explanation: NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY salary) assigns employees to 4 equal-size buckets globally (not per department). This is deliberate — the question asks for the global salary position. The CTE computes the quartile assignment; the outer query aggregates by department. top_quartile_count uses CASE WHEN to count only Q4 employees within each department, revealing which departments attract top-market salaries.
hints: Quartiles can be computed globally or per department — determine which scope the question asks for before defining the window partition.
The CTE attaches the quartile to each employee row; then GROUP BY department aggregates those rows.

title: Time to second order by acquisition channel
description: The growth team wants to know how quickly users re-order after their first completed purchase, broken down by acquisition channel. Write a query that returns `acquisition_channel`, `users_with_1plus_orders` (distinct users with at least one completed order), `users_reordered` (users with at least two completed orders), and `avg_days_to_reorder` (average days between first and second completed order for users who reordered, rounded to 1 dp). Order by `avg_days_to_reorder` ascending.
expected_query:
WITH user_order_sequence AS (
    SELECT user_id, CAST(order_date AS DATE) AS order_day,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY order_date) AS order_num
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
),
first_second AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           MAX(CASE WHEN order_num = 1 THEN order_day END) AS first_order,
           MAX(CASE WHEN order_num = 2 THEN order_day END) AS second_order
    FROM user_order_sequence
    GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT u.acquisition_channel,
       COUNT(DISTINCT fs.user_id) AS users_with_1plus_orders,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN fs.second_order IS NOT NULL THEN fs.user_id END) AS users_reordered,
       ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN fs.second_order IS NOT NULL
           THEN (fs.second_order - fs.first_order) END), 1) AS avg_days_to_reorder
FROM first_second fs
JOIN users u ON fs.user_id = u.user_id
GROUP BY u.acquisition_channel
ORDER BY avg_days_to_reorder ASC
solution_query:
WITH user_order_sequence AS (
    SELECT user_id, CAST(order_date AS DATE) AS order_day,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY order_date) AS order_num
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
),
first_second AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           MAX(CASE WHEN order_num = 1 THEN order_day END) AS first_order,
           MAX(CASE WHEN order_num = 2 THEN order_day END) AS second_order
    FROM user_order_sequence
    GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT u.acquisition_channel,
       COUNT(DISTINCT fs.user_id) AS users_with_1plus_orders,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN fs.second_order IS NOT NULL THEN fs.user_id END) AS users_reordered,
       ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN fs.second_order IS NOT NULL
           THEN (fs.second_order - fs.first_order) END), 1) AS avg_days_to_reorder
FROM first_second fs
JOIN users u ON fs.user_id = u.user_id
GROUP BY u.acquisition_channel
ORDER BY avg_days_to_reorder ASC;
explanation: ROW_NUMBER() assigns sequence positions within each user's order history. The second CTE pivots order_num=1 and order_num=2 into separate columns using MAX(CASE WHEN). Users with only one order get second_order = NULL. avg_days_to_reorder uses CASE WHEN inside AVG to exclude non-reorderers from the average — AVG automatically ignores NULLs, so CASE WHEN returning NULL for those users handles the exclusion.
