hints: First establish each order's position in the user's purchase history, then bring the first and second order dates into the same row for subtraction.
CASE WHEN inside AVG returns NULL for users with no second order — AVG ignores NULLs, so only reorderers contribute to the average.

title: Category product diversity: active rate and price range
description: The catalogue team wants a comprehensive diversity snapshot per product category. Write a query that returns `category_name`, `total_products`, `brand_count` (distinct brands within the category), `active_products` (products with is_active = true), `avg_price` (rounded to 2 dp), `min_price` (rounded to 2 dp), `max_price` (rounded to 2 dp), `price_range` (max_price - min_price, rounded to 2 dp), and `active_pct` (active_products / total_products × 100, rounded to 1 dp). Order by `total_products` descending.
expected_query:
SELECT c.category_name,
       COUNT(p.product_id) AS total_products,
       COUNT(DISTINCT p.brand) AS brand_count,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN p.is_active = true THEN 1 END) AS active_products,
       ROUND(AVG(p.price), 2) AS avg_price,
       ROUND(MIN(p.price), 2) AS min_price,
       ROUND(MAX(p.price), 2) AS max_price,
       ROUND(MAX(p.price) - MIN(p.price), 2) AS price_range,
       ROUND(COUNT(CASE WHEN p.is_active = true THEN 1 END) * 100.0 / COUNT(p.product_id), 1) AS active_pct
FROM categories c
JOIN products p ON c.category_id = p.category_id
GROUP BY c.category_name
ORDER BY total_products DESC
solution_query:
SELECT c.category_name,
       COUNT(p.product_id) AS total_products,
       COUNT(DISTINCT p.brand) AS brand_count,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN p.is_active = true THEN 1 END) AS active_products,
       ROUND(AVG(p.price), 2) AS avg_price,
       ROUND(MIN(p.price), 2) AS min_price,
       ROUND(MAX(p.price), 2) AS max_price,
       ROUND(MAX(p.price) - MIN(p.price), 2) AS price_range,
       ROUND(COUNT(CASE WHEN p.is_active = true THEN 1 END) * 100.0 / COUNT(p.product_id), 1) AS active_pct
FROM categories c
JOIN products p ON c.category_id = p.category_id
GROUP BY c.category_name
ORDER BY total_products DESC;
explanation: Single GROUP BY aggregation across multiple metric types: COUNT(DISTINCT brand) for diversity, COUNT(CASE WHEN is_active) for active inventory, MIN/MAX for price range. price_range = MAX - MIN directly in the SELECT avoids a self-join. active_pct divides by COUNT(product_id) (total products, including inactive) so the denominator is consistent with total_products.
hints: Active and total product counts can be computed in a single pass — a conditional expression can act as a filter inside an aggregation without requiring separate queries or multiple scans.
price_range = MAX(price) - MIN(price) in a single SELECT — you don't need a subquery to compute both max and min.

title: Plan tier revenue share within each month
description: The finance team wants to see how each plan tier's contribution to total monthly revenue shifts over time. Write a query that returns `plan_tier`, `order_month` (YYYY-MM), `revenue` (sum of net_amount for completed orders, rounded to 2 dp), and `share_of_month_pct` (this plan tier's revenue as a percentage of all completed revenue in that month, rounded to 1 dp). Order by `order_month` ascending, then `share_of_month_pct` descending.
expected_query:
WITH monthly_plan AS (
    SELECT u.plan_tier,
           strftime(CAST(o.order_date AS DATE), '%Y-%m') AS order_month,
           SUM(o.net_amount) AS revenue
    FROM users u
    JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY u.plan_tier, order_month
)
SELECT plan_tier, order_month, ROUND(revenue, 2) AS revenue,
       ROUND(revenue * 100.0 / SUM(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY order_month), 1) AS share_of_month_pct
FROM monthly_plan
ORDER BY order_month, share_of_month_pct DESC
solution_query:
WITH monthly_plan AS (
    SELECT u.plan_tier,
           strftime(CAST(o.order_date AS DATE), '%Y-%m') AS order_month,
           SUM(o.net_amount) AS revenue
    FROM users u
    JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY u.plan_tier, order_month
)
SELECT plan_tier, order_month, ROUND(revenue, 2) AS revenue,
       ROUND(revenue * 100.0 / SUM(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY order_month), 1) AS share_of_month_pct
FROM monthly_plan
ORDER BY order_month, share_of_month_pct DESC;
explanation: SUM(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY order_month) computes total monthly revenue for each month without collapsing rows — each plan tier row gets the month's total as a denominator. Dividing the plan tier's revenue by this month total gives the share. The pattern 'value / SUM(value) OVER (PARTITION BY ...)' is the canonical way to compute proportional contributions without a self-join.
hints: SUM OVER (PARTITION BY order_month) gives the monthly total on each row — divide each row's revenue by this to get its share.
Build monthly plan-tier aggregates in a CTE; window functions can't be applied directly over GROUP BY expressions in the same SELECT.

title: Product view-to-cart conversion rate
description: The product team wants to identify which products have the best view-to-cart conversion in user sessions. Write a query that returns `product_name`, `brand`, `category_name`, `view_sessions` (distinct sessions with a 'view_product' event for this product), `cart_sessions` (distinct sessions with an 'add_to_cart' event for this product), and `view_to_cart_pct` (cart_sessions / view_sessions × 100, rounded to 1 dp). Include only products with at least one view session. Order by `view_to_cart_pct` descending, then `product_name` ascending. Limit to 20 rows.
expected_query:
WITH view_cart AS (
    SELECT product_id,
           COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event_name = 'view_product' THEN session_id END) AS view_sessions,
           COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event_name = 'add_to_cart' THEN session_id END) AS cart_sessions
    FROM events
    GROUP BY product_id
)
SELECT p.product_name, p.brand, c.category_name,
       vc.view_sessions,
       vc.cart_sessions,
       ROUND(vc.cart_sessions * 100.0 / NULLIF(vc.view_sessions, 0), 1) AS view_to_cart_pct
FROM view_cart vc
JOIN products p ON vc.product_id = p.product_id
JOIN categories c ON p.category_id = c.category_id
WHERE vc.view_sessions > 0
ORDER BY view_to_cart_pct DESC, product_name ASC
LIMIT 20
solution_query:
WITH view_cart AS (
    SELECT product_id,
           COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event_name = 'view_product' THEN session_id END) AS view_sessions,
           COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event_name = 'add_to_cart' THEN session_id END) AS cart_sessions
    FROM events
    GROUP BY product_id
)
SELECT p.product_name, p.brand, c.category_name,
       vc.view_sessions,
       vc.cart_sessions,
       ROUND(vc.cart_sessions * 100.0 / NULLIF(vc.view_sessions, 0), 1) AS view_to_cart_pct
FROM view_cart vc
JOIN products p ON vc.product_id = p.product_id
JOIN categories c ON p.category_id = c.category_id
WHERE vc.view_sessions > 0
ORDER BY view_to_cart_pct DESC, product_name ASC
LIMIT 20;
explanation: COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event_name = 'view_product' THEN session_id END) counts unique sessions where this product was viewed — COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) without the CASE would count all event types. NULLIF(view_sessions, 0) guards against zero-view products (though WHERE view_sessions > 0 already filters them — NULLIF is defensive belt-and-suspenders practice). This is a funnel metric computed at the product level using session deduplication.
hints: When measuring reach for a specific event type, you need unique session counts — but only sessions in which that event occurred. A condition can be embedded inside an aggregation to avoid discarding unrelated rows.
NULLIF(view_sessions, 0) prevents division-by-zero, though WHERE view_sessions > 0 already handles it — both guard the same edge case.

title: Per-user cumulative spend over order history
description: The analytics team wants to show each user's order history with a running spend total. Write a query that returns `user_id`, `order_day` (CAST order_date as DATE), `order_id`, `order_sequence` (ROW_NUMBER within user, ordered by order_date), and `cumulative_spend` (running SUM of net_amount within user, ordered by order_date, from first order to current row). Include only completed orders. Order by `user_id` ascending, then `order_day` ascending. Limit to 30 rows.
expected_query:
SELECT user_id, CAST(order_date AS DATE) AS order_day,
       order_id,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY order_date) AS order_sequence,
       SUM(net_amount) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY order_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS cumulative_spend
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'completed'
ORDER BY user_id, order_day
LIMIT 30
solution_query:
SELECT user_id, CAST(order_date AS DATE) AS order_day,
       order_id,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY order_date) AS order_sequence,
       SUM(net_amount) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY order_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS cumulative_spend
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'completed'
ORDER BY user_id, order_day
LIMIT 30;
explanation: Two window functions share the same PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY order_date basis: ROW_NUMBER() for sequence, SUM() with ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW for the running total. UNBOUNDED PRECEDING means 'start from the very first row in the partition' — this is the explicit form of the default running window. ROWS (not RANGE) ensures ties in order_date don't collapse into the same frame.
hints: ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW is the explicit frame for a running total — RANGE would handle date ties differently.
Both window functions share the same PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY order_date — you can specify this once per window spec or repeat it.

title: Employee salary gap to department maximum
description: HR wants to see all employees, ordered by salary gap to the department maximum, largest gap first. Write a query that returns `employee_id`, `employee_name`, `salary`, `department_name`, `dept_max_salary` (the department's highest salary, rounded to 2 dp), `gap_to_max` (dept_max_salary - salary, rounded to 2 dp), and `gap_pct` ((dept_max_salary - salary) / dept_max_salary × 100, rounded to 1 dp). Order by `gap_to_max` descending. Limit to 20 rows.
expected_query:
WITH dept_max AS (
    SELECT department_id, MAX(salary) AS max_salary
    FROM employees
    GROUP BY department_id
)
SELECT e.employee_id, e.employee_name, e.salary, d.department_name,
       ROUND(dm.max_salary, 2) AS dept_max_salary,
       ROUND(dm.max_salary - e.salary, 2) AS gap_to_max,
       ROUND((dm.max_salary - e.salary) * 100.0 / dm.max_salary, 1) AS gap_pct
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id
JOIN dept_max dm ON e.department_id = dm.department_id
ORDER BY gap_to_max DESC
LIMIT 20
solution_query:
WITH dept_max AS (
    SELECT department_id, MAX(salary) AS max_salary
    FROM employees
    GROUP BY department_id
)
SELECT e.employee_id, e.employee_name, e.salary, d.department_name,
       ROUND(dm.max_salary, 2) AS dept_max_salary,
       ROUND(dm.max_salary - e.salary, 2) AS gap_to_max,
       ROUND((dm.max_salary - e.salary) * 100.0 / dm.max_salary, 1) AS gap_pct
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id
JOIN dept_max dm ON e.department_id = dm.department_id
ORDER BY gap_to_max DESC
LIMIT 20;
explanation: The CTE computes MAX(salary) per department. Joining it to employees gives each employee row their department's maximum alongside their own salary. The gap and gap_pct are arithmetic expressions in SELECT — no additional aggregation needed. An alternative using MAX() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id) achieves the same without a CTE, but the CTE approach makes the logic more explicit.
hints: Each employee's salary gap requires knowing the department maximum — compute that at the department level first, then make it available row by row.
The gap is just subtraction; the gap_pct is (gap / max) × 100 — both are plain arithmetic in SELECT, not aggregates.

title: Events users triggered before their first completed purchase
description: The product team wants to understand what actions users take before they first buy. Write a query that returns `event_name`, `users_with_event` (distinct users who triggered this event at least once before the calendar date of their first completed order — treat both event_time and order_date as dates, excluding same-calendar-day events), `total_events` (total occurrences of this event across all users before their first purchase), and `avg_events_per_user` (total_events / users_with_event, rounded to 1 dp). Include only users who eventually made a completed purchase. Order by `users_with_event` descending.
expected_query:
WITH first_purchases AS (
    SELECT user_id, MIN(CAST(order_date AS DATE)) AS first_purchase_date
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY user_id
),
pre_purchase_events AS (
    SELECT e.user_id, e.event_name,
           COUNT(*) AS event_count
    FROM events e
    JOIN first_purchases fp ON e.user_id = fp.user_id
    WHERE CAST(e.event_time AS DATE) < fp.first_purchase_date
    GROUP BY e.user_id, e.event_name
)
SELECT event_name,
       COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS users_with_event,
       SUM(event_count) AS total_events,
       ROUND(SUM(event_count) * 1.0 / COUNT(DISTINCT user_id), 1) AS avg_events_per_user
FROM pre_purchase_events
GROUP BY event_name
ORDER BY users_with_event DESC
solution_query:
WITH first_purchases AS (
    SELECT user_id, MIN(CAST(order_date AS DATE)) AS first_purchase_date
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY user_id
),
pre_purchase_events AS (
    SELECT e.user_id, e.event_name,
           COUNT(*) AS event_count
    FROM events e
    JOIN first_purchases fp ON e.user_id = fp.user_id
    WHERE CAST(e.event_time AS DATE) < fp.first_purchase_date
    GROUP BY e.user_id, e.event_name
)
SELECT event_name,
       COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS users_with_event,
       SUM(event_count) AS total_events,
       ROUND(SUM(event_count) * 1.0 / COUNT(DISTINCT user_id), 1) AS avg_events_per_user
FROM pre_purchase_events
GROUP BY event_name
ORDER BY users_with_event DESC;
explanation: Two CTEs: first_purchases finds each purchaser's first order date; pre_purchase_events joins events to first_purchases and filters to events before that date, then counts per user-event. The main query aggregates across users to get event-level metrics. INNER JOIN in pre_purchase_events implicitly excludes non-purchasers — only users with a first_purchase_date appear.
hints: You only want events that happened before each user's first purchase — establish that first purchase date as a boundary, then use it to filter events.
The main aggregation is two levels: per-user-event counts in the CTE, then cross-user aggregation in the outer query.

title: Acquisition channel cohort: average order value over time
description: The growth team wants to track how average order value evolves for each acquisition channel's monthly cohorts. Write a query that returns `acquisition_channel`, `cohort_month` (YYYY-MM from signup_date), `orders` (completed orders placed by that cohort), `avg_order_value` (rounded to 2 dp; NULL for cohorts with no orders), `cohort_users`, and `orders_per_user` (orders / cohort_users, rounded to 2 dp). Include only cohort-months with at least 3 users. Order by `acquisition_channel` ascending, then `cohort_month` ascending. Limit to 30 rows.
expected_query:
WITH user_cohorts AS (
    SELECT user_id, acquisition_channel,
           strftime(signup_date, '%Y-%m') AS cohort_month
    FROM users
),
cohort_orders AS (
    SELECT uc.acquisition_channel, uc.cohort_month,
           COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS orders,
           ROUND(AVG(o.net_amount), 2) AS avg_order_value,
           COUNT(DISTINCT uc.user_id) AS cohort_users
    FROM user_cohorts uc
    LEFT JOIN orders o ON uc.user_id = o.user_id AND o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY uc.acquisition_channel, uc.cohort_month
    HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT uc.user_id) >= 3
)
SELECT acquisition_channel, cohort_month, orders, avg_order_value, cohort_users,
       ROUND(orders * 1.0 / cohort_users, 2) AS orders_per_user
FROM cohort_orders
ORDER BY acquisition_channel, cohort_month
LIMIT 30
solution_query:
WITH user_cohorts AS (
    SELECT user_id, acquisition_channel,
           strftime(signup_date, '%Y-%m') AS cohort_month
    FROM users
),
cohort_orders AS (
    SELECT uc.acquisition_channel, uc.cohort_month,
           COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS orders,
           ROUND(AVG(o.net_amount), 2) AS avg_order_value,
           COUNT(DISTINCT uc.user_id) AS cohort_users
    FROM user_cohorts uc
    LEFT JOIN orders o ON uc.user_id = o.user_id AND o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY uc.acquisition_channel, uc.cohort_month
    HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT uc.user_id) >= 3
)
SELECT acquisition_channel, cohort_month, orders, avg_order_value, cohort_users,
       ROUND(orders * 1.0 / cohort_users, 2) AS orders_per_user
FROM cohort_orders
ORDER BY acquisition_channel, cohort_month
LIMIT 30;
explanation: LEFT JOIN preserves users with no completed orders — they appear as cohort members with orders=0 and avg_order_value=NULL. HAVING filters cohort-months with fewer than 3 users (too small to be meaningful). orders_per_user is computed in the outer query from the CTE result — it's a ratio of two already-computed values, not a window function.
hints: Every user belongs to a signup cohort regardless of purchase history — non-buyers should appear with zero orders rather than be absent from their cohort.
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) >= 3 filters after grouping — it's counting cohort size, not order count.

title: Support ticket issue type by plan tier with priority mix
description: The support quality team wants to understand which plan tiers generate more high-priority tickets per issue type. Write a query that returns `issue_type`, `plan_tier`, `ticket_count`, `avg_resolution_hours` (rounded to 1 dp), `high_priority_count` (tickets with priority 'high' or 'urgent'), and `high_priority_pct` (high_priority_count / ticket_count × 100, rounded to 1 dp). Order by `ticket_count` descending.
expected_query:
SELECT t.issue_type, u.plan_tier,
       COUNT(*) AS ticket_count,
       ROUND(AVG(t.resolution_hours), 1) AS avg_resolution_hours,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN t.priority IN ('high','urgent') THEN 1 END) AS high_priority_count,
       ROUND(COUNT(CASE WHEN t.priority IN ('high','urgent') THEN 1 END) * 100.0 / COUNT(*), 1) AS high_priority_pct
FROM support_tickets t
JOIN users u ON t.user_id = u.user_id
GROUP BY t.issue_type, u.plan_tier
ORDER BY ticket_count DESC
solution_query:
SELECT t.issue_type, u.plan_tier,
       COUNT(*) AS ticket_count,
       ROUND(AVG(t.resolution_hours), 1) AS avg_resolution_hours,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN t.priority IN ('high','urgent') THEN 1 END) AS high_priority_count,
       ROUND(COUNT(CASE WHEN t.priority IN ('high','urgent') THEN 1 END) * 100.0 / COUNT(*), 1) AS high_priority_pct
FROM support_tickets t
JOIN users u ON t.user_id = u.user_id
GROUP BY t.issue_type, u.plan_tier
ORDER BY ticket_count DESC;
explanation: Joining support_tickets to users adds plan_tier. GROUP BY issue_type + plan_tier creates the cross-tab. IN ('high','urgent') captures both high-severity priority levels. The high_priority_pct uses COUNT(*) as denominator (total tickets in the segment) — this correctly expresses the fraction of that segment's tickets that are high-priority.
hints: Use IN ('high','urgent') inside CASE WHEN to match both high-severity priority values in one expression.
The denominator for high_priority_pct is COUNT(*) — total tickets in the issue_type × plan_tier group, not just high-priority ones.

title: Average time between events within a session by device and source
description: The UX team wants to measure how long users spend between interactions within a session. Write a query that groups sessions with multiple events by `traffic_source` and `device_type`, and returns `traffic_source`, `device_type`, `sessions_with_multiple_events`, `avg_event_count` (average number of events per session, rounded to 1 dp), and `avg_min_between_events` (for each session, take the mean number of minutes between its consecutive events; then average those per-session means across the group, rounded to 2 dp). Order by `avg_event_count` descending.
expected_query:
WITH event_with_lag AS (
    SELECT session_id, event_time,
           LAG(event_time) OVER (PARTITION BY session_id ORDER BY event_time) AS prev_event_time
    FROM events
),
session_stats AS (
    SELECT session_id,
           COUNT(*) AS event_count,
           AVG(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (event_time - prev_event_time)) / 60.0) AS avg_minutes_between_events
    FROM event_with_lag
    GROUP BY session_id
    HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
)
SELECT s.traffic_source, s.device_type,
       COUNT(DISTINCT ss.session_id) AS sessions_with_multiple_events,
       ROUND(AVG(ss.event_count), 1) AS avg_event_count,
       ROUND(AVG(ss.avg_minutes_between_events), 2) AS avg_min_between_events
FROM session_stats ss
JOIN sessions s ON ss.session_id = s.session_id
GROUP BY s.traffic_source, s.device_type
ORDER BY avg_event_count DESC
solution_query:
WITH event_with_lag AS (
    SELECT session_id, event_time,
           LAG(event_time) OVER (PARTITION BY session_id ORDER BY event_time) AS prev_event_time
    FROM events
),
session_stats AS (
    SELECT session_id,
           COUNT(*) AS event_count,
           AVG(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (event_time - prev_event_time)) / 60.0) AS avg_minutes_between_events
    FROM event_with_lag
    GROUP BY session_id
    HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
)
SELECT s.traffic_source, s.device_type,
       COUNT(DISTINCT ss.session_id) AS sessions_with_multiple_events,
       ROUND(AVG(ss.event_count), 1) AS avg_event_count,
       ROUND(AVG(ss.avg_minutes_between_events), 2) AS avg_min_between_events
FROM session_stats ss
JOIN sessions s ON ss.session_id = s.session_id
GROUP BY s.traffic_source, s.device_type
ORDER BY avg_event_count DESC;
explanation: LAG(event_time) OVER (PARTITION BY session_id ORDER BY event_time) gives each event's predecessor within its session; the first event has none (NULL). EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (event_time - prev_event_time)) / 60 turns each gap into minutes. Per session, event_count = COUNT(*) counts ALL events (N), while AVG over the gaps skips the first event's NULL gap (so the mean gap is over the N-1 consecutive pairs) — left unrounded at this stage. HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 keeps only multi-event sessions. The outer query then averages the per-session event counts and per-session mean gaps within each traffic_source × device_type group, rounding only the final figures (avg_event_count to 1 dp, avg_min_between_events to 2 dp).
hints: Break it into two per-session measures — how many events the session had, and the typical minutes between its consecutive events — then average each of those measures across the traffic-source × device group.

Getting the gap between consecutive events needs each event’s predecessor within the session; the first event has no predecessor, so it adds to the event count but contributes no gap. Keep only sessions with more than one event.

title: First vs last order value by plan tier
description: The retention team hypothesizes that users' order sizes change over their lifetime. Considering only users with 2+ completed orders, write a query that returns, per `plan_tier`: `users` (count of such users), `avg_lifetime_orders` (average number of completed orders per user, rounded to 1 dp), `avg_first_order_value` (average net_amount of each user's first completed order, rounded to 2 dp), and `avg_last_order_value` (average net_amount of each user's most recent completed order, rounded to 2 dp). Each average weights every qualifying user equally. Order by `avg_lifetime_orders` descending.
expected_query:
WITH order_seq AS (
    SELECT user_id, net_amount,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY order_date) AS seq,
           COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id) AS total_orders
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
),
per_user AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           MAX(total_orders) AS total_orders,
           MAX(CASE WHEN seq = 1 THEN net_amount END) AS first_order_value,
           MAX(CASE WHEN seq = total_orders THEN net_amount END) AS last_order_value
    FROM order_seq
    WHERE total_orders > 1
    GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT u.plan_tier,
       COUNT(DISTINCT pu.user_id) AS users,
       ROUND(AVG(pu.total_orders), 1) AS avg_lifetime_orders,
       ROUND(AVG(pu.first_order_value), 2) AS avg_first_order_value,
       ROUND(AVG(pu.last_order_value), 2) AS avg_last_order_value
FROM per_user pu
JOIN users u ON pu.user_id = u.user_id
GROUP BY u.plan_tier
ORDER BY avg_lifetime_orders DESC
solution_query:
WITH order_seq AS (
    SELECT user_id, net_amount,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY order_date) AS seq,
           COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id) AS total_orders
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
),
per_user AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           MAX(total_orders) AS total_orders,
           MAX(CASE WHEN seq = 1 THEN net_amount END) AS first_order_value,
           MAX(CASE WHEN seq = total_orders THEN net_amount END) AS last_order_value
    FROM order_seq
    WHERE total_orders > 1
    GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT u.plan_tier,
       COUNT(DISTINCT pu.user_id) AS users,
       ROUND(AVG(pu.total_orders), 1) AS avg_lifetime_orders,
       ROUND(AVG(pu.first_order_value), 2) AS avg_first_order_value,
       ROUND(AVG(pu.last_order_value), 2) AS avg_last_order_value
FROM per_user pu
JOIN users u ON pu.user_id = u.user_id
GROUP BY u.plan_tier
ORDER BY avg_lifetime_orders DESC;
explanation: Restrict to completed orders, then keep only users with 2+ of them. ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY order_date) marks each user's first (seq=1) order, and COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id) as total_orders identifies their last (seq=total_orders). Collapsing to one row per user (per_user) before aggregating ensures each user contributes equally — so avg_lifetime_orders is a true per-user average, not an order-count-weighted one. The outer query averages the per-user values within each plan_tier.
hints: Identifying the last order requires knowing both a row's position in the sequence and the user's total order count — derive both from the same window partition.
Restrict to users with 2+ completed orders, then reduce to one row per user before averaging, so every user is weighted equally rather than weighted by how many orders they placed.

title: Product co-purchase pairs (frequently bought together)
description: The recommendation team wants to find product pairs frequently purchased in the same completed order. Write a query that returns `product_a_name`, `product_b_name`, and `co_purchase_count` (number of distinct completed orders containing both products). Only include each pair once (where product_a's product_id is strictly less than product_b's). Order by `co_purchase_count` descending, then `product_a_name` ascending, then `product_b_name` ascending. Limit to 10 rows.
expected_query:
WITH order_product_pairs AS (
    SELECT a.order_id, a.product_id AS product_a, b.product_id AS product_b
    FROM order_items a
    JOIN order_items b ON a.order_id = b.order_id AND a.product_id < b.product_id
    JOIN orders o ON a.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
)
SELECT pa.product_name AS product_a_name, pb.product_name AS product_b_name,
       COUNT(DISTINCT opp.order_id) AS co_purchase_count
FROM order_product_pairs opp
JOIN products pa ON opp.product_a = pa.product_id
JOIN products pb ON opp.product_b = pb.product_id
GROUP BY pa.product_name, pb.product_name
ORDER BY co_purchase_count DESC, product_a_name, product_b_name
LIMIT 10
solution_query:
WITH order_product_pairs AS (
    SELECT a.order_id, a.product_id AS product_a, b.product_id AS product_b
    FROM order_items a
    JOIN order_items b ON a.order_id = b.order_id AND a.product_id < b.product_id
    JOIN orders o ON a.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
)
SELECT pa.product_name AS product_a_name, pb.product_name AS product_b_name,
       COUNT(DISTINCT opp.order_id) AS co_purchase_count
FROM order_product_pairs opp
JOIN products pa ON opp.product_a = pa.product_id
JOIN products pb ON opp.product_b = pb.product_id
GROUP BY pa.product_name, pb.product_name
ORDER BY co_purchase_count DESC, product_a_name, product_b_name
LIMIT 10;
explanation: Self-joining order_items with AND a.product_id < b.product_id generates all ordered product pairs within each order — the < condition prevents duplicates (A,B and B,A) and self-pairs (A,A). Joining to orders filters to completed orders. COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) counts orders, not product-pair rows (an order with 3 of the same pair would still count once). This is the canonical pattern for market basket analysis.
hints: Generating all product pairs within an order requires pairing each item with every other item in the same order — the key challenge is producing each pair exactly once.
COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) counts qualifying orders — not rows — so the unit of analysis is 'how many orders contained both products'.

title: User churn after support ticket: activity status
description: The retention team wants to classify users by their behaviour after their last support ticket. Write a query that returns `user_id`, `last_ticket_date` (most recent created_at, as DATE), `last_order_date` (most recent completed order_date, as DATE; NULL if no completed orders), and `churn_status`: 'never_ordered' if no completed orders exist, 'churned_after_ticket' if last_order_date is before last_ticket_date, 'still_active' otherwise. Order by `churn_status` ascending, then `user_id` ascending. Limit to 30 rows.
expected_query:
WITH last_ticket AS (
    SELECT user_id, MAX(created_at) AS last_ticket_date
    FROM support_tickets
    GROUP BY user_id
),
last_order AS (
    SELECT user_id, MAX(CAST(order_date AS DATE)) AS last_order_date
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT lt.user_id,
       CAST(lt.last_ticket_date AS DATE) AS last_ticket_date,
       lo.last_order_date,
       CASE
           WHEN lo.last_order_date IS NULL THEN 'never_ordered'
           WHEN lo.last_order_date < CAST(lt.last_ticket_date AS DATE) THEN 'churned_after_ticket'
           ELSE 'still_active'
       END AS churn_status
FROM last_ticket lt
LEFT JOIN last_order lo ON lt.user_id = lo.user_id
ORDER BY churn_status, lt.user_id
LIMIT 30
solution_query:
WITH last_ticket AS (
    SELECT user_id, MAX(created_at) AS last_ticket_date
    FROM support_tickets
    GROUP BY user_id
),
last_order AS (
    SELECT user_id, MAX(CAST(order_date AS DATE)) AS last_order_date
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT lt.user_id,
       CAST(lt.last_ticket_date AS DATE) AS last_ticket_date,
       lo.last_order_date,
       CASE
           WHEN lo.last_order_date IS NULL THEN 'never_ordered'
           WHEN lo.last_order_date < CAST(lt.last_ticket_date AS DATE) THEN 'churned_after_ticket'
           ELSE 'still_active'
       END AS churn_status
FROM last_ticket lt
LEFT JOIN last_order lo ON lt.user_id = lo.user_id
ORDER BY churn_status, lt.user_id
LIMIT 30;
explanation: Two CTEs compute the most recent ticket date and the most recent completed order date per user. LEFT JOIN from last_ticket to last_order preserves users who never ordered (their last_order_date is NULL). The CASE checks NULL first (never_ordered), then compares dates to determine churn direction. CAST(created_at AS DATE) aligns the timestamp to a date for comparison with last_order_date.
hints: Check IS NULL first in CASE WHEN — if last_order_date is NULL, the later date comparison would error or give unexpected results.
LEFT JOIN from last_ticket (not last_order) — you want all users who filed tickets, including those who never ordered.

title: Revenue per sold SKU by category
description: The catalogue team wants to understand which categories generate the most revenue per active (sold) product SKU. Write a query that returns `category_name`, `total_skus` (all products in the category), `sold_skus` (products appearing in at least one completed order), `category_revenue` (total line_amount from completed orders, rounded to 2 dp), and `revenue_per_sold_sku` (category_revenue / sold_skus, rounded to 2 dp). Order by `revenue_per_sold_sku` descending.
expected_query:
WITH sku_revenue AS (
    SELECT oi.product_id,
           SUM(oi.line_amount) AS total_revenue
    FROM order_items oi
    JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY oi.product_id
)
SELECT c.category_name,
       COUNT(DISTINCT p.product_id) AS total_skus,
       COUNT(DISTINCT sr.product_id) AS sold_skus,
       ROUND(SUM(sr.total_revenue), 2) AS category_revenue,
       ROUND(SUM(sr.total_revenue) / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT sr.product_id), 0), 2) AS revenue_per_sold_sku
FROM categories c
JOIN products p ON c.category_id = p.category_id
LEFT JOIN sku_revenue sr ON p.product_id = sr.product_id
GROUP BY c.category_name
ORDER BY revenue_per_sold_sku DESC
solution_query:
WITH sku_revenue AS (
    SELECT oi.product_id,
           SUM(oi.line_amount) AS total_revenue
    FROM order_items oi
    JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY oi.product_id
)
SELECT c.category_name,
       COUNT(DISTINCT p.product_id) AS total_skus,
       COUNT(DISTINCT sr.product_id) AS sold_skus,
       ROUND(SUM(sr.total_revenue), 2) AS category_revenue,
       ROUND(SUM(sr.total_revenue) / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT sr.product_id), 0), 2) AS revenue_per_sold_sku
FROM categories c
JOIN products p ON c.category_id = p.category_id
LEFT JOIN sku_revenue sr ON p.product_id = sr.product_id
GROUP BY c.category_name
ORDER BY revenue_per_sold_sku DESC;
explanation: The CTE computes per-product revenue. LEFT JOIN from products to sku_revenue preserves unsold products (sr columns are NULL). COUNT(DISTINCT p.product_id) counts all SKUs; COUNT(DISTINCT sr.product_id) counts only sold ones (NULL product_ids from unsold products are excluded by COUNT DISTINCT). NULLIF prevents division by zero for categories where no products were sold.
hints: Categories with no sold products should still appear in the result — the combination approach must not silently drop categories that have no matching entries in the sales data.
NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT sr.product_id), 0) prevents division by zero for categories with no sold SKUs.

title: Payment retry recovery rate by first attempt status
description: The payments team wants to know how often a failed first payment attempt eventually recovers with a successful paid payment. Write a query that groups orders by the status of their FIRST payment attempt, then returns `first_status`, `orders` (distinct order count with that first attempt status), `eventually_paid` (orders where ANY payment row has status = 'paid'), and `recovery_rate_pct` (eventually_paid / orders × 100, rounded to 1 dp). Order by `recovery_rate_pct` descending.
expected_query:
WITH payment_attempts AS (
    SELECT order_id, status,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY payment_date) AS attempt_num
    FROM payments
),
first_attempt AS (
    SELECT order_id, status AS first_status
    FROM payment_attempts
    WHERE attempt_num = 1
),
any_paid AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT order_id FROM payments WHERE status = 'paid'
)
SELECT fa.first_status,
       COUNT(DISTINCT fa.order_id) AS orders,
       COUNT(DISTINCT ap.order_id) AS eventually_paid,
       ROUND(COUNT(DISTINCT ap.order_id) * 100.0 / COUNT(DISTINCT fa.order_id), 1) AS recovery_rate_pct
FROM first_attempt fa
LEFT JOIN any_paid ap ON fa.order_id = ap.order_id
GROUP BY fa.first_status
ORDER BY recovery_rate_pct DESC
solution_query:
WITH payment_attempts AS (
    SELECT order_id, status,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY payment_date) AS attempt_num
    FROM payments
),
first_attempt AS (
    SELECT order_id, status AS first_status
    FROM payment_attempts
    WHERE attempt_num = 1
),
any_paid AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT order_id FROM payments WHERE status = 'paid'
)
SELECT fa.first_status,
       COUNT(DISTINCT fa.order_id) AS orders,
       COUNT(DISTINCT ap.order_id) AS eventually_paid,
       ROUND(COUNT(DISTINCT ap.order_id) * 100.0 / COUNT(DISTINCT fa.order_id), 1) AS recovery_rate_pct
FROM first_attempt fa
LEFT JOIN any_paid ap ON fa.order_id = ap.order_id
GROUP BY fa.first_status
ORDER BY recovery_rate_pct DESC;
explanation: Three CTEs: (1) ROW_NUMBER ranks payments within each order by date; (2) WHERE attempt_num=1 isolates the first attempt per order; (3) any_paid collects orders that eventually got paid. LEFT JOIN preserves orders where recovery never happened. COUNT(DISTINCT ap.order_id) counts recoveries — NULL order_ids from unjoined rows aren't counted. The recovery_rate_pct reveals how often initial failure leads to eventual success.
hints: To analyze the first payment attempt per order, establish the chronological position of each payment within its order, then isolate the first-attempt rows.
LEFT JOIN any_paid so orders with no successful payment still appear in first_attempt with eventually_paid = 0.

title: Average events per session for active users
description: A platform engagement team wants to characterise power users. For each user who has participated in at least 5 distinct sessions, compute their average number of events per session (rounded to 2 decimal places). Return user_id, session_count, and avg_events_per_session, ordered by avg_events_per_session descending.
expected_query:
WITH session_events AS (
  SELECT
    e.session_id,
    s.user_id,
    COUNT(e.event_id) AS event_count
  FROM events e
  JOIN sessions s ON e.session_id = s.session_id
  GROUP BY e.session_id, s.user_id
),
user_stats AS (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    COUNT(session_id) AS session_count,
    AVG(event_count) AS avg_events_per_session
  FROM session_events
  GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT
  user_id,
  session_count,
  ROUND(avg_events_per_session, 2) AS avg_events_per_session
FROM user_stats
WHERE session_count >= 5
ORDER BY avg_events_per_session DESC
solution_query:
WITH session_events AS (
  SELECT
    e.session_id,
    s.user_id,
    COUNT(e.event_id) AS event_count
  FROM events e
  JOIN sessions s ON e.session_id = s.session_id
  GROUP BY e.session_id, s.user_id
),
user_stats AS (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    COUNT(session_id) AS session_count,
    AVG(event_count) AS avg_events_per_session
  FROM session_events
  GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT
  user_id,
  session_count,
  ROUND(avg_events_per_session, 2) AS avg_events_per_session
FROM user_stats
WHERE session_count >= 5
ORDER BY avg_events_per_session DESC
explanation: Two aggregation levels are needed: first count events per session (session_events CTE), then average those counts per user (user_stats CTE). Filtering WHERE session_count >= 5 ensures only statistically meaningful users are included. The two-level CTE structure is the key insight — AVG(event_count) averages the per-session counts, not the raw event rows.
hints: First aggregate events per session_id to get event_count, then average those per user.
Post-filter on session_count >= 5 in the outer query after computing user-level stats.

title: 30-day repeat purchase retention by cohort month
description: A growth analyst wants to measure early repeat-purchase behaviour. For each cohort month (based on a user's first completed order date), compute: cohort_size (total users), retained (users who made another completed order strictly after their first order date and within 30 calendar days of it — i.e. the second order's date is > first_order_date and <= first_order_date + 30 days), and retention_rate_pct (rounded to 1 decimal). Output columns: cohort_month (YYYY-MM string), cohort_size, retained, retention_rate_pct. Order by cohort_month.
expected_query:
WITH first_orders AS (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(CAST(order_date AS DATE)) AS first_order_date
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY user_id
),
retained AS (
  SELECT
    fo.user_id,
    fo.first_order_date,
    CASE WHEN EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM orders o2
      WHERE o2.user_id = fo.user_id
        AND o2.status = 'completed'
        AND CAST(o2.order_date AS DATE) > fo.first_order_date
        AND CAST(o2.order_date AS DATE) <= fo.first_order_date + 30
    ) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS retained_30d
  FROM first_orders fo
)
SELECT
  strftime(first_order_date, '%Y-%m') AS cohort_month,
  COUNT(*) AS cohort_size,
  SUM(retained_30d) AS retained,
  ROUND(100.0 * SUM(retained_30d) / COUNT(*), 1) AS retention_rate_pct
FROM retained
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1
solution_query:
WITH first_orders AS (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(CAST(order_date AS DATE)) AS first_order_date
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY user_id
),
retained AS (
  SELECT
    fo.user_id,
    fo.first_order_date,
    CASE WHEN EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM orders o2
      WHERE o2.user_id = fo.user_id
        AND o2.status = 'completed'
        AND CAST(o2.order_date AS DATE) > fo.first_order_date
        AND CAST(o2.order_date AS DATE) <= fo.first_order_date + 30
    ) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS retained_30d
  FROM first_orders fo
)
SELECT
  strftime(first_order_date, '%Y-%m') AS cohort_month,
  COUNT(*) AS cohort_size,
  SUM(retained_30d) AS retained,
  ROUND(100.0 * SUM(retained_30d) / COUNT(*), 1) AS retention_rate_pct
FROM retained
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1
explanation: Three-stage logic: (1) find each user's first completed order date, (2) use an EXISTS subquery to check for a subsequent completed order within 30 days, (3) aggregate into cohort months. CAST(order_date AS DATE) is required because order_date is stored as a timestamp. Adding 30 to a DATE in DuckDB adds 30 days (integer arithmetic on dates).
hints: Retention has two parts: anchoring each user's first-order date, then checking whether a subsequent order appeared within 30 days of it.
CAST(order_date AS DATE) + 30 adds 30 days to a date in DuckDB.

title: Monthly cart-to-purchase conversion rate
description: A product analyst wants to track the funnel efficiency over time. For each calendar month, compute: the number of distinct users who fired an add_to_cart event, the number who fired a purchase event, and the conversion rate (purchased / added_to_cart as a percentage, rounded to 1 decimal). Order by month.
expected_query:
WITH monthly_funnel AS (
  SELECT
    strftime(event_time, '%Y-%m') AS month,
    COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event_name = 'add_to_cart' THEN user_id END) AS added_to_cart,
    COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event_name = 'purchase' THEN user_id END) AS purchased
  FROM events
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT
  month,
  added_to_cart,
  purchased,
  ROUND(100.0 * purchased / NULLIF(added_to_cart, 0), 1) AS conversion_rate_pct
FROM monthly_funnel
ORDER BY month
solution_query:
WITH monthly_funnel AS (
  SELECT
    strftime(event_time, '%Y-%m') AS month,
    COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event_name = 'add_to_cart' THEN user_id END) AS added_to_cart,
    COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event_name = 'purchase' THEN user_id END) AS purchased
  FROM events
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT
  month,
  added_to_cart,
  purchased,
  ROUND(100.0 * purchased / NULLIF(added_to_cart, 0), 1) AS conversion_rate_pct
FROM monthly_funnel
ORDER BY month
explanation: COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event_name = 'X' THEN user_id END) is the standard pattern for counting distinct users who fired a specific event type within a group — it avoids a self-join or PIVOT. NULLIF prevents division by zero in months where nobody added to cart.
hints: You need unique user counts, but only for users who performed a specific event — embedding the event filter inside the aggregation preserves all rows for other calculations in the same pass.
Wrap the denominator in NULLIF(..., 0) to handle months with zero cart events.

title: Month-over-month revenue change by brand
description: A brand performance team wants to track revenue momentum. Using completed orders, compute monthly revenue per brand, then add a prev_month_revenue column and a mom_change_pct column (month-over-month percentage change, rounded to 1 decimal). Return all brand-month rows. Output columns: brand, month (YYYY-MM string), revenue, prev_month_revenue, mom_change_pct. Order by brand, month.
expected_query:
WITH monthly_rev AS (
  SELECT
    p.brand,
    strftime(CAST(o.order_date AS DATE), '%Y-%m') AS month,
    SUM(oi.line_amount) AS revenue
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY p.brand, month
)
SELECT
  brand,
  month,
  ROUND(revenue, 2) AS revenue,
  ROUND(LAG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY brand ORDER BY month), 2) AS prev_month_revenue,
  ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY brand ORDER BY month)) /
    NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY brand ORDER BY month), 0), 1) AS mom_change_pct
FROM monthly_rev
ORDER BY brand, month
solution_query:
WITH monthly_rev AS (
  SELECT
    p.brand,
    strftime(CAST(o.order_date AS DATE), '%Y-%m') AS month,
    SUM(oi.line_amount) AS revenue
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY p.brand, month
)
SELECT
  brand,
  month,
  ROUND(revenue, 2) AS revenue,
  ROUND(LAG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY brand ORDER BY month), 2) AS prev_month_revenue,
  ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY brand ORDER BY month)) /
    NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY brand ORDER BY month), 0), 1) AS mom_change_pct
FROM monthly_rev
ORDER BY brand, month
explanation: LAG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY brand ORDER BY month) looks back one row within each brand's ordered time series. NULLIF on the denominator prevents divide-by-zero for a brand's first month. Using line_amount from order_items avoids recalculating quantity * unit_price.
hints: Month-over-month change requires each month's value alongside its predecessor — build the monthly totals first, then compare within each brand's time series.
Wrap the LAG() denominator in NULLIF(..., 0) to guard against division by zero in the first month.

title: Early support ticket rate by plan tier
description: A customer success team suspects that certain plan tiers generate disproportionate early complaints. For each plan tier, compute: total_ordering_users (users with at least one completed order), users_with_early_ticket (users who opened a support ticket on the same day as their first completed order or up to 7 calendar days after it — inclusive window: day 0 through day 7), and pct (rounded to 1 decimal). Order by plan_tier.
expected_query:
WITH first_orders AS (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(CAST(order_date AS DATE)) AS first_order_date
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY user_id
),
early_tickets AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT st.user_id
  FROM support_tickets st
  JOIN first_orders fo ON st.user_id = fo.user_id
  WHERE CAST(st.created_at AS DATE) BETWEEN fo.first_order_date
    AND fo.first_order_date + 7
)
SELECT
  u.plan_tier,
  COUNT(DISTINCT fo.user_id) AS total_ordering_users,
  COUNT(DISTINCT et.user_id) AS users_with_early_ticket,
  ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT et.user_id) / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT fo.user_id), 0), 1) AS pct
FROM first_orders fo
JOIN users u ON fo.user_id = u.user_id
LEFT JOIN early_tickets et ON fo.user_id = et.user_id
GROUP BY u.plan_tier
ORDER BY u.plan_tier
solution_query:
WITH first_orders AS (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(CAST(order_date AS DATE)) AS first_order_date
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY user_id
),
early_tickets AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT st.user_id
  FROM support_tickets st
  JOIN first_orders fo ON st.user_id = fo.user_id
  WHERE CAST(st.created_at AS DATE) BETWEEN fo.first_order_date
    AND fo.first_order_date + 7
)
SELECT
  u.plan_tier,
  COUNT(DISTINCT fo.user_id) AS total_ordering_users,
  COUNT(DISTINCT et.user_id) AS users_with_early_ticket,
  ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT et.user_id) / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT fo.user_id), 0), 1) AS pct
FROM first_orders fo
JOIN users u ON fo.user_id = u.user_id
LEFT JOIN early_tickets et ON fo.user_id = et.user_id
GROUP BY u.plan_tier
ORDER BY u.plan_tier
explanation: Two CTEs scope the population: first_orders anchors the 7-day window per user, early_tickets identifies users who triggered within that window. A LEFT JOIN on early_tickets preserves all ordering users in the denominator — users without an early ticket get NULL which COUNT(DISTINCT) ignores. CAST(created_at AS DATE) handles the timestamp-to-date comparison.
hints: Build a CTE for each user's first order date, then a second CTE for users with a ticket within 7 days using BETWEEN.
LEFT JOIN the ticket CTE so users without early tickets are preserved in the denominator count.

title: Days-to-second-order reorder bucket distribution
description: A retention team wants to understand reorder velocity. For users who placed at least two completed orders, compute the number of days between their first and second order, then bucket users into: '0-7 days', '8-30 days', '31-90 days', '91+ days'. Return reorder_bucket and user_count. Order by the bucket's lower bound (shortest gap first).
expected_query:
WITH ordered_purchases AS (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    CAST(order_date AS DATE) AS order_date,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY order_date) AS order_num
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'completed'
),
first_two AS (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    MAX(CASE WHEN order_num = 1 THEN order_date END) AS first_order,
    MAX(CASE WHEN order_num = 2 THEN order_date END) AS second_order
  FROM ordered_purchases
  WHERE order_num <= 2
  GROUP BY user_id
  HAVING COUNT(*) = 2
),
gaps AS (
  SELECT (second_order - first_order) AS gap_days
  FROM first_two
)
SELECT
  CASE
    WHEN gap_days <= 7 THEN '0-7 days'
    WHEN gap_days <= 30 THEN '8-30 days'
    WHEN gap_days <= 90 THEN '31-90 days'
    ELSE '91+ days'
  END AS reorder_bucket,
  COUNT(*) AS user_count
FROM gaps
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY MIN(gap_days)
solution_query:
WITH ordered_purchases AS (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    CAST(order_date AS DATE) AS order_date,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY order_date) AS order_num
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'completed'
),
first_two AS (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    MAX(CASE WHEN order_num = 1 THEN order_date END) AS first_order,
    MAX(CASE WHEN order_num = 2 THEN order_date END) AS second_order
  FROM ordered_purchases
  WHERE order_num <= 2
  GROUP BY user_id
  HAVING COUNT(*) = 2
),
gaps AS (
  SELECT (second_order - first_order) AS gap_days
  FROM first_two
)
SELECT
  CASE
    WHEN gap_days <= 7 THEN '0-7 days'
    WHEN gap_days <= 30 THEN '8-30 days'
    WHEN gap_days <= 90 THEN '31-90 days'
    ELSE '91+ days'
  END AS reorder_bucket,
  COUNT(*) AS user_count
FROM gaps
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY MIN(gap_days)
explanation: ROW_NUMBER() assigns order sequence per user. The pivot using MAX(CASE WHEN order_num = 1 ...) brings first and second order onto one row. DATE subtraction gives integer days. HAVING COUNT(*) = 2 ensures both orders exist before pivoting. ORDER BY MIN(gap_days) produces natural bucket ordering without hardcoding string sort order.
hints: To compute the gap between a user's first and second order, bring both dates into the same row — establish order sequence numbers first, then pivot.
DATE subtraction in DuckDB returns integer days — use this to compute gap_days directly.

title: Products generating the first 80% of revenue
description: A finance team wants to identify which products drive the bulk of the business (Pareto analysis). Using completed orders, find all products whose cumulative revenue contribution (sorted from highest to lowest revenue) falls within the first 80% of total revenue — include the tipping product (the product at which the running cumulative revenue first reaches or exceeds 80% of total). Return product_id, product_name, revenue (rounded to 2 dp), and cum_pct (cumulative percentage of total revenue, rounded to 1 dp). For determinism when products share the same revenue, break ties by product_id ascending in both the cumulative-sum window ORDER BY and the final ORDER BY. Order by revenue descending, product_id ascending.
expected_query:
WITH product_rev AS (
  SELECT
    p.product_id,
    p.product_name,
    SUM(oi.line_amount) AS revenue
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
  JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name
),
with_running AS (
  SELECT *,
    SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC, product_id ASC ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS cumulative_rev,
    SUM(revenue) OVER () AS total_rev
  FROM product_rev
)
SELECT product_id, product_name, ROUND(revenue, 2) AS revenue,
       ROUND(100.0 * cumulative_rev / total_rev, 1) AS cum_pct
FROM with_running
WHERE (cumulative_rev - revenue) < 0.80 * total_rev
ORDER BY revenue DESC
solution_query:
WITH product_rev AS (
  SELECT
    p.product_id,
    p.product_name,
    SUM(oi.line_amount) AS revenue
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
  JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name
),
with_running AS (
  SELECT *,
    SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC, product_id ASC ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS cumulative_rev,
    SUM(revenue) OVER () AS total_rev
  FROM product_rev
)
SELECT product_id, product_name, ROUND(revenue, 2) AS revenue,
       ROUND(100.0 * cumulative_rev / total_rev, 1) AS cum_pct
FROM with_running
WHERE (cumulative_rev - revenue) < 0.80 * total_rev
ORDER BY revenue DESC
explanation: SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) computes a running total including the current row. The WHERE clause (cumulative_rev - revenue) < 0.80 * total_rev tests whether the running total *before* adding this row is still below 80% — including any row that pushes the total past the threshold.
hints: Sort products from highest to lowest revenue and accumulate — the cutoff is when the running total crosses 80% of the grand total.
The cutoff condition is (cumulative_rev - revenue) < 0.80 * total_rev — this includes the last product that tips the running total past 80%.

title: Completed orders with no matching paid payment
description: A data quality audit finds that some orders marked 'completed' have no corresponding payment with status='paid'. For each such product (via order_items), return product_id, product_name, and orders_without_payment (count of distinct order_ids with no paid payment). Order by orders_without_payment descending, then product_id ascending.
expected_query:
WITH completed_orders AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT o.order_id, p.product_id, p.product_name
  FROM orders o
  JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
  JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
),
paid_orders AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT order_id FROM payments WHERE status = 'paid'
)
SELECT
  co.product_id,
  co.product_name,
  COUNT(DISTINCT co.order_id) AS orders_without_payment
FROM completed_orders co
LEFT JOIN paid_orders po ON co.order_id = po.order_id
WHERE po.order_id IS NULL
GROUP BY co.product_id, co.product_name
ORDER BY orders_without_payment DESC, product_id ASC
solution_query:
WITH completed_orders AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT o.order_id, p.product_id, p.product_name
  FROM orders o
  JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
  JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
),
paid_orders AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT order_id FROM payments WHERE status = 'paid'
)
SELECT
  co.product_id,
  co.product_name,
  COUNT(DISTINCT co.order_id) AS orders_without_payment
FROM completed_orders co
LEFT JOIN paid_orders po ON co.order_id = po.order_id
WHERE po.order_id IS NULL
GROUP BY co.product_id, co.product_name
ORDER BY orders_without_payment DESC, product_id ASC
explanation: A LEFT JOIN followed by WHERE right_key IS NULL is the standard anti-join pattern — it finds rows in the left set with no match in the right set. This is more robust than NOT IN when the right set could contain NULLs. The two CTEs cleanly separate the two sets before joining.
hints: To find completed orders with no paid payment, look for orders with no corresponding record in the payments table — the pattern for surfacing absent relationships is the key technique here.
Isolate paid orders in a separate CTE first to keep the anti-join logic readable.

title: Salary percentile rank within department
description: HR wants to understand how each employee ranks relative to their department peers. Return employee_id, employee_name, department_name, salary, and salary_percentile (PERCENT_RANK within department, multiplied by 100 and rounded to 1 decimal). Order by department_name, then salary descending.
expected_query:
SELECT
  e.employee_id,
  e.employee_name,
  d.department_name,
  e.salary,
  ROUND(100.0 * PERCENT_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY e.department_id ORDER BY e.salary), 1) AS salary_percentile
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id
ORDER BY d.department_name, e.salary DESC
solution_query:
SELECT
  e.employee_id,
  e.employee_name,
  d.department_name,
  e.salary,
  ROUND(100.0 * PERCENT_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY e.department_id ORDER BY e.salary), 1) AS salary_percentile
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id
ORDER BY d.department_name, e.salary DESC
explanation: PERCENT_RANK() returns a value in [0, 1] where 0 is the lowest earner and 1 is the highest within the partition. Multiplying by 100 converts to a 0–100 scale. The lowest earner in each department gets 0.0% and the highest gets 100.0%.
hints: To express how a salary compares to others in the same department, think in terms of relative standing — what fraction of colleagues earn less than this person?
The lowest earner in each department gets percentile 0; the highest gets 100.

title: Departments where median salary exceeds mean salary
description: Following the percentile analysis, a finance partner notices that some departments appear to have outliers pulling the average down. Identify departments where the median salary is higher than the mean salary (indicating negative skew). Return department_name, mean_salary (rounded to 2 decimal places), median_salary (rounded to 2 decimal places), and median_minus_mean (rounded to 2 decimal places), ordered by that gap descending. Use PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) for the median.
expected_query:
WITH dept_stats AS (
  SELECT
    d.department_name,
    AVG(e.salary) AS mean_salary,
    PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY e.salary) AS median_salary
  FROM employees e
  JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id
  GROUP BY d.department_name
)
SELECT
  department_name,
  ROUND(mean_salary, 2) AS mean_salary,
  ROUND(median_salary, 2) AS median_salary,
  ROUND(median_salary - mean_salary, 2) AS median_minus_mean
FROM dept_stats
WHERE median_salary > mean_salary
ORDER BY (median_salary - mean_salary) DESC
solution_query:
WITH dept_stats AS (
  SELECT
    d.department_name,
    AVG(e.salary) AS mean_salary,
    PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY e.salary) AS median_salary
  FROM employees e
  JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id
  GROUP BY d.department_name
)
SELECT
  department_name,
  ROUND(mean_salary, 2) AS mean_salary,
  ROUND(median_salary, 2) AS median_salary,
  ROUND(median_salary - mean_salary, 2) AS median_minus_mean
FROM dept_stats
WHERE median_salary > mean_salary
ORDER BY (median_salary - mean_salary) DESC
explanation: PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary) computes the median using linear interpolation. When median > mean, the distribution is negatively skewed — a few low earners pull the mean below the median. This is a useful diagnostic when evaluating compensation equity.
hints: Mean and median serve different purposes — the median is the midpoint value in sorted order. SQL has an ordered-set aggregate that computes this per group.
When median > mean the distribution is negatively skewed — a few very low values pull the average down.

title: Average order value by support ticket history
description: A CX team wants to test whether users who have ever filed a support ticket have a different buying pattern. For each user with at least one completed order, compute their average order value, then segment users into 'With support ticket' vs 'No support ticket'. Return user_segment, user_count, and avg_order_value (rounded to 2 decimal places). Order by user_segment.
expected_query:
WITH user_aov AS (
  SELECT
    o.user_id,
    AVG(o.net_amount) AS aov
  FROM orders o
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY o.user_id
),
ticket_users AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM support_tickets
)
SELECT
  CASE WHEN tu.user_id IS NOT NULL THEN 'With support ticket' ELSE 'No support ticket' END AS user_segment,
  COUNT(DISTINCT ua.user_id) AS user_count,
  ROUND(AVG(ua.aov), 2) AS avg_order_value
FROM user_aov ua
LEFT JOIN ticket_users tu ON ua.user_id = tu.user_id
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1
solution_query:
WITH user_aov AS (
  SELECT
    o.user_id,
    AVG(o.net_amount) AS aov
  FROM orders o
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY o.user_id
),
ticket_users AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM support_tickets
)
SELECT
  CASE WHEN tu.user_id IS NOT NULL THEN 'With support ticket' ELSE 'No support ticket' END AS user_segment,
  COUNT(DISTINCT ua.user_id) AS user_count,
  ROUND(AVG(ua.aov), 2) AS avg_order_value
FROM user_aov ua
LEFT JOIN ticket_users tu ON ua.user_id = tu.user_id
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1
explanation: A LEFT JOIN on support ticket users preserves buyers with no tickets (NULL join key). CASE WHEN tu.user_id IS NOT NULL converts the NULL flag into a readable label. AVG(ua.aov) averages the per-user AOV — not the raw order amounts — so each user contributes equally regardless of order volume.
hints: Every buyer belongs to one of two segments — those with at least one support ticket and those without. The combination must preserve buyers who have no ticket on record.
CASE WHEN tu.user_id IS NOT NULL THEN 'With ...' handles the NULL resulting from no match.

title: Week-over-week unique active user change
description: A product team wants to monitor engagement momentum. Cover the last 56 days of activity (anchored to the maximum event_time in the dataset), bucketed by ISO week using date_trunc('week', event_time); partial weeks at the edges are expected. Compute unique_users, the previous week's unique_users (prev_week_users), and the absolute week-over-week change (wow_change). Output columns: week_start (TIMESTAMP — the Monday start of each ISO week, as returned by date_trunc), unique_users, prev_week_users, wow_change. Order by week_start ascending.
expected_query:
WITH weekly_users AS (
  SELECT
    date_trunc('week', event_time) AS week_start,
    COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS unique_users
  FROM events
  WHERE event_time >= (SELECT MAX(event_time) FROM events) - INTERVAL '56 days'
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT
  week_start,
  unique_users,
  LAG(unique_users) OVER (ORDER BY week_start) AS prev_week_users,
  unique_users - LAG(unique_users) OVER (ORDER BY week_start) AS wow_change
FROM weekly_users
ORDER BY week_start
solution_query:
WITH weekly_users AS (
  SELECT
    date_trunc('week', event_time) AS week_start,
    COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS unique_users
  FROM events
  WHERE event_time >= (SELECT MAX(event_time) FROM events) - INTERVAL '56 days'
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT
  week_start,
  unique_users,
  LAG(unique_users) OVER (ORDER BY week_start) AS prev_week_users,
  unique_users - LAG(unique_users) OVER (ORDER BY week_start) AS wow_change
FROM weekly_users
ORDER BY week_start
explanation: Anchoring the window to MAX(event_time) makes the query dataset-agnostic. LAG() over the ordered CTE looks one row back — no self-join needed. The first week's LAG returns NULL (no prior week), which is expected and informative.
hints: Week-over-week change requires each week's user count next to the prior week's — compute weekly totals first, then look back one row in the ordered time series.
Use MAX(event_time) as the anchor to avoid hardcoding a date.

title: Top-ranked products by unique buyers
description: A sales team wants to identify the most broadly appealing products (distinct buyers, not just order volume). Using completed orders, compute unique_buyers per product, then return all products whose DENSE_RANK ≤ 5; ties at the cutoff are included, so the result may exceed 5 rows. Include product_id, product_name, unique_buyers, and buyer_rank. Order by buyer_rank, then product_id.
expected_query:
WITH product_buyers AS (
  SELECT
    p.product_id,
    p.product_name,
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.user_id) AS unique_buyers
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name
),
ranked AS (
  SELECT *,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY unique_buyers DESC) AS buyer_rank
  FROM product_buyers
)
SELECT product_id, product_name, unique_buyers, buyer_rank
FROM ranked
WHERE buyer_rank <= 5
ORDER BY buyer_rank, product_id
solution_query:
WITH product_buyers AS (
  SELECT
    p.product_id,
    p.product_name,
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.user_id) AS unique_buyers
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name
)
,ranked AS (
  SELECT *,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY unique_buyers DESC) AS buyer_rank
  FROM product_buyers
)
SELECT product_id, product_name, unique_buyers, buyer_rank
FROM ranked
WHERE buyer_rank <= 5
ORDER BY buyer_rank, product_id
explanation: DENSE_RANK() is preferred over ROW_NUMBER() here because tied products should share the same rank — a tie at rank 3 should not push a product to rank 4. WHERE buyer_rank <= 5 returns all products with ranks 1 through 5, including any ties at rank 5.
hints: When selecting the top 5, decide what should happen when two products are tied at the cutoff — some approaches give tied items the same position, others break the tie.
Filter WHERE buyer_rank <= 5 — if two products are tied at rank 5, both are included.

title: Revenue gap between orders and payments tables
description: A finance team suspects the orders and payments tables have discrepancies. For completed orders, compare each order's net_amount to the sum of its paid payment amounts. Return a summary: orders_with_gap (count of orders where |discrepancy| > 0.01), total_revenue_gap, avg_gap_per_order, min_discrepancy, and max_discrepancy — all rounded to 2 decimal places.
expected_query:
WITH order_totals AS (
  SELECT order_id, net_amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed'
),
payment_totals AS (
  SELECT order_id, SUM(amount) AS paid_amount
  FROM payments
  WHERE status = 'paid'
  GROUP BY order_id
),
gaps AS (
  SELECT
    ot.order_id,
    ot.net_amount,
    COALESCE(pt.paid_amount, 0) AS paid_amount,
    ot.net_amount - COALESCE(pt.paid_amount, 0) AS discrepancy
  FROM order_totals ot
  LEFT JOIN payment_totals pt ON ot.order_id = pt.order_id
)
SELECT
  COUNT(*) AS orders_with_gap,
  ROUND(SUM(discrepancy), 2) AS total_revenue_gap,
  ROUND(AVG(discrepancy), 2) AS avg_gap_per_order,
  ROUND(MIN(discrepancy), 2) AS min_discrepancy,
  ROUND(MAX(discrepancy), 2) AS max_discrepancy
FROM gaps
WHERE ABS(discrepancy) > 0.01
solution_query:
WITH order_totals AS (
  SELECT order_id, net_amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed'
),
payment_totals AS (
  SELECT order_id, SUM(amount) AS paid_amount
  FROM payments
  WHERE status = 'paid'
  GROUP BY order_id
),
gaps AS (
  SELECT
    ot.order_id,
    ot.net_amount,
    COALESCE(pt.paid_amount, 0) AS paid_amount,
    ot.net_amount - COALESCE(pt.paid_amount, 0) AS discrepancy
  FROM order_totals ot
  LEFT JOIN payment_totals pt ON ot.order_id = pt.order_id
)
SELECT
  COUNT(*) AS orders_with_gap,
  ROUND(SUM(discrepancy), 2) AS total_revenue_gap,
  ROUND(AVG(discrepancy), 2) AS avg_gap_per_order,
  ROUND(MIN(discrepancy), 2) AS min_discrepancy,
  ROUND(MAX(discrepancy), 2) AS max_discrepancy
FROM gaps
WHERE ABS(discrepancy) > 0.01
explanation: Three CTEs separate concerns: order amounts, payment sums, and the discrepancy calculation. COALESCE handles orders with no payment record (gap = full order amount). ABS(discrepancy) > 0.01 filters floating-point near-zeros. This is a canonical data reconciliation pattern used in finance and billing audits.
hints: When reconciling two tables, the direction of the combination determines which gaps are visible — orders with no payment record must not be silently dropped.
Use COALESCE(paid_amount, 0) to handle NULLs from the LEFT JOIN before computing discrepancy.

title: Signup-to-first-order latency percentile distribution
description: A growth team wants to understand how quickly new users convert to buyers. Consider only users whose first-ever completed order was on or after their signup_date. For those users, compute the number of days from signup_date to that first completed order date, then return the 25th, 50th, 75th, and 90th percentiles of that day count as continuous/interpolated percentiles (PERCENTILE_CONT), left unrounded; the average (rounded to 1 decimal); and the user count. Output columns: p25_days, p50_days, p75_days, p90_days, avg_days, total_users.
expected_query:
WITH first_orders AS (
  SELECT
    u.user_id,
    u.signup_date,
    MIN(CAST(o.order_date AS DATE)) AS first_order_date
  FROM users u
  JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY u.user_id, u.signup_date
),
days_to_order AS (
  SELECT (first_order_date - signup_date) AS days_gap
  FROM first_orders
  WHERE first_order_date >= signup_date
)
SELECT
  PERCENTILE_CONT(0.25) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY days_gap) AS p25_days,
  PERCENTILE_CONT(0.50) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY days_gap) AS p50_days,
  PERCENTILE_CONT(0.75) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY days_gap) AS p75_days,
  PERCENTILE_CONT(0.90) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY days_gap) AS p90_days,
  ROUND(AVG(days_gap), 1) AS avg_days,
  COUNT(*) AS total_users
FROM days_to_order
solution_query:
WITH first_orders AS (
  SELECT
    u.user_id,
    u.signup_date,
    MIN(CAST(o.order_date AS DATE)) AS first_order_date
  FROM users u
  JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY u.user_id, u.signup_date
),
days_to_order AS (
  SELECT (first_order_date - signup_date) AS days_gap
  FROM first_orders
  WHERE first_order_date >= signup_date
)
SELECT
  PERCENTILE_CONT(0.25) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY days_gap) AS p25_days,
  PERCENTILE_CONT(0.50) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY days_gap) AS p50_days,
  PERCENTILE_CONT(0.75) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY days_gap) AS p75_days,
  PERCENTILE_CONT(0.90) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY days_gap) AS p90_days,
  ROUND(AVG(days_gap), 1) AS avg_days,
  COUNT(*) AS total_users
FROM days_to_order
explanation: DATE - DATE in DuckDB returns integer days, so first_order_date - signup_date is the gap directly. PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY ...) is the SQL standard median/percentile function. The WHERE first_order_date >= signup_date guards against data anomalies where an order precedes signup.
hints: DATE - DATE in DuckDB returns integer days — use this to compute days_gap directly.
PERCENTILE_CONT(p) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY col) computes percentiles — use it four times for p25/p50/p75/p90.

title: 30-day signup-to-purchase conversion rate by month
description: A growth team wants to track how quickly new user cohorts convert to buyers. For each signup month, return total_signups, fast_converters (users whose first completed order was within 30 days of signup), and conversion_rate_pct (rounded to 1 decimal). Output columns: signup_month (YYYY-MM string), total_signups, fast_converters, conversion_rate_pct. Order by signup_month.
expected_query:
WITH signups AS (
  SELECT user_id, signup_date FROM users
),
first_orders AS (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(CAST(order_date AS DATE)) AS first_order_date
  FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY user_id
),
fast_converters AS (
  SELECT
    s.user_id,
    s.signup_date,
    (fo.first_order_date - s.signup_date) AS days_to_convert
  FROM signups s
  LEFT JOIN first_orders fo ON s.user_id = fo.user_id
)
SELECT
  strftime(signup_date, '%Y-%m') AS signup_month,
  COUNT(*) AS total_signups,
  SUM(CASE WHEN days_to_convert IS NOT NULL AND days_to_convert <= 30 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS fast_converters,
  ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN days_to_convert IS NOT NULL AND days_to_convert <= 30 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS conversion_rate_pct
FROM fast_converters
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1
solution_query:
WITH signups AS (
  SELECT user_id, signup_date FROM users
),
first_orders AS (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(CAST(order_date AS DATE)) AS first_order_date
  FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY user_id
),
fast_converters AS (
  SELECT
    s.user_id,
    s.signup_date,
    (fo.first_order_date - s.signup_date) AS days_to_convert
  FROM signups s
  LEFT JOIN first_orders fo ON s.user_id = fo.user_id
)
SELECT
  strftime(signup_date, '%Y-%m') AS signup_month,
  COUNT(*) AS total_signups,
  SUM(CASE WHEN days_to_convert IS NOT NULL AND days_to_convert <= 30 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS fast_converters,
  ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN days_to_convert IS NOT NULL AND days_to_convert <= 30 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS conversion_rate_pct
FROM fast_converters
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1
explanation: Three CTEs build up the logic: signups anchors the population, first_orders finds each user's earliest purchase, fast_converters computes the days gap. A LEFT JOIN on first_orders preserves users with no purchase (their gap is NULL). The CASE WHEN in the outer aggregation counts only users with a gap ≤ 30 days.
hints: The conversion rate includes non-purchasers in the denominator — the approach must keep users with no orders in the result, not silently exclude them.
In the final aggregation, use CASE WHEN days_to_convert IS NOT NULL AND days_to_convert <= 30 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END.

title: Order basket size distribution
description: An e-commerce analyst wants to understand how large orders typically are. For completed orders, compute the total quantity of items per order, then bucket orders into: '1 item', '2-3 items', '4-5 items', '6+ items'. Return basket_size, order_count, and pct_of_orders (rounded to 1 decimal). Order by the bucket's lower bound (shortest first).
expected_query:
WITH order_item_counts AS (
  SELECT oi.order_id, SUM(oi.quantity) AS total_items
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY oi.order_id
)
SELECT
  CASE
    WHEN total_items = 1 THEN '1 item'
    WHEN total_items <= 3 THEN '2-3 items'
    WHEN total_items <= 5 THEN '4-5 items'
    ELSE '6+ items'
  END AS basket_size,
  COUNT(*) AS order_count,
  ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_orders
FROM order_item_counts
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY MIN(total_items)
solution_query:
WITH order_item_counts AS (
  SELECT oi.order_id, SUM(oi.quantity) AS total_items
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY oi.order_id
)
SELECT
  CASE
    WHEN total_items = 1 THEN '1 item'
    WHEN total_items <= 3 THEN '2-3 items'
    WHEN total_items <= 5 THEN '4-5 items'
    ELSE '6+ items'
  END AS basket_size,
  COUNT(*) AS order_count,
  ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_orders
FROM order_item_counts
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY MIN(total_items)
explanation: SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER () is a window function applied after GROUP BY — it sums all group counts to get the grand total for percentage computation. ORDER BY MIN(total_items) sorts buckets naturally (1, 2, 4, 6) rather than alphabetically.
hints: Two steps: compute total item quantity per order, then assign each order to a size bucket based on that total.
SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER () gives the grand total after grouping — divide each bucket count by this for the percentage.

title: Session abandonment rate by traffic source
description: A marketing team wants to understand which acquisition channels have the highest session abandonment (sessions with no purchase event). For each traffic_source, return total_sessions, abandoned_sessions (no purchase event in the session), and abandonment_rate_pct (rounded to 1 decimal). Order by abandonment_rate_pct descending.
expected_query:
WITH session_purchase AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT session_id FROM events WHERE event_name = 'purchase'
),
session_info AS (
  SELECT
    s.session_id,
    s.traffic_source,
    CASE WHEN sp.session_id IS NOT NULL THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS abandoned
  FROM sessions s
  LEFT JOIN session_purchase sp ON s.session_id = sp.session_id
)
SELECT
  traffic_source,
  COUNT(*) AS total_sessions,
  SUM(abandoned) AS abandoned_sessions,
  ROUND(100.0 * SUM(abandoned) / COUNT(*), 1) AS abandonment_rate_pct
FROM session_info
GROUP BY traffic_source
ORDER BY abandonment_rate_pct DESC
solution_query:
WITH session_purchase AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT session_id FROM events WHERE event_name = 'purchase'
),
session_info AS (
  SELECT
    s.session_id,
    s.traffic_source,
    CASE WHEN sp.session_id IS NOT NULL THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS abandoned
  FROM sessions s
  LEFT JOIN session_purchase sp ON s.session_id = sp.session_id
)
SELECT
  traffic_source,
  COUNT(*) AS total_sessions,
  SUM(abandoned) AS abandoned_sessions,
  ROUND(100.0 * SUM(abandoned) / COUNT(*), 1) AS abandonment_rate_pct
FROM session_info
GROUP BY traffic_source
ORDER BY abandonment_rate_pct DESC
explanation: First CTE identifies sessions that had at least one purchase event. LEFT JOIN preserves sessions with no purchase (NULL join key). CASE WHEN converts the NULL flag into a 0/1 abandoned indicator. SUM(abandoned) / COUNT(*) gives the abandonment rate per source.
hints: Start with all sessions and flag which ones contain a purchase — sessions without that flag are the abandoned ones.
CASE WHEN sp.session_id IS NOT NULL THEN 0 ELSE 1 END creates the abandoned flag for SUM().

title: Customer lifetime value by acquisition channel
description: A growth analyst wants to assess which acquisition channels produce the highest-value customers. For each acquisition_channel (including NULL as a distinct channel value representing users with no recorded channel), return the number of buyers (users with at least one completed order), avg_ltv (average total net_amount per buyer, rounded to 2 decimal places), and total_revenue (sum of all completed-order net_amounts for that channel's buyers, rounded to 2 decimal places). Order by avg_ltv descending.
expected_query:
WITH user_ltv AS (
  SELECT
    u.user_id,
    u.acquisition_channel,
    SUM(o.net_amount) AS total_spent
  FROM users u
  JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY u.user_id, u.acquisition_channel
)
SELECT
  acquisition_channel,
  COUNT(*) AS buyers,
  ROUND(AVG(total_spent), 2) AS avg_ltv,
  ROUND(SUM(total_spent), 2) AS total_revenue
FROM user_ltv
GROUP BY acquisition_channel
ORDER BY avg_ltv DESC
solution_query:
WITH user_ltv AS (
  SELECT
    u.user_id,
