    u.acquisition_channel,
    SUM(o.net_amount) AS total_spent
  FROM users u
  JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
  WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY u.user_id, u.acquisition_channel
)
SELECT
  acquisition_channel,
  COUNT(*) AS buyers,
  ROUND(AVG(total_spent), 2) AS avg_ltv,
  ROUND(SUM(total_spent), 2) AS total_revenue
FROM user_ltv
GROUP BY acquisition_channel
ORDER BY avg_ltv DESC
explanation: Two-level aggregation: first sum orders per user (user_ltv CTE), then average those per-user totals by channel (outer query). This matters because AVG(net_amount) directly would weight by order count rather than user — a user with 10 small orders would count more than a user with 1 large order.
hints: First aggregate total spending per user in a CTE, then average those per-user totals by channel.
Direct AVG(net_amount) would weight by order count, not user count — always aggregate to user level first.

title: Department payroll share of total company payroll
description: Finance wants a payroll breakdown. For each department, return department_name, headcount (employee count), dept_payroll (total salary, rounded to 2 decimal places), and payroll_share_pct (department payroll as a percentage of company total, rounded to 1 decimal). Order by dept_payroll descending.
expected_query:
SELECT
  d.department_name,
  COUNT(e.employee_id) AS headcount,
  ROUND(SUM(e.salary), 2) AS dept_payroll,
  ROUND(100.0 * SUM(e.salary) / SUM(SUM(e.salary)) OVER (), 1) AS payroll_share_pct
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id
GROUP BY d.department_name
ORDER BY dept_payroll DESC
solution_query:
SELECT
  d.department_name,
  COUNT(e.employee_id) AS headcount,
  ROUND(SUM(e.salary), 2) AS dept_payroll,
  ROUND(100.0 * SUM(e.salary) / SUM(SUM(e.salary)) OVER (), 1) AS payroll_share_pct
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id
GROUP BY d.department_name
ORDER BY dept_payroll DESC
explanation: SUM(SUM(e.salary)) OVER () is an aggregate-inside-a-window-function — the inner SUM() aggregates per group, the outer SUM() OVER () sums all groups to produce the grand total. This avoids a CTE or self-join just to compute the total.
hints: Department payroll share needs the department total and the company-wide total simultaneously — a window over the grouped result can supply the company total without a separate query.
No CTE needed for this pattern — the nested aggregate window function handles it in one pass.

title: Revenue from repeat buyers vs one-time buyers
description: A retention analyst wants to quantify the value of repeat customers. Segment users with completed orders into 'One-time buyer' (exactly 1 completed order) and 'Repeat buyer' (2+ completed orders). Return segment, user_count, total_revenue, and avg_revenue_per_user (both rounded to 2 decimal places). Order by segment.
expected_query:
WITH user_order_count AS (
  SELECT user_id,
    COUNT(*) AS order_count,
    SUM(net_amount) AS total_spent
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY user_id
),
buyer_segments AS (
  SELECT
    CASE WHEN order_count = 1 THEN 'One-time buyer' ELSE 'Repeat buyer' END AS segment,
    total_spent
  FROM user_order_count
)
SELECT
  segment,
  COUNT(*) AS user_count,
  ROUND(SUM(total_spent), 2) AS total_revenue,
  ROUND(AVG(total_spent), 2) AS avg_revenue_per_user
FROM buyer_segments
GROUP BY segment
ORDER BY segment
solution_query:
WITH user_order_count AS (
  SELECT user_id,
    COUNT(*) AS order_count,
    SUM(net_amount) AS total_spent
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY user_id
),
buyer_segments AS (
  SELECT
    CASE WHEN order_count = 1 THEN 'One-time buyer' ELSE 'Repeat buyer' END AS segment,
    total_spent
  FROM user_order_count
)
SELECT
  segment,
  COUNT(*) AS user_count,
  ROUND(SUM(total_spent), 2) AS total_revenue,
  ROUND(AVG(total_spent), 2) AS avg_revenue_per_user
FROM buyer_segments
GROUP BY segment
ORDER BY segment
explanation: Two CTEs: user_order_count aggregates per-user, buyer_segments applies the segmentation logic. The outer query then aggregates the segments. Three-level thinking: row → user → segment. AVG(total_spent) averages per-user lifetime values — if you used AVG(net_amount) directly you'd weight by order count instead of user count.
hints: First aggregate order count and total spend per user, then apply CASE WHEN order_count = 1 to assign segment.
Aggregate at segment level in the outer query — not at the order level, to avoid weighting by order volume.

title: User acquisition funnel by signup cohort
description: A product analyst wants to track how each signup cohort progresses through the funnel: signup → any event → first completed order. For each signup_month, return signed_up, had_first_event, made_first_purchase, event_rate_pct, and purchase_rate_pct (both rounded to 1 decimal). had_first_event = the user has any event on record (lifetime, across all of `events`); made_first_purchase = the user has at least one completed order on record (lifetime, across all of `orders` with status = 'completed'). Neither is required to occur after signup or in the same cohort period — these are lifetime funnel presence flags. Output columns: signup_month (YYYY-MM string), signed_up, had_first_event, made_first_purchase, event_rate_pct, purchase_rate_pct. Order by signup_month.
expected_query:
WITH signups AS (
  SELECT user_id, signup_date FROM users
),
first_events AS (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(CAST(event_time AS DATE)) AS first_event_date
  FROM events
  GROUP BY user_id
),
first_orders AS (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(CAST(order_date AS DATE)) AS first_order_date
  FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT
  strftime(s.signup_date, '%Y-%m') AS signup_month,
  COUNT(*) AS signed_up,
  COUNT(fe.user_id) AS had_first_event,
  COUNT(fo.user_id) AS made_first_purchase,
  ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(fe.user_id) / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0), 1) AS event_rate_pct,
  ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(fo.user_id) / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0), 1) AS purchase_rate_pct
FROM signups s
LEFT JOIN first_events fe ON s.user_id = fe.user_id
LEFT JOIN first_orders fo ON s.user_id = fo.user_id
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1
solution_query:
WITH signups AS (
  SELECT user_id, signup_date FROM users
),
first_events AS (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(CAST(event_time AS DATE)) AS first_event_date
  FROM events
  GROUP BY user_id
),
first_orders AS (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(CAST(order_date AS DATE)) AS first_order_date
  FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT
  strftime(s.signup_date, '%Y-%m') AS signup_month,
  COUNT(*) AS signed_up,
  COUNT(fe.user_id) AS had_first_event,
  COUNT(fo.user_id) AS made_first_purchase,
  ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(fe.user_id) / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0), 1) AS event_rate_pct,
  ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(fo.user_id) / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0), 1) AS purchase_rate_pct
FROM signups s
LEFT JOIN first_events fe ON s.user_id = fe.user_id
LEFT JOIN first_orders fo ON s.user_id = fo.user_id
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1
explanation: Two LEFT JOINs bring in event and order presence per user. COUNT(fe.user_id) counts non-NULL values — users who had no event contribute NULL (not counted), automatically computing the correct numerator. This is cleaner than SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) for funnel counts.
hints: A funnel preserves all users at every stage — users who did not reach a step should appear with a count of zero, not disappear from the result entirely.
COUNT(fe.user_id) counts only users who matched the event join — NULLs from non-matches are not counted.

title: Support ticket SLA compliance by priority
description: A support lead defines SLA as: tickets resolved within 24 hours. For each priority level, return total_tickets, within_sla (resolved tickets with resolution_hours <= 24), total_resolved, sla_compliance_pct (within_sla / total_resolved as %, rounded to 1 decimal), and avg_resolution_hours (rounded to 1 decimal). Order by urgency: urgent → high → medium → low.
expected_query:
SELECT
  priority,
  COUNT(*) AS total_tickets,
  SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'resolved' AND resolution_hours <= 24 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS within_sla,
  SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'resolved' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS total_resolved,
  ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'resolved' AND resolution_hours <= 24 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) /
    NULLIF(SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'resolved' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 0), 1) AS sla_compliance_pct,
  ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN status = 'resolved' THEN resolution_hours END), 1) AS avg_resolution_hours
FROM support_tickets
GROUP BY priority
ORDER BY
  CASE priority WHEN 'urgent' THEN 1 WHEN 'high' THEN 2 WHEN 'medium' THEN 3 ELSE 4 END
solution_query:
SELECT
  priority,
  COUNT(*) AS total_tickets,
  SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'resolved' AND resolution_hours <= 24 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS within_sla,
  SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'resolved' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS total_resolved,
  ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'resolved' AND resolution_hours <= 24 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) /
    NULLIF(SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'resolved' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 0), 1) AS sla_compliance_pct,
  ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN status = 'resolved' THEN resolution_hours END), 1) AS avg_resolution_hours
FROM support_tickets
GROUP BY priority
ORDER BY
  CASE priority WHEN 'urgent' THEN 1 WHEN 'high' THEN 2 WHEN 'medium' THEN 3 ELSE 4 END
explanation: Multiple CASE WHEN expressions in one GROUP BY pass compute three different conditional counts simultaneously. AVG(CASE WHEN status = 'resolved' THEN resolution_hours END) automatically ignores NULL (unresolved tickets) — equivalent to filtering then averaging. ORDER BY CASE sorts by business priority order rather than alphabetically.
hints: SLA compliance requires counting several things from the same ticket set — all can be derived in one pass using conditional aggregation.
ORDER BY CASE priority WHEN 'urgent' THEN 1 ... END to sort by business severity rather than alphabetically.

title: User recency segmentation: Active, Lapsing, Churned
description: A CRM team wants to classify users by how recently they were active. Anchor to the most recent event date in the dataset (treating event_time as a date). Classify each user by days since their last activity date: 'Active' (30 or fewer days ago), 'Lapsing' (31 to 90 days ago, inclusive of day 90), or 'Churned' (more than 90 days ago, i.e. 91 or more). Return segment, user_count, and avg_days_since_activity (rounded to 1 decimal). Order: Active first, then Lapsing, then Churned.
expected_query:
WITH last_event AS (
  SELECT user_id, MAX(CAST(event_time AS DATE)) AS last_activity_date
  FROM events
  GROUP BY user_id
),
anchor AS (
  SELECT MAX(CAST(event_time AS DATE)) AS max_date FROM events
),
segmented AS (
  SELECT
    le.user_id,
    (a.max_date - le.last_activity_date) AS days_since_last_activity,
    CASE
      WHEN (a.max_date - le.last_activity_date) <= 30 THEN 'Active'
      WHEN (a.max_date - le.last_activity_date) <= 90 THEN 'Lapsing'
      ELSE 'Churned'
    END AS segment
  FROM last_event le
  JOIN anchor a ON 1=1
)
SELECT
  segment,
  COUNT(*) AS user_count,
  ROUND(AVG(days_since_last_activity), 1) AS avg_days_since_activity
FROM segmented
GROUP BY segment
ORDER BY CASE segment WHEN 'Active' THEN 1 WHEN 'Lapsing' THEN 2 ELSE 3 END
solution_query:
WITH last_event AS (
  SELECT user_id, MAX(CAST(event_time AS DATE)) AS last_activity_date
  FROM events
  GROUP BY user_id
),
anchor AS (
  SELECT MAX(CAST(event_time AS DATE)) AS max_date FROM events
),
segmented AS (
  SELECT
    le.user_id,
    (a.max_date - le.last_activity_date) AS days_since_last_activity,
    CASE
      WHEN (a.max_date - le.last_activity_date) <= 30 THEN 'Active'
      WHEN (a.max_date - le.last_activity_date) <= 90 THEN 'Lapsing'
      ELSE 'Churned'
    END AS segment
  FROM last_event le
  JOIN anchor a ON 1=1
)
SELECT
  segment,
  COUNT(*) AS user_count,
  ROUND(AVG(days_since_last_activity), 1) AS avg_days_since_activity
FROM segmented
GROUP BY segment
ORDER BY CASE segment WHEN 'Active' THEN 1 WHEN 'Lapsing' THEN 2 ELSE 3 END
explanation: A CROSS JOIN with the single-row anchor CTE distributes the maximum date to every user row without a correlated subquery. DATE subtraction gives integer days. CASE WHEN applies the threshold logic. The final CASE in ORDER BY maps business segments to a sort order.
hints: Every user needs to be compared against the same reference date — compute that date once in isolation, then make it available to every user row efficiently.
DATE - DATE in DuckDB gives integer days — use this directly for the threshold checks.

title: Average order value by category diversity
description: A merchandising team hypothesises that multi-category orders are higher value. For completed orders, count distinct categories per order, then bucket into '1 category', '2 categories', '3+ categories'. Return category_diversity, order_count, and avg_net_amount (rounded to 2 decimal places). Order by the bucket's lower bound.
expected_query:
WITH order_category_count AS (
  SELECT
    oi.order_id,
    COUNT(DISTINCT p.category_id) AS category_count
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
  GROUP BY oi.order_id
)
SELECT
  CASE
    WHEN occ.category_count = 1 THEN '1 category'
    WHEN occ.category_count = 2 THEN '2 categories'
    ELSE '3+ categories'
  END AS category_diversity,
  COUNT(*) AS order_count,
  ROUND(AVG(o.net_amount), 2) AS avg_net_amount
FROM order_category_count occ
JOIN orders o ON occ.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY MIN(occ.category_count)
solution_query:
WITH order_category_count AS (
  SELECT
    oi.order_id,
    COUNT(DISTINCT p.category_id) AS category_count
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
  GROUP BY oi.order_id
)
SELECT
  CASE
    WHEN occ.category_count = 1 THEN '1 category'
    WHEN occ.category_count = 2 THEN '2 categories'
    ELSE '3+ categories'
  END AS category_diversity,
  COUNT(*) AS order_count,
  ROUND(AVG(o.net_amount), 2) AS avg_net_amount
FROM order_category_count occ
JOIN orders o ON occ.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY MIN(occ.category_count)
explanation: Two levels: first compute distinct categories per order (CTE), then join back to orders to get net_amount, apply bucket labels, and aggregate. ORDER BY MIN(category_count) ensures buckets sort in ascending bucket-size order regardless of the string labels.
hints: First measure how many different categories each order covers, then group orders into diversity buckets based on that breadth.
ORDER BY MIN(occ.category_count) sorts buckets naturally — '1 category' before '2 categories' before '3+' — regardless of string sort order.

title: Conversion rate denominator — observation window completeness
description: A funnel analysis reports a 7-day signup-to-first-purchase conversion rate. A skeptical stakeholder asks: 'Did every user in that cohort actually have 7 full days to convert?' Write a query that classifies every user as either `observation_complete` (signed up at least 7 days before the latest order in the dataset) or `observation_truncated` (signed up too recently to have a 7-day window). Return `group_label`, `user_count`, and `pct_of_cohort` (rounded to 1 decimal), ordered by group_label.
expected_query:
WITH cutoff AS (
    SELECT MAX(order_date) - INTERVAL '7 days' AS cutoff_date FROM orders
),
cohort AS (
    SELECT u.user_id,
           CASE WHEN u.signup_date <= c.cutoff_date
                THEN 'observation_complete'
                ELSE 'observation_truncated'
           END AS group_label
    FROM users u
    JOIN cutoff c ON 1=1
),
counts AS (
    SELECT group_label, COUNT(*) AS user_count
    FROM cohort
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT group_label,
       user_count,
       ROUND(100.0 * user_count / SUM(user_count) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_cohort
FROM counts
ORDER BY group_label
solution_query:
WITH cutoff AS (
    SELECT MAX(order_date) - INTERVAL '7 days' AS cutoff_date FROM orders
),
cohort AS (
    SELECT u.user_id,
           CASE WHEN u.signup_date <= c.cutoff_date
                THEN 'observation_complete'
                ELSE 'observation_truncated'
           END AS group_label
    FROM users u
    JOIN cutoff c ON 1=1
),
counts AS (
    SELECT group_label, COUNT(*) AS user_count
    FROM cohort
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT group_label,
       user_count,
       ROUND(100.0 * user_count / SUM(user_count) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_cohort
FROM counts
ORDER BY group_label;
explanation: The cutoff CTE derives a data-anchored boundary: the latest order date minus 7 days. The cohort CTE classifies each user as observation_complete or truncated relative to that boundary. The counts CTE aggregates by group and the outer query adds window-based percentage. If a large share falls into observation_truncated, the reported conversion rate is systematically understated — a critical sanity flag before presenting the metric.
hints: You need two things: each user's signup date and a cutoff that is 7 days before the latest activity in the dataset. The cutoff can be derived from the orders table without hardcoding a date.
Once you have the cutoff, classifying each user is a date comparison — then count each group and express each as a share of the total cohort.

title: Salary distribution shape before reporting department averages
description: Your report will state the average salary by department. Before publishing it, your manager asks you to verify that the average is a reliable summary and not distorted by outliers. Write a query that, for each department, returns the minimum, 25th-percentile, median, 75th-percentile, and maximum salary using PERCENTILE_CONT (the interpolating variant, not PERCENTILE_DISC). Return `department_name`, `min_salary`, `p25_salary`, `median_salary`, `p75_salary`, and `max_salary`, ordered by department_name.
expected_query:
SELECT d.department_name,
       MIN(e.salary)                                                   AS min_salary,
       PERCENTILE_CONT(0.25) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY e.salary)        AS p25_salary,
       PERCENTILE_CONT(0.50) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY e.salary)        AS median_salary,
       PERCENTILE_CONT(0.75) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY e.salary)        AS p75_salary,
       MAX(e.salary)                                                   AS max_salary
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id
GROUP BY d.department_name
ORDER BY d.department_name
solution_query:
SELECT d.department_name,
       MIN(e.salary)                                                   AS min_salary,
       PERCENTILE_CONT(0.25) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY e.salary)        AS p25_salary,
       PERCENTILE_CONT(0.50) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY e.salary)        AS median_salary,
       PERCENTILE_CONT(0.75) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY e.salary)        AS p75_salary,
       MAX(e.salary)                                                   AS max_salary
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id
GROUP BY d.department_name
ORDER BY d.department_name;
explanation: The min/max are standard aggregates. The quartile and median values use PERCENTILE_CONT(fraction) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary), an ordered-set aggregate that interpolates the value at a given quantile within each department group. A department with a large gap between p75 and max has salary outliers that would inflate the mean — this distribution check makes that visible before the summary goes out.
hints: The min and max are standard aggregates. The percentile values require an ordered-set aggregate that computes the value at a given quantile within each group — SQL has a built-in function for this.
Once you have the five distribution markers per department, compare p50 to the mean you would have reported — departments with a large p75-to-max gap are candidates for a caveat in your report.

title: Orphan order audit — completed orders with no line items
description: A per-order revenue pipeline joins `orders` to `order_items` to sum line amounts. Before trusting the output, verify that no completed order is silently excluded due to missing item rows. Write a diagnostic query that returns a single row with three figures: `total_completed_orders` (distinct orders with status='completed'), `orders_with_items` (completed orders that have at least one matching row in order_items), and `orders_without_items` (the gap between the two).
expected_query:
SELECT
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)                                          AS total_completed_orders,
    COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id)                                         AS orders_with_items,
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) - COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id)           AS orders_without_items
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
solution_query:
SELECT
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)                                          AS total_completed_orders,
    COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id)                                         AS orders_with_items,
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) - COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id)           AS orders_without_items
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed';
explanation: A LEFT JOIN from orders to order_items preserves completed orders even when no matching item rows exist. COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) counts all completed orders; COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) counts only those with at least one item row; the difference surfaces orphans. If orders_without_items > 0, any downstream revenue query that drops the unmatched orders will undercount both order volume and revenue.
hints: You need two counts: completed orders in the orders table, and completed orders that have at least one line item. Preserve all completed orders in the combination so you can detect the missing-item case.
The gap between the two counts reveals orphan orders — completed orders with no item rows that would produce NULL revenue in a downstream pipeline.

title: Collapse redundant orders CTEs — eliminate duplicate table scans
description:
The query below scans the `orders` table twice — once for order counts and once for revenue — then stitches the two results together. Rewrite it to scan `orders` exactly once while producing the same daily metrics.

```sql
WITH daily_orders AS (
    SELECT DATE_TRUNC('day', order_date)::DATE AS day, COUNT(*) AS order_count
    FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed' GROUP BY 1
),
daily_revenue AS (
    SELECT DATE_TRUNC('day', order_date)::DATE AS day, ROUND(SUM(net_amount),2) AS total_revenue
    FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed' GROUP BY 1
),
daily_signups AS (
    SELECT DATE_TRUNC('day', signup_date)::DATE AS day, COUNT(*) AS signup_count
    FROM users GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT o.day, o.order_count, r.total_revenue, s.signup_count
FROM daily_orders o
JOIN daily_revenue r ON o.day = r.day
LEFT JOIN daily_signups s ON o.day = s.day
ORDER BY o.day
```

Return `day`, `order_count`, `total_revenue`, and `signup_count`, ordered by `day` ascending.

Because both removed CTEs filter to `status = 'completed'`, the merged single-scan version is semantically equivalent.
expected_query:
WITH daily_orders_revenue AS (
    SELECT DATE_TRUNC('day', order_date)::DATE AS day,
           COUNT(*)                            AS order_count,
           ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2)           AS total_revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY 1
),
daily_signups AS (
    SELECT DATE_TRUNC('day', signup_date)::DATE AS day,
           COUNT(*) AS signup_count
    FROM users
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT o.day, o.order_count, o.total_revenue, s.signup_count
FROM daily_orders_revenue o
LEFT JOIN daily_signups s ON o.day = s.day
ORDER BY o.day
solution_query:
WITH daily_orders_revenue AS (
    SELECT DATE_TRUNC('day', order_date)::DATE AS day,
           COUNT(*)                            AS order_count,
           ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2)           AS total_revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY 1
),
daily_signups AS (
    SELECT DATE_TRUNC('day', signup_date)::DATE AS day,
           COUNT(*) AS signup_count
    FROM users
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT o.day, o.order_count, o.total_revenue, s.signup_count
FROM daily_orders_revenue o
LEFT JOIN daily_signups s ON o.day = s.day
ORDER BY o.day;
explanation: The original scans orders twice with the same filter and the same grouping key, then inner-joins the two CTEs. Two aggregations over the same source, same filter, and same grain can always be collapsed into one CTE — the daily_orders_revenue CTE computes both metrics in a single pass. The INNER JOIN between daily_orders and daily_revenue becomes unnecessary; only the LEFT JOIN to daily_signups remains.
hints: Two of the three CTEs scan the same source table with the same filter and the same time granularity — their metrics can be combined into a single aggregation pass without changing the result.

When two aggregations share the same source, the same filter, and the same grouping dimension, merging them into one CTE eliminates one full pass over the source data and removes a downstream combination step.

title: Push event filter before join to reduce cardinality
description:
The query below joins all 45,000 event rows to the sessions table before filtering to purchase events. Rewrite it to filter events to purchases first, then join — reducing the join's input from 45,000 rows to roughly 3,700.

```sql
SELECT s.device_type, s.traffic_source,
       COUNT(DISTINCT e.session_id) AS sessions_with_purchase
FROM events e
JOIN sessions s ON e.session_id = s.session_id
WHERE e.event_name = 'purchase'
GROUP BY s.device_type, s.traffic_source
ORDER BY sessions_with_purchase DESC, s.device_type, s.traffic_source
```

Return `device_type`, `traffic_source`, and `sessions_with_purchase`, ordered by `sessions_with_purchase` descending, then `device_type` and `traffic_source` ascending.
expected_query:
WITH purchase_sessions AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT session_id
    FROM events
    WHERE event_name = 'purchase'
)
SELECT s.device_type, s.traffic_source,
       COUNT(ps.session_id) AS sessions_with_purchase
FROM purchase_sessions ps
JOIN sessions s ON ps.session_id = s.session_id
GROUP BY s.device_type, s.traffic_source
ORDER BY sessions_with_purchase DESC, s.device_type, s.traffic_source
solution_query:
WITH purchase_sessions AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT session_id
    FROM events
    WHERE event_name = 'purchase'
)
SELECT s.device_type, s.traffic_source,
       COUNT(ps.session_id) AS sessions_with_purchase
FROM purchase_sessions ps
JOIN sessions s ON ps.session_id = s.session_id
GROUP BY s.device_type, s.traffic_source
ORDER BY sessions_with_purchase DESC, s.device_type, s.traffic_source;
explanation: Filtering events to purchases inside a CTE before the join reduces the join's left-side cardinality from ~45K to ~3.7K rows — a 12x reduction. The DISTINCT in the CTE also deduplicates session IDs so the outer query can use COUNT instead of COUNT(DISTINCT). Query optimisers may reorder predicates, but explicit pre-filtering makes the intent clear and is robust across planning strategies.
hints: Only purchase events contribute to the output — filtering to that subset before combining with sessions reduces the number of rows the combination must process by roughly 12x.
After isolating the relevant event rows, deduplicate by session so each session appears at most once before combining with session attributes.

title: Top 10 spenders — pre-aggregate and limit instead of window-then-filter
description:
The query below uses a window function to number all users by total spend, then filters to the top 10. This numbers every user before discarding most of them. Rewrite it to compute the top 10 more directly — aggregate spend per user, sort, and limit without numbering every row.

```sql
WITH user_spend AS (
    SELECT user_id, ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS total_spend
    FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed' GROUP BY user_id
),
ranked AS (
    SELECT user_id, total_spend,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY total_spend DESC, user_id) AS rn
    FROM user_spend
)
SELECT u.user_id, u.name, r.total_spend
FROM ranked r
JOIN users u ON r.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE r.rn <= 10
ORDER BY r.total_spend DESC, r.user_id
```

Return `user_id`, `name`, and `total_spend`, ordered by `total_spend` descending, then `user_id` ascending.
expected_query:
WITH user_spend AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS total_spend
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY user_id
    ORDER BY total_spend DESC, user_id
    LIMIT 10
)
SELECT u.user_id, u.name, us.total_spend
FROM user_spend us
JOIN users u ON us.user_id = u.user_id
ORDER BY us.total_spend DESC, us.user_id
solution_query:
WITH user_spend AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS total_spend
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY user_id
    ORDER BY total_spend DESC, user_id
    LIMIT 10
)
SELECT u.user_id, u.name, us.total_spend
FROM user_spend us
JOIN users u ON us.user_id = u.user_id
ORDER BY us.total_spend DESC, us.user_id;
explanation: The original numbers every user's spend with ROW_NUMBER() across the full aggregated result, then discards all but 10 rows. Moving the sort and LIMIT into the CTE stops materialization at 10 rows — no window function is needed when the goal is simply the top-N by a single sort key. Both approaches use the same tie-breaking (total_spend DESC, user_id ASC) so results are identical.
hints: The two-CTE version numbers every user's spend before filtering to 10 — but the numbering is only needed to apply the cutoff. What if you applied the cutoff directly at the aggregation step instead?
Once spend is aggregated per user, applying a sort and a row limit inside that aggregation step stops you from materialising results you will never use.

title: Category revenue ranking with parent and gap
description: For each product category compute `total_revenue` (rounded to 2 dp), `revenue_rank` (1 = highest, using `RANK()`), `parent_category`, and `revenue_vs_top` — how far each category's revenue is below the top category (positive number, rounded to 2 dp). Return `category_name`, `total_revenue`, `revenue_rank`, `parent_category`, and `revenue_vs_top`. Order by `revenue_rank` ascending, then `category_name` ascending to break ties within the same rank.
expected_query:
WITH cat_revenue AS (
    SELECT c.category_name, c.category_id, ROUND(SUM(oi.line_amount),2) AS total_revenue
    FROM order_items oi
    JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
    JOIN categories c ON p.category_id = c.category_id
    GROUP BY c.category_name, c.category_id
)
SELECT cr.category_name, cr.total_revenue,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY cr.total_revenue DESC) AS revenue_rank,
       c.parent_category,
       ROUND(MAX(cr.total_revenue) OVER () - cr.total_revenue, 2) AS revenue_vs_top
FROM cat_revenue cr
JOIN categories c ON cr.category_id = c.category_id
ORDER BY revenue_rank, category_name ASC
solution_query:
WITH cat_revenue AS (
    SELECT c.category_name, c.category_id,
           ROUND(SUM(oi.line_amount), 2) AS total_revenue
    FROM order_items oi
    JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
    JOIN categories c ON p.category_id = c.category_id
    GROUP BY c.category_name, c.category_id
)
SELECT cr.category_name, cr.total_revenue,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY cr.total_revenue DESC) AS revenue_rank,
       c.parent_category,
       ROUND(MAX(cr.total_revenue) OVER () - cr.total_revenue, 2) AS revenue_vs_top
FROM cat_revenue cr
JOIN categories c ON cr.category_id = c.category_id
ORDER BY revenue_rank, category_name ASC;
explanation: The CTE computes per-category revenue. RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total_revenue DESC) assigns global rank. MAX(total_revenue) OVER () — with no PARTITION BY — returns the single highest revenue across all rows, enabling the gap calculation. A second JOIN to categories fetches parent_category, which wasn't needed during aggregation.
hints: Assign each category a position in the global revenue ranking before computing the gap to the top.
MAX(...) OVER () with no PARTITION BY returns the maximum across all result rows — use it to compute the gap to the top.

title: Department salary rank and above-average count
description: For each department, compute the headcount, average salary (rounded to 2 dp), salary rank across all departments (1 = highest average salary, using `RANK()`), and the count of employees whose individual salary exceeds the company-wide average. Return `department_name`, `headcount`, `avg_salary`, `salary_rank`, and `above_avg_count`, ordered by `salary_rank` ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT d.department_name, COUNT(e.employee_id) AS headcount,
       ROUND(AVG(e.salary),2) AS avg_salary,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY AVG(e.salary) DESC) AS salary_rank,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN e.salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees) THEN 1 END) AS above_avg_count
FROM departments d
JOIN employees e ON d.department_id = e.department_id
GROUP BY d.department_name, d.department_id
ORDER BY salary_rank
solution_query:
SELECT d.department_name,
       COUNT(e.employee_id) AS headcount,
       ROUND(AVG(e.salary), 2) AS avg_salary,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY AVG(e.salary) DESC) AS salary_rank,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN e.salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees) THEN 1 END) AS above_avg_count
FROM departments d
JOIN employees e ON d.department_id = e.department_id
GROUP BY d.department_name, d.department_id
ORDER BY salary_rank;
explanation: RANK() OVER (ORDER BY AVG(e.salary) DESC) applies a window function to the aggregated value — valid after GROUP BY. The scalar subquery (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees) computes the company-wide average and is used inside CASE WHEN for the above_avg_count. GROUP BY must include department_id to ensure unique grouping.
hints: A position/ordering function can be applied to the per-department averages that aggregation produces.
Use a scalar subquery to compute the company-wide average salary inside CASE WHEN.

title: Top 2 spenders per country
description: Finance wants to identify the top two highest-spending users in each country based on completed orders. Write a query that returns `country`, `user_id`, `name`, `total_spend` (sum of `net_amount` from completed orders, rounded to 2 dp), and `spend_rank` (DENSE_RANK within country, 1 = highest spender). Include only rows where `spend_rank <= 2`. Order by `country` ascending, then `spend_rank` ascending.
expected_query:
WITH user_spend AS (
    SELECT u.country, u.user_id, u.name,
           ROUND(SUM(o.net_amount), 2) AS total_spend
    FROM users u
    JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY u.country, u.user_id, u.name
),
ranked AS (
    SELECT *,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY country ORDER BY total_spend DESC) AS spend_rank
    FROM user_spend
)
SELECT country, user_id, name, total_spend, spend_rank
FROM ranked
WHERE spend_rank <= 2
ORDER BY country, spend_rank
solution_query:
WITH user_spend AS (
    SELECT u.country, u.user_id, u.name,
           ROUND(SUM(o.net_amount), 2) AS total_spend
    FROM users u
    JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY u.country, u.user_id, u.name
),
ranked AS (
    SELECT *,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY country ORDER BY total_spend DESC) AS spend_rank
    FROM user_spend
)
SELECT country, user_id, name, total_spend, spend_rank
FROM ranked
WHERE spend_rank <= 2
ORDER BY country, spend_rank;
explanation: The CTE computes per-user total spend, then DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY country ORDER BY total_spend DESC) assigns ranks within each country. DENSE_RANK means ties both get rank 1 (and then rank 2 is skipped), so the result correctly handles countries where two users tied. The outer WHERE spend_rank <= 2 filters to the top two.
hints: Compute total spend per user in a CTE, then apply the window function in a second CTE before filtering.
DENSE_RANK handles ties by giving tied users the same rank — ROW_NUMBER would arbitrarily break ties.

title: 7-day rolling average of daily completed revenue
description: The finance team wants to smooth out daily revenue volatility. For each day with at least one completed order, compute `order_day` (YYYY-MM-DD), `daily_revenue` (sum of `net_amount` for completed orders on that day, rounded to 2 dp), and `rolling_7d_avg_revenue` — the average of `daily_revenue` over a 7-calendar-day window: the current day plus the 6 calendar days immediately before it (a calendar-date window, NOT the 6 previous order-rows; days with no completed orders simply contribute no value to the average), rounded to 2 dp. Output columns: order_day, daily_revenue, rolling_7d_avg_revenue. Order by `order_day` ascending.
expected_query: WITH daily AS (SELECT CAST(order_date AS DATE) AS order_day, ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS daily_revenue FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed' GROUP BY order_day) SELECT order_day, daily_revenue, ROUND(AVG(daily_revenue) OVER (ORDER BY order_day RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 6 DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS rolling_7d_avg_revenue FROM daily ORDER BY order_day
solution_query: WITH daily AS (SELECT CAST(order_date AS DATE) AS order_day, ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS daily_revenue FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed' GROUP BY order_day) SELECT order_day, daily_revenue, ROUND(AVG(daily_revenue) OVER (ORDER BY order_day RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 6 DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS rolling_7d_avg_revenue FROM daily ORDER BY order_day;
explanation: A 7-calendar-day trailing window requires RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 6 DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. RANGE with an INTERVAL operand compares actual date values, so the window always covers the 7-day calendar span ending on order_day — even when some days have no completed orders (and therefore no row in the daily CTE). ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW counts 6 prior rows, not 6 prior calendar days, and silently spans more than 7 calendar days whenever order-less days create gaps in the row sequence.
hints: Build a CTE with daily totals first, then apply the window function on the CTE's result.

ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING counts 6 prior rows — if some calendar days have no completed orders they are absent from the CTE, and those rows span more than 7 calendar days. Use RANGE with an INTERVAL to compare actual dates instead.

title: Category revenue rank within each brand

title: Monthly new user signups with cumulative total and share
description: The growth team tracks signup momentum. Write a query that returns `signup_month` (YYYY-MM from `signup_date`), `new_users` (users who signed up that month), `cumulative_users` (running total of all users up to and including that month), and `share_of_total_pct` (new_users / all-time total signups × 100, rounded to 1 dp). Order by `signup_month` ascending.
expected_query:
WITH monthly_signups AS (
    SELECT strftime(signup_date, '%Y-%m') AS signup_month,
           COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS new_users
    FROM users
    GROUP BY signup_month
)
SELECT signup_month,
       new_users,
       SUM(new_users) OVER (ORDER BY signup_month) AS cumulative_users,
       ROUND(new_users * 100.0 / SUM(new_users) OVER (), 1) AS share_of_total_pct
FROM monthly_signups
ORDER BY signup_month
solution_query:
WITH monthly_signups AS (
    SELECT strftime(signup_date, '%Y-%m') AS signup_month,
           COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS new_users
    FROM users
    GROUP BY signup_month
)
SELECT signup_month,
       new_users,
       SUM(new_users) OVER (ORDER BY signup_month) AS cumulative_users,
       ROUND(new_users * 100.0 / SUM(new_users) OVER (), 1) AS share_of_total_pct
FROM monthly_signups
ORDER BY signup_month;
explanation: Two window functions in one SELECT: SUM() OVER (ORDER BY signup_month) produces a running total (cumulative users); SUM() OVER () with no ORDER BY and no frame spec computes the grand total (same value on every row), used as the denominator for share_of_total_pct. These two window specs co-exist in the same query — each window is independent.
hints: You need two window calculations simultaneously: one that accumulates month by month, and one that gives the fixed total across all months.
The grand total denominator (SUM OVER ()) is the same value on every row — dividing monthly new_users by it gives each month's share.

title: Most expensive completed order per user
description: A finance analyst wants to identify each user’s highest-value completed order for a VIP scoring model. For each user with at least one completed order, return their user_id, the order_id of their most expensive completed order, its net_amount, and the order_date. If a user has multiple completed orders tied at their maximum net_amount, pick the smallest order_id. Output columns: user_id, order_id, net_amount, order_date. Order by net_amount descending, then order_id ascending.
expected_query: WITH ranked AS (SELECT o.user_id, o.order_id, o.net_amount, o.order_date, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY o.user_id ORDER BY o.net_amount DESC, o.order_id ASC) AS rn FROM orders o WHERE o.status = 'completed') SELECT user_id, order_id, ROUND(net_amount, 2) AS net_amount, order_date FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY net_amount DESC, order_id ASC
solution_query: WITH ranked AS (SELECT o.user_id, o.order_id, o.net_amount, o.order_date, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY o.user_id ORDER BY o.net_amount DESC, o.order_id ASC) AS rn FROM orders o WHERE o.status = 'completed') SELECT user_id, order_id, ROUND(net_amount, 2) AS net_amount, order_date FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY net_amount DESC, order_id ASC;
explanation: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY net_amount DESC, order_id ASC) assigns rank 1 to the most expensive completed order per user, with ties broken by the smallest order_id — making the pick deterministic when two orders share the same net_amount. Filtering WHERE rn = 1 returns exactly one row per user. The outer ORDER BY net_amount DESC, order_id ASC surfaces the highest-value users first with a stable secondary key.
hints: Each user should appear exactly once — the challenge is picking one row per user based on a ranking criterion, keeping only the maximum per user.
When two orders tie on net_amount, the window ORDER BY needs a secondary key — smallest order_id wins — to guarantee exactly one row is ranked 1 per user.
Wrap in a CTE, then filter WHERE rn = 1 in the outer query; match the outer ORDER BY to the question's stated output order.

title: Highest-average-quantity product per category

title: 3-month rolling average order count
description: An operations analyst wants to smooth out month-to-month noise in order volume. For each calendar month, compute the order_count (completed orders) and a rolling_3m_avg — the average of the current and two preceding months' counts (rounded to 1 decimal). Order by month.
expected_query:

    strftime(CAST(order_date AS DATE), '%Y-%m') AS month,
    COUNT(*) AS order_count
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT
  month,
  order_count,
  ROUND(AVG(order_count) OVER (ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 1) AS rolling_3m_avg
FROM monthly_orders
ORDER BY month
solution_query:
WITH monthly_orders AS (
  SELECT
    strftime(CAST(order_date AS DATE), '%Y-%m') AS month,
    COUNT(*) AS order_count
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT
  month,
  order_count,
  ROUND(AVG(order_count) OVER (ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 1) AS rolling_3m_avg
FROM monthly_orders
ORDER BY month
explanation: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW defines a 3-row window (current + 2 before). AVG() over this frame gives a rolling 3-month average. The first two months will have averages over 1 and 2 months respectively (smaller frames) — this is correct and expected.
hints: A rolling 3-month average includes the current month and the two preceding months in each calculation — define that window boundary over an ordered time series.
The window frame ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW gives 3 rows: current + 2 previous.
