title: Acquisition channel modifier revenue share
description: Marketing wants to compare the revenue performance of channel sub-types. For channels that contain an underscore (e.g. `paid_search`, `paid_social`), extract the part after the underscore as the modifier; for all other channels use the full channel name as the modifier. Write a query that returns `modifier`, `user_count` (distinct users with that modifier), `completed_revenue` (sum of net_amount from completed orders, rounded to 2 dp, defaulting to 0 for modifiers with no completed orders), and `revenue_share_pct` (this modifier's completed_revenue as a percentage of total completed revenue across all modifiers, rounded to 1 dp). Order by `completed_revenue` descending.
expected_query:
WITH channel_modifiers AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           CASE WHEN POSITION('_' IN acquisition_channel) > 0
                THEN split_part(acquisition_channel, '_', 2)
                ELSE acquisition_channel
           END AS modifier
    FROM users
),
modifier_stats AS (
    SELECT cm.modifier,
           COUNT(DISTINCT cm.user_id) AS user_count,
           ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(o.net_amount), 0), 2) AS completed_revenue
    FROM channel_modifiers cm
    LEFT JOIN orders o ON cm.user_id = o.user_id AND o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY cm.modifier
)
SELECT modifier, user_count, completed_revenue,
       ROUND(100.0 * completed_revenue / SUM(completed_revenue) OVER (), 1) AS revenue_share_pct
FROM modifier_stats
ORDER BY completed_revenue DESC
solution_query:
WITH channel_modifiers AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           CASE WHEN POSITION('_' IN acquisition_channel) > 0
                THEN split_part(acquisition_channel, '_', 2)
                ELSE acquisition_channel
           END AS modifier
    FROM users
),
modifier_stats AS (
    SELECT cm.modifier,
           COUNT(DISTINCT cm.user_id) AS user_count,
           ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(o.net_amount), 0), 2) AS completed_revenue
    FROM channel_modifiers cm
    LEFT JOIN orders o ON cm.user_id = o.user_id AND o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY cm.modifier
)
SELECT modifier, user_count, completed_revenue,
       ROUND(100.0 * completed_revenue / SUM(completed_revenue) OVER (), 1) AS revenue_share_pct
FROM modifier_stats
ORDER BY completed_revenue DESC;
explanation: POSITION('_' IN ...) > 0 detects channels with a sub-type separator; split_part extracts the second token. For channels without an underscore, the full channel name becomes the modifier. LEFT JOIN in the aggregation CTE preserves modifiers whose users have no completed orders (COALESCE handles the resulting NULL SUM). The window function SUM(...) OVER () in the final SELECT computes the grand total across all modifier rows, enabling each row to express its share without a self-join or subquery.
hints: Use POSITION('_' IN acquisition_channel) > 0 to detect channels with a modifier suffix, then split_part to extract the part after the underscore.
Compute per-modifier totals in a CTE first; then apply SUM(completed_revenue) OVER () in the outer SELECT to divide each row by the grand total without a self-join.

title: Product view-to-purchase conversion rate
description: The merchandising team wants to know which products convert the most viewers into buyers. For each product that was viewed at least once, compute `unique_viewers` (distinct users who triggered a `view_product` event for that product), `unique_buyers` (distinct users who completed an order containing that product — default 0 if none), and `conversion_pct` (unique_buyers / unique_viewers × 100, rounded to 1 dp). Return `product_name`, `unique_viewers`, `unique_buyers`, and `conversion_pct`. Order by `unique_viewers` descending, then `product_name` ascending to break ties.
expected_query:
WITH viewers AS (
    SELECT e.product_id,
           COUNT(DISTINCT e.user_id) AS unique_viewers
    FROM events e
    WHERE e.event_name = 'view_product'
      AND e.product_id IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY e.product_id
),
buyers AS (
    SELECT oi.product_id,
           COUNT(DISTINCT o.user_id) AS unique_buyers
    FROM order_items oi
    JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY oi.product_id
)
SELECT p.product_name,
       v.unique_viewers,
       COALESCE(b.unique_buyers, 0) AS unique_buyers,
       ROUND(100.0 * COALESCE(b.unique_buyers, 0) / v.unique_viewers, 1) AS conversion_pct
FROM viewers v
JOIN products p ON v.product_id = p.product_id
LEFT JOIN buyers b ON v.product_id = b.product_id
ORDER BY unique_viewers DESC, product_name ASC
solution_query:
WITH viewers AS (
    SELECT e.product_id,
           COUNT(DISTINCT e.user_id) AS unique_viewers
    FROM events e
    WHERE e.event_name = 'view_product'
      AND e.product_id IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY e.product_id
),
buyers AS (
    SELECT oi.product_id,
           COUNT(DISTINCT o.user_id) AS unique_buyers
    FROM order_items oi
    JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY oi.product_id
)
SELECT p.product_name,
       v.unique_viewers,
       COALESCE(b.unique_buyers, 0) AS unique_buyers,
       ROUND(100.0 * COALESCE(b.unique_buyers, 0) / v.unique_viewers, 1) AS conversion_pct
FROM viewers v
JOIN products p ON v.product_id = p.product_id
LEFT JOIN buyers b ON v.product_id = b.product_id
ORDER BY unique_viewers DESC, product_name ASC;
explanation: Separating viewers and buyers into CTEs avoids the classic double-counting trap: if you join events directly to order_items before aggregating, a user who viewed a product 3 times and bought it twice would appear 6 times (3 × 2) in the join result. Aggregating viewers and buyers independently in CTEs, then joining the pre-aggregated rows, ensures each metric counts unique users exactly once. LEFT JOIN from viewers to buyers preserves products that were viewed but never purchased (conversion_pct = 0).
hints: Aggregate viewers and buyers in separate CTEs before joining them — joining events to order_items before aggregating creates a row-multiplication that inflates both counts.
Use LEFT JOIN from viewers to buyers so products with no purchases still appear with conversion_pct = 0 rather than being dropped from the result.

title: Monthly revenue by payment method without double-counting
description: Finance wants a monthly breakdown of completed order revenue by payment method. Each completed order can have multiple payment rows (retries, partial payments) — attributing the full order's net_amount to each payment row would inflate revenue figures. De-duplicate by assigning each order to its earliest paid payment. Return `payment_month` (formatted `YYYY-MM`), `payment_method`, `order_count` (distinct order IDs attributed to that method+month), `total_net_amount` (sum of net_amount for those orders, rounded to 2 dp), and `payment_count`. `payment_count` is the number of (de-duplicated by `rn=1`) payment rows in that (month, method) — equal to `order_count` by construction; keep both columns for clarity in the result schema. Order by `payment_month` ascending, then `order_count` descending.
expected_query:
WITH order_method AS (
    SELECT o.order_id, o.net_amount,
           STRFTIME('%Y-%m', p.payment_date) AS payment_month,
           p.payment_method,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY o.order_id
               ORDER BY p.payment_date, p.payment_id
           ) AS rn
    FROM orders o
    JOIN payments p ON o.order_id = p.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed' AND p.status = 'paid'
)
SELECT payment_month, payment_method,
       COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS order_count,
       ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS total_net_amount,
       COUNT(*) AS payment_count
FROM order_method
WHERE rn = 1
GROUP BY payment_month, payment_method
ORDER BY payment_month ASC, order_count DESC
solution_query:
WITH order_method AS (
    SELECT o.order_id, o.net_amount,
           STRFTIME('%Y-%m', p.payment_date) AS payment_month,
           p.payment_method,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY o.order_id
               ORDER BY p.payment_date, p.payment_id
           ) AS rn
    FROM orders o
    JOIN payments p ON o.order_id = p.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed' AND p.status = 'paid'
)
SELECT payment_month, payment_method,
       COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS order_count,
       ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS total_net_amount,
       COUNT(*) AS payment_count
FROM order_method
WHERE rn = 1
GROUP BY payment_month, payment_method
ORDER BY payment_month ASC, order_count DESC;
explanation: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY payment_date, payment_id) assigns rank 1 to the earliest paid payment per order. Filtering WHERE rn = 1 in the outer query retains exactly one payment row per order, so net_amount is summed once per order rather than once per payment row. The tie-breaker on payment_id ensures deterministic rank assignment when two payments share the same timestamp. payment_count (COUNT(*) after dedup) is always equal to order_count in this dataset but surfaces as a useful sanity-check column for QA.
hints: Each completed order may have multiple paid payment rows — direct aggregation treats every retry or partial payment as a separate order, inflating the total. Before summing, identify the single canonical payment that represents each order.
Include payment_id as a tie-breaker in the ORDER BY inside ROW_NUMBER to guarantee a deterministic winner when two payments share the same payment_date.

title: Funnel with deep-browse definition: ≥2 distinct products viewed
description: Same funnel as before. The product team redefines 'viewed' as deep-browse: a session must have view_product events for at least 2 distinct product_ids to qualify. Rebuild the funnel with this updated definition. Output columns: traffic_source, sessions_started, deep_browse_sessions (the new 'viewed' count), with_add_to_cart, with_start_checkout, with_purchased. Order by sessions_started descending.
expected_query:
WITH session_events AS (
    SELECT s.session_id, s.traffic_source,
           COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'view_product' THEN e.product_id END) AS distinct_viewed_products,
           MAX(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'add_to_cart' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS had_cart,
           MAX(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'start_checkout' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS had_checkout,
           MAX(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'purchase' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS had_purchase
    FROM sessions s
    LEFT JOIN events e ON e.session_id = s.session_id
    GROUP BY s.session_id, s.traffic_source
)
SELECT traffic_source,
       COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) AS sessions_started,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN distinct_viewed_products >= 2 THEN session_id END) AS deep_browse_sessions,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN had_cart = 1 THEN session_id END) AS with_add_to_cart,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN had_checkout = 1 THEN session_id END) AS with_start_checkout,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN had_purchase = 1 THEN session_id END) AS with_purchased
FROM session_events
GROUP BY traffic_source
ORDER BY sessions_started DESC
solution_query:
WITH session_events AS (
    SELECT s.session_id, s.traffic_source,
           COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'view_product' THEN e.product_id END) AS distinct_viewed_products,
           MAX(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'add_to_cart' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS had_cart,
           MAX(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'start_checkout' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS had_checkout,
           MAX(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'purchase' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS had_purchase
    FROM sessions s
    LEFT JOIN events e ON e.session_id = s.session_id
    GROUP BY s.session_id, s.traffic_source
)
SELECT traffic_source,
       COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) AS sessions_started,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN distinct_viewed_products >= 2 THEN session_id END) AS deep_browse_sessions,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN had_cart = 1 THEN session_id END) AS with_add_to_cart,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN had_checkout = 1 THEN session_id END) AS with_start_checkout,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN had_purchase = 1 THEN session_id END) AS with_purchased
FROM session_events
GROUP BY traffic_source
ORDER BY sessions_started DESC;
explanation: The two-level aggregation is necessary: the inner CTE resolves the per-session deep-browse flag (COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) per session), then the outer query counts sessions by traffic_source. Trying to compute COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) and COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) in the same aggregation level would mix granularities. The business rule change — from 'any view' to '≥2 distinct product views' — drops deep_browse_sessions by ~29% in organic traffic (2531 → ~1803), showing that the original funnel overstated product engagement by counting single-product peek sessions.
hints: Deep-browse sessions require a two-level approach: first determine per-session which products were viewed (and how many unique ones), then apply the qualifying filter before measuring funnel progress.
COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event_name='view_product' THEN product_id END) per session_id gives the number of distinct products viewed in that session.

title: Funnel data quality: duplicate event rows and their inflation effect
description: The funnel query uses COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) per event stage, which silently masks duplicate event rows. Before trusting the funnel numbers, quantify the duplication. Write a query that shows, for each of the four funnel event types, the raw row count vs the deduplicated session count and the inflation ratio. Output columns: event_name, raw_row_count (total event rows of that type), distinct_sessions (COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) for that event_name), inflation_ratio (raw_row_count / distinct_sessions, rounded to 2 decimal places). Include only the four funnel event types: 'view_product', 'add_to_cart', 'start_checkout', 'purchase'. Order by event_name ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT event_name,
       COUNT(*) AS raw_row_count,
       COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) AS distinct_sessions,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) * 1.0 / COUNT(DISTINCT session_id), 2) AS inflation_ratio
FROM events
WHERE event_name IN ('view_product', 'add_to_cart', 'start_checkout', 'purchase')
GROUP BY event_name
ORDER BY event_name
solution_query:
SELECT event_name,
       COUNT(*) AS raw_row_count,
       COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) AS distinct_sessions,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) * 1.0 / COUNT(DISTINCT session_id), 2) AS inflation_ratio
FROM events
WHERE event_name IN ('view_product', 'add_to_cart', 'start_checkout', 'purchase')
GROUP BY event_name
ORDER BY event_name;
explanation: COUNT(*) counts all event rows including repeats; COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) counts unique sessions that fired the event at least once. Their ratio reveals the average number of events per session for that type — inflation_ratio > 1.0 means multiple events of the same type per session. Results show view_product fires ~2.66× per session on average (a user scrolls past the same product multiple times), while purchase fires ~1.17× (a user rarely completes two purchases in the same session). The parent funnel query used COUNT(DISTINCT session_id), so it correctly counted sessions that reached each stage — but a naive COUNT(*) funnel would have been inflated ~2.66× at the top of the funnel.
hints: Two metrics on the same data that should be equal will reveal duplication when they diverge: per-session event presence vs. raw event-row count for the same stage.
Multiply by 1.0 before dividing to avoid integer division in the ratio.

title: Reconciliation data quality audit: classify all months by source completeness
description: Extend the parent's FULL OUTER JOIN reconciliation to classify every month by data quality status: 'balanced' (both order_revenue > 0 and payment_revenue > 0), 'orders_only' (order_revenue > 0 but no matching payment month), or 'payments_only' (payment_revenue > 0 but no matching order month). Return all months from both sources with columns: month (YYYY-MM format), order_revenue, payment_revenue, discrepancy (rounded to 2 dp), data_quality_tag. Order by month ascending. Note: in this dataset all months may be 'balanced' — an all-balanced result is a valuable finding, not an empty query.
expected_query:
WITH monthly_orders AS (
    SELECT STRFTIME('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month,
           ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS order_revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY 1
),
monthly_payments AS (
    SELECT STRFTIME('%Y-%m', payment_date) AS month,
           ROUND(SUM(amount), 2) AS payment_revenue
    FROM payments
    WHERE status = 'paid'
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT COALESCE(o.month, p.month) AS month,
       COALESCE(o.order_revenue, 0) AS order_revenue,
       COALESCE(p.payment_revenue, 0) AS payment_revenue,
       ROUND(COALESCE(o.order_revenue, 0) - COALESCE(p.payment_revenue, 0), 2) AS discrepancy,
       CASE
           WHEN o.month IS NULL THEN 'payments_only'
           WHEN p.month IS NULL THEN 'orders_only'
           ELSE 'balanced'
       END AS data_quality_tag
FROM monthly_orders o
FULL OUTER JOIN monthly_payments p ON o.month = p.month
ORDER BY 1
solution_query:
WITH monthly_orders AS (
    SELECT STRFTIME('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month,
           ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS order_revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY 1
),
monthly_payments AS (
    SELECT STRFTIME('%Y-%m', payment_date) AS month,
           ROUND(SUM(amount), 2) AS payment_revenue
    FROM payments
    WHERE status = 'paid'
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT COALESCE(o.month, p.month) AS month,
       COALESCE(o.order_revenue, 0) AS order_revenue,
       COALESCE(p.payment_revenue, 0) AS payment_revenue,
       ROUND(COALESCE(o.order_revenue, 0) - COALESCE(p.payment_revenue, 0), 2) AS discrepancy,
       CASE
           WHEN o.month IS NULL THEN 'payments_only'
           WHEN p.month IS NULL THEN 'orders_only'
           ELSE 'balanced'
       END AS data_quality_tag
FROM monthly_orders o
FULL OUTER JOIN monthly_payments p ON o.month = p.month
ORDER BY 1;
explanation: The FULL OUTER JOIN preserves months present in only one source via NULL propagation. CASE WHEN o.month IS NULL detects payments_only months (the orders CTE produced no row for that month); WHEN p.month IS NULL detects orders_only months. In this dataset all 36 months appear in both sources, so every row gets tag='balanced' — this is the expected finding in a healthy system. If a month appeared only in orders (e.g. due to a payment processing delay), tag='orders_only'; vice versa for 'payments_only'. The data quality tag turns a raw discrepancy report into a triaged action list: balanced months need amount investigation; one-sided months flag a data pipeline gap.
hints: A full outer merge already surfaces months present in only one source as NULL on the absent side — classifying them is a matter of reading which side returned NULL for a given month.
An empty result is a legitimate finding: it means every month has both sides and the discrepancies are real mismatches.

title: Reconciliation via UNION ALL: eliminate the full outer join
description: The FULL OUTER JOIN approach works correctly. An alternative uses UNION ALL with conditional aggregation to avoid the join entirely: tag each raw row with a 'src' column, UNION ALL both tables, then GROUP BY month with CASE WHEN to split the two streams. Rewrite the monthly reconciliation query using this approach. Output the same columns as the parent: month (YYYY-MM format), order_revenue, payment_revenue, discrepancy. Results must match the parent query exactly.
expected_query:
SELECT month,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN src = 'order' THEN amt ELSE 0 END), 2) AS order_revenue,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN src = 'payment' THEN amt ELSE 0 END), 2) AS payment_revenue,
       ROUND(
           SUM(CASE WHEN src = 'order' THEN amt ELSE 0 END) -
           SUM(CASE WHEN src = 'payment' THEN amt ELSE 0 END),
           2
       ) AS discrepancy
FROM (
    SELECT STRFTIME('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month, net_amount AS amt, 'order' AS src
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    UNION ALL
    SELECT STRFTIME('%Y-%m', payment_date), amount, 'payment'
    FROM payments
    WHERE status = 'paid'
) combined
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month
solution_query:
SELECT month,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN src = 'order' THEN amt ELSE 0 END), 2) AS order_revenue,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN src = 'payment' THEN amt ELSE 0 END), 2) AS payment_revenue,
       ROUND(
           SUM(CASE WHEN src = 'order' THEN amt ELSE 0 END) -
           SUM(CASE WHEN src = 'payment' THEN amt ELSE 0 END),
           2
       ) AS discrepancy
FROM (
    SELECT STRFTIME('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month, net_amount AS amt, 'order' AS src
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    UNION ALL
    SELECT STRFTIME('%Y-%m', payment_date), amount, 'payment'
    FROM payments
    WHERE status = 'paid'
) combined
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month;
explanation: The UNION ALL approach tags each row with a source flag, stacks both tables into a single relation, then uses one GROUP BY pass to split the streams with CASE WHEN. It avoids the sort-merge join that FULL OUTER JOIN requires, and naturally handles months present in only one table — rows from the missing side simply contribute 0 to the SUM(CASE WHEN ...) for the other side. When to prefer UNION ALL over FULL OUTER JOIN: (1) when the join key is a derived column (STRFTIME result) rather than a stored key — a FULL OUTER JOIN on a derived column prevents predicate pushdown; (2) when both tables are large and the sort-merge join cost is measurable; (3) when the ETL system guarantees no cross-table month gaps (the edge case from the prior follow-up). FULL OUTER JOIN is clearer to read; UNION ALL is often faster in columnar engines.
hints: Stacking both result sets and aggregating by month is semantically equivalent to a full outer merge — when both sides produce the same bucket key, there is no asymmetric lookup needed.
SUM(CASE WHEN src='order' THEN amt ELSE 0 END) naturally returns 0 for months that exist only in the payments stream — no COALESCE needed.

title: SLA compliance by country and issue type with Global rollup
description: The VP of Support wants the same SLA compliance breakdown segmented by user country (from the users table). Use the same issue_type thresholds: technical=72h, billing=48h, account=48h, shipping=96h, product=72h. Return rows for each (country, issue_type) combination where total_tickets in that group >= 50, PLUS one 'Global' row per issue_type showing overall compliance across all countries. Columns: country, issue_type, sla_hours, total_tickets, resolved_tickets, within_sla, sla_pct (rounded to 1 dp, NULL if resolved_tickets = 0). Order by issue_type ascending, then country ascending with 'Global' last within each issue_type.
expected_query:
WITH sla_thresholds (issue_type, sla_hours) AS (
    VALUES ('technical', 72), ('billing', 48), ('account', 48),
           ('shipping', 96), ('product', 72)
),
country_level AS (
    SELECT u.country, st.issue_type, sl.sla_hours,
           COUNT(*) AS total_tickets,
           COUNT(CASE WHEN st.status = 'resolved' THEN 1 END) AS resolved_tickets,
           COUNT(CASE WHEN st.status = 'resolved' AND st.resolution_hours <= sl.sla_hours THEN 1 END) AS within_sla
    FROM support_tickets st
    JOIN users u ON u.user_id = st.user_id
    JOIN sla_thresholds sl ON sl.issue_type = st.issue_type
    GROUP BY u.country, st.issue_type, sl.sla_hours
    HAVING COUNT(*) >= 50
),
global_level AS (
    SELECT 'Global' AS country, st.issue_type, sl.sla_hours,
           COUNT(*) AS total_tickets,
           COUNT(CASE WHEN st.status = 'resolved' THEN 1 END) AS resolved_tickets,
           COUNT(CASE WHEN st.status = 'resolved' AND st.resolution_hours <= sl.sla_hours THEN 1 END) AS within_sla
    FROM support_tickets st
    JOIN sla_thresholds sl ON sl.issue_type = st.issue_type
    GROUP BY st.issue_type, sl.sla_hours
)
SELECT country, issue_type, sla_hours, total_tickets, resolved_tickets, within_sla,
       ROUND(100.0 * within_sla / NULLIF(resolved_tickets, 0), 1) AS sla_pct
FROM (
    SELECT * FROM country_level
    UNION ALL
    SELECT * FROM global_level
) combined
ORDER BY issue_type, CASE WHEN country = 'Global' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END, country
solution_query:
WITH sla_thresholds (issue_type, sla_hours) AS (
    VALUES ('technical', 72), ('billing', 48), ('account', 48),
           ('shipping', 96), ('product', 72)
),
country_level AS (
    SELECT u.country, st.issue_type, sl.sla_hours,
           COUNT(*) AS total_tickets,
           COUNT(CASE WHEN st.status = 'resolved' THEN 1 END) AS resolved_tickets,
           COUNT(CASE WHEN st.status = 'resolved' AND st.resolution_hours <= sl.sla_hours THEN 1 END) AS within_sla
    FROM support_tickets st
    JOIN users u ON u.user_id = st.user_id
    JOIN sla_thresholds sl ON sl.issue_type = st.issue_type
    GROUP BY u.country, st.issue_type, sl.sla_hours
    HAVING COUNT(*) >= 50
),
global_level AS (
    SELECT 'Global' AS country, st.issue_type, sl.sla_hours,
           COUNT(*) AS total_tickets,
           COUNT(CASE WHEN st.status = 'resolved' THEN 1 END) AS resolved_tickets,
           COUNT(CASE WHEN st.status = 'resolved' AND st.resolution_hours <= sl.sla_hours THEN 1 END) AS within_sla
    FROM support_tickets st
    JOIN sla_thresholds sl ON sl.issue_type = st.issue_type
    GROUP BY st.issue_type, sl.sla_hours
)
SELECT country, issue_type, sla_hours, total_tickets, resolved_tickets, within_sla,
       ROUND(100.0 * within_sla / NULLIF(resolved_tickets, 0), 1) AS sla_pct
FROM (
    SELECT * FROM country_level
    UNION ALL
    SELECT * FROM global_level
) combined
ORDER BY issue_type, CASE WHEN country = 'Global' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END, country;
explanation: Two separate CTEs avoid a GROUPING SETS dependency: country_level applies the ≥50 ticket HAVING filter at the country×issue_type grain; global_level recomputes the full aggregate without any country filter. UNION ALL combines them — HAVING in global_level is deliberately omitted (the VP wants every issue_type globally regardless of volume). The CASE WHEN country = 'Global' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END sort key pushes 'Global' to the bottom of each issue_type group while alphabetical country ordering applies above it. In this dataset only the US meets the ≥50 threshold for each issue_type; all other countries appear only in the Global row.
hints: The country-level rows and the Global rollup use different filtering rules, which makes them hard to compute in a single pass — separate computations for each output type, then combine.
To sort 'Global' last within each issue_type, use CASE WHEN country = 'Global' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END as the secondary sort key.

title: Cross-entity aggregation at monthly grain: session count and order revenue per month
description: The same double-counting risk applies at any grouping key. Generalise the per-user CTE approach to the monthly grain: compute, per calendar month, session_count (distinct session_ids from sessions), completed_order_count (distinct completed order_ids), and completed_order_revenue (SUM of net_amount for completed orders, rounded to 2 dp). Include all months that appear in either sessions or orders. Output columns: month (YYYY-MM), session_count, completed_order_count, completed_order_revenue. Order by month ascending.
expected_query:
WITH monthly_sessions AS (
    SELECT STRFTIME('%Y-%m', session_start) AS month,
           COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) AS session_count
    FROM sessions
    GROUP BY 1
),
monthly_orders AS (
    SELECT STRFTIME('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month,
           COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS completed_order_count,
           ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS completed_order_revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT COALESCE(ms.month, mo.month) AS month,
       COALESCE(ms.session_count, 0) AS session_count,
       COALESCE(mo.completed_order_count, 0) AS completed_order_count,
       COALESCE(mo.completed_order_revenue, 0) AS completed_order_revenue
FROM monthly_sessions ms
FULL OUTER JOIN monthly_orders mo ON mo.month = ms.month
ORDER BY 1
solution_query:
WITH monthly_sessions AS (
    SELECT STRFTIME('%Y-%m', session_start) AS month,
           COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) AS session_count
    FROM sessions
    GROUP BY 1
),
monthly_orders AS (
    SELECT STRFTIME('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month,
           COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS completed_order_count,
           ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS completed_order_revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT COALESCE(ms.month, mo.month) AS month,
       COALESCE(ms.session_count, 0) AS session_count,
       COALESCE(mo.completed_order_count, 0) AS completed_order_count,
       COALESCE(mo.completed_order_revenue, 0) AS completed_order_revenue
FROM monthly_sessions ms
FULL OUTER JOIN monthly_orders mo ON mo.month = ms.month
ORDER BY 1;
explanation: The structural pattern is identical to the per-user version: pre-aggregate each fact table to one row per key (month instead of user_id), then JOIN the summaries. The join type changes from LEFT to FULL OUTER: at the monthly grain, some months might have sessions with no completed orders (e.g., a new marketing campaign month) or completed orders with no session data (legacy orders from before session tracking was deployed) — FULL OUTER captures both. This is the invariant: pre-aggregate independently, join summaries, choose the join type based on which universe is the denominator. The monthly grain also reveals a business truth not visible per-user: session volume and order volume trend together month-over-month but diverge in specific periods.
hints: The fan-out problem from the per-user version applies at monthly grain too — aggregate each entity to one row per month before combining the two streams.
Switch from LEFT JOIN to FULL OUTER JOIN at the monthly grain — some months may have sessions but no orders, or orders but no sessions.

title: Extend cross-entity user report with a third pre-aggregation: distinct products viewed
description: Extend the per-user report from the parent question to include a fourth column: distinct_products_viewed — the number of distinct product_ids the user viewed (event_name = 'view_product') across all their events. Add a product_views CTE that computes this from the events table, then LEFT JOIN it to the existing result. Output columns: user_id, session_count, completed_order_count, completed_order_revenue, distinct_products_viewed (0 for users with no view events). Order by user_id ascending.
expected_query:
WITH session_counts AS (
    SELECT user_id, COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) AS session_count
    FROM sessions
    GROUP BY user_id
),
order_totals AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS completed_order_count,
           ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS completed_order_revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY user_id
),
product_views AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) AS distinct_products_viewed
    FROM events
    WHERE event_name = 'view_product'
    GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT sc.user_id,
       sc.session_count,
       COALESCE(ot.completed_order_count, 0) AS completed_order_count,
       COALESCE(ot.completed_order_revenue, 0) AS completed_order_revenue,
       COALESCE(pv.distinct_products_viewed, 0) AS distinct_products_viewed
FROM session_counts sc
LEFT JOIN order_totals ot ON ot.user_id = sc.user_id
LEFT JOIN product_views pv ON pv.user_id = sc.user_id
ORDER BY sc.user_id
solution_query:
WITH session_counts AS (
    SELECT user_id, COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) AS session_count
    FROM sessions
    GROUP BY user_id
),
order_totals AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS completed_order_count,
           ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS completed_order_revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY user_id
),
product_views AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) AS distinct_products_viewed
    FROM events
    WHERE event_name = 'view_product'
    GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT sc.user_id,
       sc.session_count,
       COALESCE(ot.completed_order_count, 0) AS completed_order_count,
       COALESCE(ot.completed_order_revenue, 0) AS completed_order_revenue,
       COALESCE(pv.distinct_products_viewed, 0) AS distinct_products_viewed
FROM session_counts sc
LEFT JOIN order_totals ot ON ot.user_id = sc.user_id
LEFT JOIN product_views pv ON pv.user_id = sc.user_id
ORDER BY sc.user_id;
explanation: Adding a third dimension follows the same structural rule: a separate CTE pre-aggregates to one row per user_id, then LEFT JOINs to the driver table. Each additional dimension costs one scan of the source table plus one hash join — O(source rows + user count), not multiplicative. The performance implication: 3 independent CTEs cost 3 sequential table scans with 2 hash joins; joining events raw into the main query instead would immediately re-introduce the fan-out problem (sessions × events × orders). The CTE architecture scales linearly in dimensions; a raw-join architecture scales multiplicatively. Note that events is the largest table here (45K rows) — the product_views CTE filters to view_product events before aggregating, reducing the hash join cardinality.
hints: Add a third CTE that pre-aggregates events to one row per user_id — the same pattern as session_counts and order_totals.
Each additional CTE adds one sequential scan and one hash join; the cost scales linearly. Joining raw events into the main query would re-introduce the fan-out.

title: Product inactivity: catalog flag vs finance sales-based definition
description: The parent audit flagged 9 inactive products (is_active = 'false') with recent completed orders. But the finance team uses a different inactivity definition: a product is inactive if it had no completed order in calendar year 2025 (between 2025-01-01 and 2025-12-31). Write a query that classifies all 260 products into four groups based on which definition(s) apply: 'catalog_inactive_only' (is_active = 'false' but did sell in 2025), 'finance_inactive_only' (is_active = true but did not sell in 2025), 'both_definitions' (is_active = 'false' AND did not sell in 2025), 'neither' (is_active = true AND did sell in 2025). Output columns: definition, product_count.
expected_query:
WITH product_2025_sales AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT p.product_id
    FROM products p
    JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
    JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
      AND CAST(o.order_date AS DATE) BETWEEN '2025-01-01' AND '2025-12-31'
),
categorized AS (
    SELECT p.product_id,
           p.is_active = 'false' AS catalog_inactive,
           ps.product_id IS NULL AS finance_inactive
    FROM products p
    LEFT JOIN product_2025_sales ps ON ps.product_id = p.product_id
)
SELECT definition, COUNT(*) AS product_count
FROM (
    SELECT CASE
               WHEN catalog_inactive AND NOT finance_inactive THEN 'catalog_inactive_only'
               WHEN NOT catalog_inactive AND finance_inactive THEN 'finance_inactive_only'
               WHEN catalog_inactive AND finance_inactive THEN 'both_definitions'
               ELSE 'neither'
           END AS definition
    FROM categorized
) classified
GROUP BY definition
solution_query:
WITH product_2025_sales AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT p.product_id
    FROM products p
    JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
    JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
      AND CAST(o.order_date AS DATE) BETWEEN '2025-01-01' AND '2025-12-31'
),
categorized AS (
    SELECT p.product_id,
           p.is_active = 'false' AS catalog_inactive,
           ps.product_id IS NULL AS finance_inactive
    FROM products p
    LEFT JOIN product_2025_sales ps ON ps.product_id = p.product_id
)
SELECT definition, COUNT(*) AS product_count
FROM (
    SELECT CASE
               WHEN catalog_inactive AND NOT finance_inactive THEN 'catalog_inactive_only'
               WHEN NOT catalog_inactive AND finance_inactive THEN 'finance_inactive_only'
               WHEN catalog_inactive AND finance_inactive THEN 'both_definitions'
               ELSE 'neither'
           END AS definition
    FROM categorized
) classified
GROUP BY definition;
explanation: The product_2025_sales CTE identifies products with at least one completed order in 2025 — using DISTINCT to deduplicate before the LEFT JOIN. The categorized CTE flags each product on both definitions independently: catalog_inactive (is_active = 'false') and finance_inactive (no row in product_2025_sales, indicated by ps.product_id IS NULL after the LEFT JOIN). The outer CASE WHEN then produces four mutually exclusive groups. Results: catalog_inactive_only = 9 (flagged by catalog but still selling in 2025), finance_inactive_only = 27 (active in catalog but not selling), both_definitions = 5 (both agree it's inactive), neither = 219. The two definitions agree on only 5 of 46 total 'inactive' products by either measure — a strong signal to align the definitions before acting on either list.
hints: The two inactivity definitions produce different product sets — set-membership operations (is this product in each set?) reveal the four possible combinations of active/inactive across both definitions.
Flag each product on both dimensions independently in a CTE, then classify into four groups with CASE WHEN in the final SELECT.

title: Sessionize events by 30-minute gap and classify session duration
description: The product team wants to understand session engagement depth. Sessionize the events table using a 30-minute inactivity gap: a new session begins whenever the gap between consecutive events for the same user exceeds 30 minutes, or at the user's first event. Then classify each session by duration: 'short' (< 5 minutes), 'medium' (5–29 minutes inclusive), 'long' (>= 30 minutes). Output columns: user_id, session_num (sequential session counter per user, starting at 1), session_start (MIN(event_time) for the session), duration_minutes (DATEDIFF in minutes between first and last event), event_count, session_class. Order by user_id, session_num ascending.
expected_query:
WITH event_gaps AS (
    SELECT user_id, event_time,
           LAG(event_time) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time) AS prev_event_time
    FROM events
),
session_starts AS (
    SELECT user_id, event_time,
           CASE WHEN prev_event_time IS NULL
                     OR DATEDIFF('minute', CAST(prev_event_time AS TIMESTAMP), CAST(event_time AS TIMESTAMP)) > 30
                THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_new_session
    FROM event_gaps
),
session_numbers AS (
    SELECT user_id, event_time,
           SUM(is_new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time) AS session_num
    FROM session_starts
),
session_summary AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           session_num,
           MIN(event_time) AS session_start,
           MAX(event_time) AS session_end,
           COUNT(*) AS event_count,
           DATEDIFF('minute', CAST(MIN(event_time) AS TIMESTAMP), CAST(MAX(event_time) AS TIMESTAMP)) AS duration_minutes
    FROM session_numbers
    GROUP BY user_id, session_num
)
SELECT user_id,
       session_num,
       session_start,
       duration_minutes,
       event_count,
       CASE
           WHEN duration_minutes < 5 THEN 'short'
           WHEN duration_minutes < 30 THEN 'medium'
           ELSE 'long'
       END AS session_class
FROM session_summary
ORDER BY user_id, session_num
solution_query:
WITH event_gaps AS (
    SELECT user_id, event_time,
           LAG(event_time) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time) AS prev_event_time
    FROM events
),
session_starts AS (
    SELECT user_id, event_time,
           CASE WHEN prev_event_time IS NULL
                     OR DATEDIFF('minute', CAST(prev_event_time AS TIMESTAMP), CAST(event_time AS TIMESTAMP)) > 30
                THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_new_session
    FROM event_gaps
),
session_numbers AS (
    SELECT user_id, event_time,
           SUM(is_new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time) AS session_num
    FROM session_starts
),
session_summary AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           session_num,
           MIN(event_time) AS session_start,
           MAX(event_time) AS session_end,
           COUNT(*) AS event_count,
           DATEDIFF('minute', CAST(MIN(event_time) AS TIMESTAMP), CAST(MAX(event_time) AS TIMESTAMP)) AS duration_minutes
    FROM session_numbers
    GROUP BY user_id, session_num
)
SELECT user_id,
       session_num,
       session_start,
       duration_minutes,
       event_count,
       CASE
           WHEN duration_minutes < 5 THEN 'short'
           WHEN duration_minutes < 30 THEN 'medium'
           ELSE 'long'
       END AS session_class
FROM session_summary
ORDER BY user_id, session_num;
explanation: Four-CTE sessionization pipeline: (1) event_gaps uses LAG to compute the gap to the previous event per user; (2) session_starts flags each event as a new session start when the gap exceeds 30 minutes or prev_event_time is NULL; (3) session_numbers uses a running SUM of the flag to assign a monotonically increasing session_num per user — this is the gaps-and-islands key insight: a cumulative sum of a 0/1 boundary flag produces a session ID that increments exactly at each boundary; (4) session_summary aggregates to one row per (user_id, session_num). Session class distribution: 58% medium, 33% long, 9% short — the product's session mix skews toward engaged mid-length sessions.
hints: Sessionization is a gaps-and-islands problem: first classify each event as 'starts a new session' or 'continues an existing session', then let a running accumulation of those boundary flags produce a session identifier.
Compute session duration as DATEDIFF('minute', MIN(event_time), MAX(event_time)) in the final aggregation CTE — not during the gap-detection phase.

description: Same sessionization task. The product analytics team adds a second boundary rule: a session also ends (and a new one begins) immediately after any 'purchase' event, regardless of elapsed time. That is, the event immediately following a 'purchase' always starts a new session. Apply both boundary rules (30-minute inactivity gap OR the event after a 'purchase' event) and return the same session classification output: user_id, session_num, session_start, duration_minutes, event_count, session_class. The CASE WHEN in session_boundaries gains a third branch: WHEN prev_event = 'purchase' THEN 1. This changes the session count significantly — purchase events effectively split post-purchase browsing into new sessions, increasing the session count from ~9,196 to ~11,915.
