title: Sessionization at scale: LAG bottleneck and alternatives for 5-billion-row events
description: The events table now holds 5 billion rows. The LAG-based sessionization requires a full sort of all events per user, which becomes prohibitively expensive at this scale. Write a query that demonstrates a pre-filtering optimisation: instead of sessionizing all events, first identify only the session boundary events — events where the gap to the previous event exceeds 30 minutes (or it is the user's first event). Return these boundary events only, with columns: user_id, event_time, gap_to_prev_minutes (NULL for first events). This is the first step of an alternative approach that avoids materialising all intermediate events. Order by user_id, event_time ascending.
expected_query:
WITH event_gaps AS (
    SELECT user_id, event_time,
           DATEDIFF('minute',
               CAST(LAG(event_time) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time) AS TIMESTAMP),
               CAST(event_time AS TIMESTAMP)
           ) AS gap_to_prev_minutes
    FROM events
)
SELECT user_id, event_time, gap_to_prev_minutes
FROM event_gaps
WHERE gap_to_prev_minutes IS NULL OR gap_to_prev_minutes > 30
ORDER BY user_id, event_time
solution_query:
WITH event_gaps AS (
    SELECT user_id, event_time,
           DATEDIFF('minute',
               CAST(LAG(event_time) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time) AS TIMESTAMP),
               CAST(event_time AS TIMESTAMP)
           ) AS gap_to_prev_minutes
    FROM events
)
SELECT user_id, event_time, gap_to_prev_minutes
FROM event_gaps
WHERE gap_to_prev_minutes IS NULL OR gap_to_prev_minutes > 30
ORDER BY user_id, event_time;
explanation: At 5B rows, a full per-user sort to compute LAG costs O(N log N) globally and requires materialising the entire sorted dataset. The boundary-event approach reduces the output to only the session start events — typically a small fraction of all events (~1 per session per user). The boundary rows can then be joined back to the full events table to assign session_start times per event without re-sorting. Further scale approaches beyond SQL: (1) partition the events table by user_id modulo P — each partition sorts independently on smaller data; (2) use a streaming sessionizer in Spark/Flink that processes each user's events in a single pass with in-memory state; (3) pre-materialise the last-event-per-user timestamp as a compaction table updated by the ETL pipeline. The SQL boundary-extraction query is correct and complete; the architectural discussion is the scale pivot.
hints: At scale, producing only the session boundary events from the full event stream — rather than session-numbering every event row — is a much smaller intermediate result to materialise.

To isolate just the boundary events, use LAG to bring the previous event's timestamp into the current row, then filter for rows where the gap exceeds the threshold — or where no previous event exists. This predicate scan is far cheaper than numbering every event first.

title: 24-hour attributed session-to-order funnel with intermediate event stages
description: Attribution requires both behavioral signals and a downstream conversion. For each traffic_source, compute a funnel showing how sessions progress through event stages and ultimately convert to completed orders within 24 hours of session start. Output columns: traffic_source, total_sessions, with_product_view (sessions with at least one 'view_product' event), with_add_to_cart, with_start_checkout, with_purchase_event (at least one 'purchase' event), converted_in_24h (sessions where the same user placed a completed order with order_date within 24 hours of session_start). Order by total_sessions descending.
expected_query:
WITH session_events AS (
    SELECT s.session_id, s.user_id, s.session_start, s.traffic_source,
           MAX(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'view_product' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS had_view,
           MAX(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'add_to_cart' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS had_cart,
           MAX(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'start_checkout' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS had_checkout,
           MAX(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'purchase' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS had_purchase_event
    FROM sessions s
    LEFT JOIN events e ON e.session_id = s.session_id
    GROUP BY s.session_id, s.user_id, s.session_start, s.traffic_source
),
with_conversion AS (
    SELECT se.session_id, se.traffic_source,
           se.had_view, se.had_cart, se.had_checkout, se.had_purchase_event,
           CASE WHEN EXISTS (
               SELECT 1 FROM orders o
               WHERE o.user_id = se.user_id
                 AND o.status = 'completed'
                 AND CAST(o.order_date AS TIMESTAMP) >= CAST(se.session_start AS TIMESTAMP)
                 AND CAST(o.order_date AS TIMESTAMP) < CAST(se.session_start AS TIMESTAMP) + INTERVAL 1 DAY
           ) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS converted_24h
    FROM session_events se
)
SELECT traffic_source,
       COUNT(*) AS total_sessions,
       SUM(had_view) AS with_product_view,
       SUM(had_cart) AS with_add_to_cart,
       SUM(had_checkout) AS with_start_checkout,
       SUM(had_purchase_event) AS with_purchase_event,
       SUM(converted_24h) AS converted_in_24h
FROM with_conversion
GROUP BY traffic_source
ORDER BY total_sessions DESC
solution_query:
WITH session_events AS (
    SELECT s.session_id, s.user_id, s.session_start, s.traffic_source,
           MAX(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'view_product' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS had_view,
           MAX(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'add_to_cart' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS had_cart,
           MAX(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'start_checkout' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS had_checkout,
           MAX(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'purchase' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS had_purchase_event
    FROM sessions s
    LEFT JOIN events e ON e.session_id = s.session_id
    GROUP BY s.session_id, s.user_id, s.session_start, s.traffic_source
),
with_conversion AS (
    SELECT se.session_id, se.traffic_source,
           se.had_view, se.had_cart, se.had_checkout, se.had_purchase_event,
           CASE WHEN EXISTS (
               SELECT 1 FROM orders o
               WHERE o.user_id = se.user_id
                 AND o.status = 'completed'
                 AND CAST(o.order_date AS TIMESTAMP) >= CAST(se.session_start AS TIMESTAMP)
                 AND CAST(o.order_date AS TIMESTAMP) < CAST(se.session_start AS TIMESTAMP) + INTERVAL 1 DAY
           ) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS converted_24h
    FROM session_events se
)
SELECT traffic_source,
       COUNT(*) AS total_sessions,
       SUM(had_view) AS with_product_view,
       SUM(had_cart) AS with_add_to_cart,
       SUM(had_checkout) AS with_start_checkout,
       SUM(had_purchase_event) AS with_purchase_event,
       SUM(converted_24h) AS converted_in_24h
FROM with_conversion
GROUP BY traffic_source
ORDER BY total_sessions DESC;
explanation: Two-layer CTE approach: session_events resolves per-session event flags by LEFT JOINing events; with_conversion adds the 24h order attribution via a correlated EXISTS subquery. The EXISTS checks: same user_id, completed status, and order_date within the [session_start, session_start + 1 day) window. converted_in_24h is intentionally low (9–15 per traffic_source) — it means 56 sessions total directly attributed to a same-day completed order. This is realistic: most users browse across multiple sessions before purchasing, and the order_date might fall in a different calendar session from the browse session. The exist-based approach is semantically clearer than a LEFT JOIN with deduplication; at scale, indexing on (user_id, order_date, status) enables efficient correlated lookup.
hints: Two separate analytical questions are being answered: which stages did a session reach (from events), and did the session result in a same-day order (from orders)? Resolve them in sequence to avoid mixing two fan-out paths.
The 24h window condition is: order_date >= session_start AND order_date < session_start + INTERVAL 1 DAY — cast both sides to TIMESTAMP for a safe comparison.

title: Attribution funnel edge case: sessions with zero events
description: A session can exist with no rows in the events table (created, but the user left before any event fired). As an edge-case check on the attribution funnel, return two checks combined with UNION ALL into one result with three columns — result_type, sessions_with_no_events, sessions_with_zero_events — where each row fills only its own metric and leaves the other NULL. Row 1 (result_type = 'zero_event_check'): sessions_with_no_events = the number of sessions that have NO matching rows in the events table at all (sessions_with_zero_events is NULL). Row 2 (result_type = 'direct_traffic_check'): among sessions with traffic_source = 'direct', sessions_with_zero_events = the number whose funnel flags are all zero — i.e. none of the four funnel events ('view_product', 'add_to_cart', 'start_checkout', 'purchase') fired (sessions_with_no_events is NULL). This verifies that the funnel — built from those four events via a LEFT JOIN with each stage flag defaulting to 0 — correctly absorbs sessions that produced no events.
expected_query:
WITH session_events AS (
    SELECT s.session_id, s.traffic_source,
           MAX(CASE WHEN e.session_id IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS has_any_event,
           MAX(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'view_product' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS had_view,
           MAX(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'add_to_cart' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS had_cart,
           MAX(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'start_checkout' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS had_checkout,
           MAX(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'purchase' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS had_purchase_event
    FROM sessions s
    LEFT JOIN events e ON e.session_id = s.session_id
    GROUP BY s.session_id, s.traffic_source
)
SELECT 'zero_event_check' AS result_type,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN has_any_event = 0 THEN 1 END) AS sessions_with_no_events,
       NULL::BIGINT AS sessions_with_zero_events
FROM session_events
UNION ALL
SELECT 'direct_traffic_check' AS result_type,
       NULL::BIGINT AS sessions_with_no_events,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN had_view = 0 AND had_cart = 0 AND had_checkout = 0 AND had_purchase_event = 0 THEN 1 END) AS sessions_with_zero_events
FROM session_events
WHERE traffic_source = 'direct'
solution_query:
WITH session_events AS (
    SELECT s.session_id, s.traffic_source,
           MAX(CASE WHEN e.session_id IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS has_any_event,
           MAX(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'view_product' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS had_view,
           MAX(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'add_to_cart' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS had_cart,
           MAX(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'start_checkout' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS had_checkout,
           MAX(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'purchase' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS had_purchase_event
    FROM sessions s
    LEFT JOIN events e ON e.session_id = s.session_id
    GROUP BY s.session_id, s.traffic_source
)
SELECT 'zero_event_check' AS result_type,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN has_any_event = 0 THEN 1 END) AS sessions_with_no_events,
       NULL::BIGINT AS sessions_with_zero_events
FROM session_events
UNION ALL
SELECT 'direct_traffic_check' AS result_type,
       NULL::BIGINT AS sessions_with_no_events,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN had_view = 0 AND had_cart = 0 AND had_checkout = 0 AND had_purchase_event = 0 THEN 1 END) AS sessions_with_zero_events
FROM session_events
WHERE traffic_source = 'direct';
explanation: Two checks share one 3-column output via UNION ALL, each row filling only its metric (NULL elsewhere). Row 1 counts sessions with no matching events at all: the LEFT JOIN leaves e.session_id NULL for such sessions, so MAX(CASE WHEN e.session_id IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 0 flags them. Row 2 counts direct-traffic sessions where none of the four funnel events fired (all had_* flags 0) — exactly how the funnel, built from the same LEFT JOIN with ELSE 0 defaults, represents a zero-event session. In this dataset every session has at least one event (and at least one funnel event), so both counts are 0; the point is that the funnel structure already absorbs zero-event sessions correctly.
hints: Decompose into two independent checks: (a) which sessions have no matching event rows at all, and (b) among direct-traffic sessions, which have all four funnel-stage flags equal to zero. A single aggregation CTE that links sessions to events can power both branches.
Combine the two checks with UNION ALL; since each branch reports a different metric, leave the other column NULL so both SELECTs share one three-column shape.

title: Generalise the funnel to an ordered N-step sequence with step-order enforcement
description: The parent funnel counts sessions that fired each event at least once, in any order. A stricter definition requires the events to occur in the correct order within a session: view_product must occur before add_to_cart, which must occur before start_checkout, which must occur before purchase. Write a query that computes, per traffic_source, the count of sessions where this strict ordering holds at each step: ordered_through_cart (MIN(view_product event_time) < MIN(add_to_cart event_time)), ordered_through_checkout (ordered_through_cart AND MIN(add_to_cart event_time) < MIN(start_checkout event_time)), ordered_through_purchase (ordered_through_checkout AND MIN(start_checkout event_time) < MIN(purchase event_time)). Output columns: traffic_source, total_sessions, ordered_through_cart, ordered_through_checkout, ordered_through_purchase. Order by total_sessions descending.
expected_query:
WITH session_min_times AS (
    SELECT s.session_id, s.traffic_source,
           MIN(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'view_product' THEN CAST(e.event_time AS TIMESTAMP) END) AS first_view,
           MIN(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'add_to_cart' THEN CAST(e.event_time AS TIMESTAMP) END) AS first_cart,
           MIN(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'start_checkout' THEN CAST(e.event_time AS TIMESTAMP) END) AS first_checkout,
           MIN(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'purchase' THEN CAST(e.event_time AS TIMESTAMP) END) AS first_purchase
    FROM sessions s
    LEFT JOIN events e ON e.session_id = s.session_id
    GROUP BY s.session_id, s.traffic_source
)
SELECT traffic_source,
       COUNT(*) AS total_sessions,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN first_view IS NOT NULL AND first_cart IS NOT NULL AND first_view < first_cart THEN 1 END) AS ordered_through_cart,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN first_view IS NOT NULL AND first_cart IS NOT NULL AND first_checkout IS NOT NULL
                       AND first_view < first_cart AND first_cart < first_checkout THEN 1 END) AS ordered_through_checkout,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN first_view IS NOT NULL AND first_cart IS NOT NULL AND first_checkout IS NOT NULL AND first_purchase IS NOT NULL
                       AND first_view < first_cart AND first_cart < first_checkout AND first_checkout < first_purchase THEN 1 END) AS ordered_through_purchase
FROM session_min_times
GROUP BY traffic_source
ORDER BY total_sessions DESC
solution_query:
WITH session_min_times AS (
    SELECT s.session_id, s.traffic_source,
           MIN(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'view_product' THEN CAST(e.event_time AS TIMESTAMP) END) AS first_view,
           MIN(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'add_to_cart' THEN CAST(e.event_time AS TIMESTAMP) END) AS first_cart,
           MIN(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'start_checkout' THEN CAST(e.event_time AS TIMESTAMP) END) AS first_checkout,
           MIN(CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'purchase' THEN CAST(e.event_time AS TIMESTAMP) END) AS first_purchase
    FROM sessions s
    LEFT JOIN events e ON e.session_id = s.session_id
    GROUP BY s.session_id, s.traffic_source
)
SELECT traffic_source,
       COUNT(*) AS total_sessions,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN first_view IS NOT NULL AND first_cart IS NOT NULL AND first_view < first_cart THEN 1 END) AS ordered_through_cart,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN first_view IS NOT NULL AND first_cart IS NOT NULL AND first_checkout IS NOT NULL
                       AND first_view < first_cart AND first_cart < first_checkout THEN 1 END) AS ordered_through_checkout,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN first_view IS NOT NULL AND first_cart IS NOT NULL AND first_checkout IS NOT NULL AND first_purchase IS NOT NULL
                       AND first_view < first_cart AND first_cart < first_checkout AND first_checkout < first_purchase THEN 1 END) AS ordered_through_purchase
FROM session_min_times
GROUP BY traffic_source
ORDER BY total_sessions DESC;
explanation: The ordered funnel requires the FIRST occurrence of each event type in the correct sequence. session_min_times computes MIN(CASE WHEN event_name='X' THEN event_time END) for each stage — NULL when a stage never occurred. The outer SELECT then chains comparisons: ordered_through_cart requires both first_view and first_cart to be non-NULL and first_view < first_cart. Each subsequent step adds one more NULL check and one more less-than comparison. The generalisation principle: for an N-step ordered funnel, you need N MIN(timestamp) columns and N-1 less-than comparisons — the pattern is O(N) in length, not exponential. Compared to the parent's unordered funnel (does any event of this type exist?), the ordered funnel is significantly stricter: ordered_through_purchase is much lower than with_purchase_event because many purchase events occur in sessions where checkout events never fired (direct purchases, mobile app events, etc.).
hints: Ordered funnel logic requires knowing the first time each event type fired within a session, not just whether it fired at all — that's a per-stage timing question, not a presence question.
Chain comparisons: first_view < first_cart checks step 1 ordering; first_cart < first_checkout checks step 2. NULL-check each stage before comparing — a missing stage breaks the chain.

title: Cumulative paid amount by payment method: first month crossing $500K threshold
description: Finance tracks cumulative paid payment amounts and wants to know when each payment method first crossed the $500,000 total milestone. For each payment_method, compute the running total of paid amounts month by month (YYYY-MM), and return the first month where that cumulative total reached or exceeded $500,000. Output columns: payment_method, threshold_crossing_month, cumulative_at_crossing (rounded to 2 dp). If a method never crosses $500K, omit it. Order by threshold_crossing_month ascending.
expected_query:
WITH monthly_payments AS (
    SELECT payment_method,
           STRFTIME('%Y-%m', payment_date) AS month,
           SUM(amount) AS monthly_amount
    FROM payments
    WHERE status = 'paid'
    GROUP BY 1, 2
),
cumulative AS (
    SELECT payment_method,
           month,
           ROUND(SUM(monthly_amount) OVER (
               PARTITION BY payment_method
               ORDER BY month
               ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
           ), 2) AS cumulative_amount
    FROM monthly_payments
)
SELECT payment_method,
       month AS threshold_crossing_month,
       cumulative_amount AS cumulative_at_crossing
FROM (
    SELECT payment_method, month, cumulative_amount,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY payment_method ORDER BY month) AS rn
    FROM cumulative
    WHERE cumulative_amount >= 500000
) first_crossing
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY threshold_crossing_month
solution_query:
WITH monthly_payments AS (
    SELECT payment_method,
           STRFTIME('%Y-%m', payment_date) AS month,
           SUM(amount) AS monthly_amount
    FROM payments
    WHERE status = 'paid'
    GROUP BY 1, 2
),
cumulative AS (
    SELECT payment_method,
           month,
           ROUND(SUM(monthly_amount) OVER (
               PARTITION BY payment_method
               ORDER BY month
               ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
           ), 2) AS cumulative_amount
    FROM monthly_payments
)
SELECT payment_method,
       month AS threshold_crossing_month,
       cumulative_amount AS cumulative_at_crossing
FROM (
    SELECT payment_method, month, cumulative_amount,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY payment_method ORDER BY month) AS rn
    FROM cumulative
    WHERE cumulative_amount >= 500000
) first_crossing
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY threshold_crossing_month;
explanation: The cumulative SUM OVER (PARTITION BY payment_method ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) computes the running total per method. ROWS is used instead of RANGE to avoid floating-point aggregation sensitivity at month boundaries. The first crossing is extracted with a ROW_NUMBER() applied after filtering to rows where cumulative_amount >= 500000 — taking rn = 1 gives the earliest qualifying month per method. Results: card crosses $500K fastest (2023-04), wallet crosses last (2025-06), consistent with their relative volumes. All four methods eventually cross $500K.
hints: The 'first crossing' is a two-step problem: first build a running cumulative total month by month per method, then identify the earliest month that crossed the threshold.
Use ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW (not RANGE) in the cumulative SUM to avoid float instability at month-end ties.

title: Cumulative threshold crossing with per-method targets
description: Finance now wants per-method milestones rather than a uniform $500K threshold. The targets are: card = $800,000; paypal = $200,000; bank_transfer = $300,000; wallet = $100,000. Using the same cumulative running total approach, return the first month each method crossed its own target. Output columns: payment_method, target_amount, threshold_crossing_month (YYYY-MM format), cumulative_at_crossing (rounded to 2 dp). Order by threshold_crossing_month ascending.
expected_query:
WITH thresholds (payment_method, target_amount) AS (
    VALUES ('card', 800000), ('paypal', 200000),
           ('bank_transfer', 300000), ('wallet', 100000)
),
monthly_payments AS (
    SELECT p.payment_method,
           STRFTIME('%Y-%m', p.payment_date) AS month,
           SUM(p.amount) AS monthly_amount,
           t.target_amount
    FROM payments p
    JOIN thresholds t ON t.payment_method = p.payment_method
    WHERE p.status = 'paid'
    GROUP BY p.payment_method, STRFTIME('%Y-%m', p.payment_date), t.target_amount
),
cumulative AS (
    SELECT payment_method, month, target_amount,
           ROUND(SUM(monthly_amount) OVER (
               PARTITION BY payment_method
               ORDER BY month
               ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
           ), 2) AS cumulative_amount
    FROM monthly_payments
)
SELECT payment_method, target_amount, month AS threshold_crossing_month, cumulative_amount AS cumulative_at_crossing
FROM (
    SELECT payment_method, target_amount, month, cumulative_amount,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY payment_method ORDER BY month) AS rn
    FROM cumulative
    WHERE cumulative_amount >= target_amount
) first_crossing
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY threshold_crossing_month
solution_query:
WITH thresholds (payment_method, target_amount) AS (
    VALUES ('card', 800000), ('paypal', 200000),
           ('bank_transfer', 300000), ('wallet', 100000)
),
monthly_payments AS (
    SELECT p.payment_method,
           STRFTIME('%Y-%m', p.payment_date) AS month,
           SUM(p.amount) AS monthly_amount,
           t.target_amount
    FROM payments p
    JOIN thresholds t ON t.payment_method = p.payment_method
    WHERE p.status = 'paid'
    GROUP BY p.payment_method, STRFTIME('%Y-%m', p.payment_date), t.target_amount
),
cumulative AS (
    SELECT payment_method, month, target_amount,
           ROUND(SUM(monthly_amount) OVER (
               PARTITION BY payment_method
               ORDER BY month
               ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
           ), 2) AS cumulative_amount
    FROM monthly_payments
)
SELECT payment_method, target_amount, month AS threshold_crossing_month, cumulative_amount AS cumulative_at_crossing
FROM (
    SELECT payment_method, target_amount, month, cumulative_amount,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY payment_method ORDER BY month) AS rn
    FROM cumulative
    WHERE cumulative_amount >= target_amount
) first_crossing
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY threshold_crossing_month;
explanation: The structural change: replace the hard-coded threshold comparison with a JOIN to a thresholds VALUES CTE. The target_amount propagates through monthly_payments into cumulative so the WHERE cumulative_amount >= target_amount comparison uses the per-method threshold. The rest of the pipeline is identical to the parent. Results: paypal and wallet cross their lower thresholds first (2023-06 and 2023-07), card crosses its higher threshold next (2023-07), and bank_transfer last (2023-12). The VALUES CTE pattern makes the thresholds auditable and easily changed — a clear improvement over a hardcoded constant in the WHERE clause.
hints: Per-entity thresholds need to be present alongside each payment row so the final comparison evaluates each method against its own target, not a shared constant.
The WHERE clause becomes WHERE cumulative_amount >= target_amount instead of a hard-coded value, comparing each row to its own method's threshold.

title: Rolling 12-month cumulative paid amount by payment method
description: The head of finance asks: 'Has each payment method's 12-month rolling volume been growing over time?' Compute, for each payment_method and each month, the rolling 12-month sum of paid amounts (the current month plus the preceding 11 months). Output columns: payment_method, month (YYYY-MM format), rolling_12m_amount (rounded to 2 dp). Include all months from 2024-01 onward (the first month where a full 12-month lookback is available from a 2023-01 start). Order by payment_method, month ascending.
expected_query:
WITH monthly_payments AS (
    SELECT payment_method,
           STRFTIME('%Y-%m', payment_date) AS month,
           SUM(amount) AS monthly_amount
    FROM payments
    WHERE status = 'paid'
    GROUP BY 1, 2
)
SELECT payment_method,
       month,
       ROUND(SUM(monthly_amount) OVER (
           PARTITION BY payment_method
           ORDER BY month
           ROWS BETWEEN 11 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ), 2) AS rolling_12m_amount
FROM monthly_payments
WHERE month >= '2024-01'
ORDER BY payment_method, month
solution_query:
WITH monthly_payments AS (
    SELECT payment_method,
           STRFTIME('%Y-%m', payment_date) AS month,
           SUM(amount) AS monthly_amount
    FROM payments
    WHERE status = 'paid'
    GROUP BY 1, 2
)
SELECT payment_method,
       month,
       ROUND(SUM(monthly_amount) OVER (
           PARTITION BY payment_method
           ORDER BY month
           ROWS BETWEEN 11 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ), 2) AS rolling_12m_amount
FROM monthly_payments
WHERE month >= '2024-01'
ORDER BY payment_method, month;
explanation: ROWS BETWEEN 11 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW with a string-ordered month (YYYY-MM strings sort lexicographically correctly) gives the rolling 12-month window. The WHERE month >= '2024-01' filter is applied after the window function executes — the window sees pre-2024 rows from monthly_payments for the lookback but only outputs rows from 2024 onward. The stakeholder question is about trend: is rolling_12m_amount increasing month-over-month per payment_method? Presenting the output as a time series per method lets the finance team answer this directly. If the lookback must be enforced strictly (no partial windows for edge months), the WHERE can be moved inside monthly_payments with additional pre-2024 rows included explicitly — but for this dataset, 2023 is fully present so the lookback is always 12 months starting from 2024-01.
hints: A rolling window that covers the current month plus the 11 months before it is a fixed-width sliding sum over a 12-period lookback — identify the window size and direction before reaching for the frame syntax.
Apply the WHERE month >= '2024-01' filter after the window calculation, not inside the CTE — the window needs the 2023 rows for the lookback.

title: Per-user month-over-month completed order count: flag 50% drops as at-risk
description: The customer success team wants to identify users showing signs of churn: a month where their completed order count dropped by 50% or more compared to the previous month. For every user who has completed orders in at least two different months, compare each ordering month's completed-order count to that of their immediately preceding ORDERING month (their previous active month, which need not be the calendar-previous month). Compute month (YYYY-MM format), order_count (completed orders that month), prev_month_count (that user's immediately preceding ordering month's count), pct_drop (rounded to 1 dp), and at_risk_flag (true when order_count * 2 <= prev_month_count). Return only rows where a previous ordering month exists (skip the user's first ordering month). Order by pct_drop descending, user_id ascending.
expected_query:
WITH monthly_user_orders AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           STRFTIME('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month,
           COUNT(*) AS order_count
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY user_id, STRFTIME('%Y-%m', order_date)
),
with_lag AS (
    SELECT user_id, month, order_count,
           LAG(order_count) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY month) AS prev_month_count
    FROM monthly_user_orders
)
SELECT user_id, month, order_count, prev_month_count,
       ROUND(100.0 * (prev_month_count - order_count) / prev_month_count, 1) AS pct_drop,
       order_count * 2 <= prev_month_count AS at_risk_flag
FROM with_lag
WHERE prev_month_count IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY pct_drop DESC, user_id
solution_query:
WITH monthly_user_orders AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           STRFTIME('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month,
           COUNT(*) AS order_count
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY user_id, STRFTIME('%Y-%m', order_date)
),
with_lag AS (
    SELECT user_id, month, order_count,
           LAG(order_count) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY month) AS prev_month_count
    FROM monthly_user_orders
)
SELECT user_id, month, order_count, prev_month_count,
       ROUND(100.0 * (prev_month_count - order_count) / prev_month_count, 1) AS pct_drop,
       order_count * 2 <= prev_month_count AS at_risk_flag
FROM with_lag
WHERE prev_month_count IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY pct_drop DESC, user_id;
explanation: Two-CTE approach: monthly_user_orders aggregates to one row per (user_id, month); with_lag applies LAG over user_id partition ordered by month to bring the prior month's count forward. The at_risk_flag uses integer arithmetic (order_count * 2 <= prev_month_count) instead of floating-point division to avoid boundary precision issues — a ≥50% drop means current ≤ 50% of previous, i.e., current * 2 ≤ previous. pct_drop orders by the largest drops first: a user dropping from 6 orders to 1 (83.3% drop) is more alarming than from 4 to 2 (50% drop). The query surfaces 314 at-risk (user, month) pairs across 153 distinct users — a meaningful segment for retention outreach.
hints: To compare a user's current-month count to their prior-month count, you need both values in the same row — a window-based lookback retrieves the prior-period value alongside the current one.
Use integer arithmetic for the 50% threshold: order_count * 2 <= prev_month_count avoids floating-point rounding at the boundary.

title: MoM order count: handling non-consecutive months (gaps in the series)
description: The LAG-based query treats consecutive data-months as consecutive calendar months. But a user with orders in January and March (no February orders) would have LAG returning January's count as March's 'previous month' — incorrectly treating a 2-month gap as a 1-month change. Revise the query to detect non-consecutive months and exclude those rows from the pct_drop calculation: return only rows where the current month (YYYY-MM format) directly follows the previous ordering month (a 1-month gap in the monthly series). Add a months_gap column (integer: months between prev_month and current month). Only compute pct_drop and at_risk_flag for rows where months_gap = 1. For rows where months_gap > 1, return NULL for pct_drop and false for at_risk_flag. Output columns: user_id, month (YYYY-MM string), order_count, prev_month_count, prev_month (YYYY-MM string), months_gap, pct_drop, at_risk_flag. Order by pct_drop DESC NULLS LAST, user_id ascending.
expected_query:
WITH monthly_user_orders AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           STRFTIME('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month,
           COUNT(*) AS order_count
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY user_id, STRFTIME('%Y-%m', order_date)
),
with_lag AS (
    SELECT user_id, month, order_count,
           LAG(order_count) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY month) AS prev_month_count,
           LAG(month) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY month) AS prev_month
    FROM monthly_user_orders
)
SELECT user_id, month, order_count, prev_month_count, prev_month,
       DATEDIFF('month',
           CAST(prev_month || '-01' AS DATE),
           CAST(month || '-01' AS DATE)
       ) AS months_gap,
       CASE WHEN DATEDIFF('month',
                   CAST(prev_month || '-01' AS DATE),
                   CAST(month || '-01' AS DATE)
               ) = 1
            THEN ROUND(100.0 * (prev_month_count - order_count) / prev_month_count, 1)
            ELSE NULL
       END AS pct_drop,
       CASE WHEN DATEDIFF('month',
                   CAST(prev_month || '-01' AS DATE),
                   CAST(month || '-01' AS DATE)
               ) = 1
            THEN order_count * 2 <= prev_month_count
            ELSE false
       END AS at_risk_flag
FROM with_lag
WHERE prev_month_count IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY pct_drop DESC NULLS LAST, user_id
solution_query:
WITH monthly_user_orders AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           STRFTIME('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month,
           COUNT(*) AS order_count
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY user_id, STRFTIME('%Y-%m', order_date)
),
with_lag AS (
    SELECT user_id, month, order_count,
           LAG(order_count) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY month) AS prev_month_count,
           LAG(month) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY month) AS prev_month
    FROM monthly_user_orders
)
SELECT user_id, month, order_count, prev_month_count, prev_month,
       DATEDIFF('month',
           CAST(prev_month || '-01' AS DATE),
           CAST(month || '-01' AS DATE)
       ) AS months_gap,
       CASE WHEN DATEDIFF('month',
                   CAST(prev_month || '-01' AS DATE),
                   CAST(month || '-01' AS DATE)
               ) = 1
            THEN ROUND(100.0 * (prev_month_count - order_count) / prev_month_count, 1)
            ELSE NULL
       END AS pct_drop,
       CASE WHEN DATEDIFF('month',
                   CAST(prev_month || '-01' AS DATE),
                   CAST(month || '-01' AS DATE)
               ) = 1
            THEN order_count * 2 <= prev_month_count
            ELSE false
       END AS at_risk_flag
FROM with_lag
WHERE prev_month_count IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY pct_drop DESC NULLS LAST, user_id;
explanation: The fix requires two LAG calls: one for prev_month_count (as before) and a new one for prev_month (the month string). DATEDIFF('month', prev_month_date, current_month_date) computes the gap — appending '-01' and casting to DATE converts the YYYY-MM string to a parseable date. A gap of 1 means truly consecutive months; a gap > 1 means the user had a month with zero orders in between. pct_drop and at_risk_flag are wrapped in CASE WHEN months_gap = 1 so only genuinely consecutive month pairs produce the at-risk signal. ORDER BY pct_drop DESC NULLS LAST pushes the gap rows (NULL pct_drop) to the end. This guards against false churn flags from users who simply order less frequently than monthly.
hints: The month-over-month comparison is only meaningful when the two months are truly adjacent in the calendar — verify the gap between data-months before computing the percentage change.
Append '-01' to the YYYY-MM string before casting to DATE: CAST(month || '-01' AS DATE) gives the first day of that month for date arithmetic.

title: Comparing two MoM at-risk definitions: gap-months-included vs consecutive-months-only
description: There are two defensible interpretations of 'month-over-month' when a user has a month with zero orders: (A) a missing month is treated as a 0-order month — any month M where the user's next ordering month is more than one calendar month later implies they had zero orders in M+1, which is a 100% drop (gap_months_included); (B) month-over-month only applies to months where the user actively ordered — gaps are excluded (consecutive_months_only). Using a LEAD-based approach for interpretation A (not a calendar spine), compute for each interpretation the total number of user-month rows that are flagged at_risk. For interpretation A, a row is at_risk when: the standard 50% drop condition holds (order_count * 2 <= prev_count AND prev_count IS NOT NULL), OR the user had orders this month (order_count > 0) and the next ordering month is more than 1 calendar month away (implying at least one 0-order month follows). Note: the month grain is stored as a YYYY-MM format string. Return interpretation_label ('gap_months_included' or 'consecutive_months_only') and total_at_risk_flags. Order by interpretation_label.
expected_query:
WITH monthly_orders AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           STRFTIME('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month,
           COUNT(*) AS order_count
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY user_id, STRFTIME('%Y-%m', order_date)
),
with_neighbors AS (
    SELECT user_id, month, order_count,
           LAG(order_count) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY month) AS prev_count,
           LEAD(month) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY month) AS next_month
    FROM monthly_orders
)
SELECT 'consecutive_months_only' AS interpretation_label,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN prev_count IS NOT NULL
                       AND order_count * 2 <= prev_count THEN 1 END) AS total_at_risk_flags
FROM with_neighbors
UNION ALL
SELECT 'gap_months_included',
       COUNT(CASE WHEN
               (prev_count IS NOT NULL AND order_count * 2 <= prev_count)
               OR (
                   order_count > 0
                   AND next_month IS NOT NULL
                   AND DATEDIFF('month',
                       CAST(month || '-01' AS DATE),
                       CAST(next_month || '-01' AS DATE)
                   ) > 1
               )
             THEN 1 END) AS total_at_risk_flags
FROM with_neighbors
ORDER BY interpretation_label
solution_query:
WITH monthly_orders AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           STRFTIME('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month,
           COUNT(*) AS order_count
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY user_id, STRFTIME('%Y-%m', order_date)
),
with_neighbors AS (
    SELECT user_id, month, order_count,
           LAG(order_count) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY month) AS prev_count,
           LEAD(month) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY month) AS next_month
    FROM monthly_orders
)
SELECT 'consecutive_months_only' AS interpretation_label,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN prev_count IS NOT NULL
                       AND order_count * 2 <= prev_count THEN 1 END) AS total_at_risk_flags
FROM with_neighbors
UNION ALL
SELECT 'gap_months_included',
       COUNT(CASE WHEN
               (prev_count IS NOT NULL AND order_count * 2 <= prev_count)
               OR (
                   order_count > 0
                   AND next_month IS NOT NULL
                   AND DATEDIFF('month',
                       CAST(month || '-01' AS DATE),
                       CAST(next_month || '-01' AS DATE)
                   ) > 1
               )
             THEN 1 END) AS total_at_risk_flags
FROM with_neighbors
ORDER BY interpretation_label;
explanation: The LEAD-based approach avoids building a full calendar spine (which would need a CROSS JOIN or VALUES enumeration). with_neighbors adds two window lookups per row: LAG for the prior ordering month's count (used by both interpretations) and LEAD for the next ordering month's string (used to detect gaps in interpretation A). For gap_months_included: a user with orders in January and March has a 1-month gap — DATEDIFF('month', Jan, Mar) = 2 > 1 — so January is flagged because the February 0-order month that follows it is a 100% drop. The DATEDIFF check uses the '-01' append trick to convert YYYY-MM strings to parseable dates. The two interpretations produce different at_risk counts: gap_months_included is always >= consecutive_months_only because it adds gap-triggered flags on top of the standard ones. This quantifies how much 'churn signal' comes purely from users who order intermittently vs. users who ordered and then reduced.
hints: For the gap-based interpretation, you do not need a full calendar spine — if a user's next ordering month is more than one calendar month away, that implies a zero-order month follows the current one.
The LEAD-based month gap check uses the same '-01' append trick: compute months between the current month and the next ordering month using the first day of each as a reference date.

title: 2024 signup cohort retention at 30, 60, and 90-day marks simultaneously
description: The growth team wants to understand how 2024 sign-up cohorts retain across three fixed time windows simultaneously. For each monthly cohort (users who signed up in 2024), compute: cohort_month (YYYY-MM format), cohort_size, ret_30d (users with at least one completed order within days 0–29 of signup), ret_60d (days 0–59), ret_90d (days 0–89), and retention rates ret_30d_pct, ret_60d_pct, ret_90d_pct (rounded to 1 dp). Order by cohort_month ascending.
expected_query:
WITH cohort_users AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           STRFTIME('%Y-%m', signup_date) AS cohort_month,
           CAST(signup_date AS DATE) AS signup_day
    FROM users
    WHERE signup_date >= '2024-01-01' AND signup_date < '2025-01-01'
),
cohort_retention AS (
    SELECT cu.cohort_month,
           COUNT(DISTINCT cu.user_id) AS cohort_size,

title: Cohort retention at scale: 200M users, daily-partitioned orders table
description: The users table now has 200 million rows and the orders table has daily partitions (orders_YYYYMMDD). The correlated EXISTS subquery approach scans orders once per user per cohort_month group — expensive at this scale. Write a query that pre-joins the cohort users to their qualifying orders using a date-range JOIN (avoiding correlated subqueries), then flags retention windows using conditional aggregation. This approach scans orders once. Output the same columns as the parent: cohort_month (YYYY-MM format), cohort_size, ret_30d, ret_60d, ret_90d, ret_30d_pct, ret_60d_pct, ret_90d_pct. THEN user_id END): an order row falling within day 0–29 contributes to all three windows; day 30–59 contributes to ret_60d and ret_90d only; day 60–89 to ret_90d only. For a daily-partitioned table, the planner can further prune to only the partitions covering signup_day through signup_day + 89 days — orders outside this range are never read. This approach scans orders at most once per relevant partition, vs three EXISTS subqueries each scanning orders independently.

The JOIN condition BETWEEN signup_day AND signup_day + INTERVAL 89 DAY acts as a pre-filter — with daily partitions, the planner only reads partitions within that range.
